To the aid of the workers in danger.

Meanwhile a person comes up to me and invites me to go with her to a field where the workers were all in turmoil: «Run and restore order! They no longer listen to the overseer; indeed they mock her, and each one thinks of doing things in her own way.»

I look to see whether I see my way. No!

«Who, if you please, are you?»

«One of those from the field in turmoil.»

«But I can do nothing for you, because your flock does not belong to me, for I am a wretched slave who cannot go where my Master does not send me. You must go and look for some good shepherd who will come to set that flock in order again.

She insisted so much; but I stood firm, because I saw no path of any kind. At last, in a kindly manner, I tried as best I could to send her away. What does this unhappy woman do? She digs in her heels and, resolute, (says to me): «If you do not come, I will stay here!»

«My God! How can you so resolutely stay, when I do not know you at all?»

My voice:

— Keep her! If she goes back, she perishes.

What sorrow! I kept her; but she was weeping for her companions, who were about to be devoured by certain evildoers: it was because of these that all that confusion had come about. And then,

— Go — she added — for pity’s sake!

My path could not be seen, the voice said nothing to me, and I felt a sharp sorrow. She went on with her account; every so often I bade her be silent, because I suffered too much from it. At last (I said to her):

— Why do you not have a shepherd?

— Oh! there was one, but, poor man, he had to withdraw, because he could not bear it; seeing that he could do nothing, he went away.

— Then you are alone? You do not even have a guide?

— Oh! — with a deep sigh — alas, we have one, but this evil has all come from her, for she was the first to throw everything into confusion.

How I felt myself torn! But I saw nothing indicating that I should take care of them. What did I do? I invited her to join me and, prostrate on the ground, we made fervent supplications to the Most High that he would free those poor workers. But never did I feel anything telling me that they would be freed. It was true heartbreak; I wept, and that poor creature did the same: it was anguish to see her.

— My Lord, my Master, my God! be moved to compassion for them and for this poor creature who, moved by sorrow at the loss of her companions, weeping, implores you to have pity and mercy on them.

This said, a great uproar is heard. It was those unhappy women who, in a frightful manner, were coming in search of help, because, terrified, or rather touched by divine grace, they were fleeing the lions to throw themselves into the arms of that God whom they had so outraged. I welcomed them as kindly as I could, and their poor companion did the same. I looked them over to see if I could recognize the guide among them, but it was not granted me. Perhaps I am mistaken (I said to myself), but she is certainly not here. With this thought I went up to the first one and asked her. Oh unhappy woman! she had gone off with the lions, taking another one with her. I tried to refresh them; and then I handed them over to my keeper, that she might look after them well and try to rid them of their bad ideas, and finally lead them and set them on the right path. While everything was being put in order, my voice:

— The path is traced: run swiftly to where the Master has prepared a great work for you.

On the rough path with bleeding feet

— Conversion of a group of women who then follow her.

Without heeding anything else, I set out. It was a road full of stones, and climbs and descents, and dry torrent beds. In short, it was a painful way; my feet were already all wounded, and I had them very swollen. I did not dare utter a word of complaint; on the contrary, I felt great satisfaction. I suffered greatly, but the relish of so sharp a torment was a sweet consolation to me; and I tried to run ever faster. Already blood was coming from my feet.

Oh! how I was consoled thinking of my Savior who, on the return from Egypt, barefoot, ran ahead of the most holy Virgin and Saint Joseph, and that these two personages felt great pain, above all when they saw blood coming from the divine soles of his feet. Oh! how anxious they became, and they offered to carry him, but He would not consent and went on along the road. 70. Oh! how sweet and very consoling it is to me to think that this wretched blood had the good fortune to be shed on these stones!

At last I came near a torrent, where there were women amusing themselves in the water. How was I to pass without being noticed? I plunged into the water, believing that they would see nothing: when the water turns red, and they run after me telling me to stop. The devil puts it into their heads that I am fleeing because I have committed a crime; and so, instead of having compassion on me, they seize me tightly, heaping a thousand insults on me; and they wanted to know who I was and where I came from.

— I am a poor slave who, by order of my Master, must go very far away.

— But you are wounded, or you have wounded someone!

— Oh! good people: I have wounded no one but my Master; he receives (wounds), because so many times I seem to have understood him and instead I do not do what he desires.

They look at one another.

— But we do not understand this talk of yours. We tell you to tell us the truth: who has wounded you, or whom have you wounded?

— Why do you put these questions to me? They point to the water. Ah! the blood!

— No one has wounded me, and neither have I wounded any creature, but it is the long way I have traveled; and since these feet are so poorly made, it was necessary that a little blood should come out so that they might be made less unworthy to appear before their Lord.

— We do not understand your talk. Are you a Jew?

— Oh! no, never! I am Catholic, Apostolic and Roman; I serve my God! And you, of what religion are you?

— Of none, because it is all tales!

— Oh! poor creatures! you move me to compassion.

And I began to weep. Meanwhile I had reached the other bank of the channel, and they were following me. Without caring about anything else, I turned to them and taught them that they were in great error; that eternity was awaiting them. I gave them a long conference. One, the youngest, I perceived was already converted; but there were two old women whose hearts were bewitched by the most loathsome earthly affections; the word would not enter. Others were also convinced, but no!

With greater vigor I showed them how great and beautiful was the way of Paradise for those who believe. They began to mock me. What did I do? I embraced my dear Crucified One tightly:

— Give strength to my words, win their hardened hearts, and may they too be saved!

This said, I grasped my Crucifix and with vigor made them understand that they were lost if they wished to remain in their mire. They burst into a flood of tears and were converted. It was a fine harvest. Full of joy, I led them with me all along the way, speaking of God and of his infinite mercy.

Forewarnings about the future of her work and about new sufferings — A «mystical dream».

As I ran, reciting the prayer of the most holy Virgin, there came upon me a delightful discourse on the future of the work of a magnificent field, where there were gracious and good workers. I remained so taken up with so beautiful a discourse! I did not notice where I was. Like one who wakes from a delightful sleep, I was troubled to see that it was late at night in a very solitary place; my track was very ruinous. I forgot all that I had so greatly relished and began to weep. My God! I am very much afraid and do not know what to do: stop? I fear not doing your most holy will; go forward? I feel I have no courage. As I said this, my voice:

— What faintheartedness!

Hearing this, I was full of shame. I set out into that forest by night: how frightening it was! every noise of those great birds gave me a violent start. How long — I began to say to my God — this darkness is! the dawn never breaks. How can it be, after so long a time that I have been walking?

Another mystical discourse came upon me, as I conversed with my angel Saint Michael, and I felt a great satisfaction. I was called before an ecclesiastical judge; he treated me very roughly. My angel, so that I should not hear too much of those words, which would greatly have offended my hearing and my soul, lowered his wings and made of them a gracious shelter for my ear, so that I heard only very few things. Having wrapped every power of mine in his beautiful caparison, he left me only sweetness and charity to forgive the one who was molesting me so much by means of the ecclesiastical superior. With the zephyr of the beating of his wings I felt myself in bliss.

Everything was bound by Him; my humanity remained a meek lamb, it had no word; it appeared silent outwardly, because it was absorbed in the sweet actions of its angel. Oh! how beautiful and mysterious, and of infinite wisdom, is what is so woven, that no human creature can ever comprehend it, but only the one to whom God gives these inexpressible sweetnesses and knowledge!

Overcome by sleep, I fell asleep, and of a sudden my mind entered a great gallery, where there was every sort of lovely fruit, and here and there groups of people conferring together. A young man comes up to me and offers me a magnificent basket of fruit: it was a delight! so lovely in its form!… I looked at it and then, politely, declined to taste it. He kept insisting, and I refused more and more. At last he threw it on the ground in a rage. Horror! from such beautiful fruit there came out a terrible stench, so that I had to move away, because I could not bear such a stench. I was frightened and looked all around me. More afraid than ever, I tried to flee; another man came toward me, dressed as a priest, in a kind of monk’s habit. He stops me near a small column and says to me:

— Do you see those writings? One day they will be victorious.

— What victory? — I said to him — what have I to do with it?

He leaves me, and I kept trying to flee. Then a young woman whom I recognized comes near me, and at once I asked her for explanations of those papers and of everything. She answered me that those writings were by a priest who had written a work well, but that the devil wished to destroy it. At last she assured me that none of those dragons would do anything to me; that great display and those groups of people were all demons, who would torment me greatly before long, and with great cunning would obtain a correspondence of action with persons; and that I would suffer greatly from it.

She disappeared. And I, awakened, kept it all fixed before me, in full detail and so clear. What can it be? Was I sleeping, or was I truly in the midst of those people?

My voice:

— This is not a material sleep, but a mystical one. All that you have seen, or, as you say, dreamed, will come true.

A banner, with the inscription: «Joys — Struggles».

Reflecting, I was traveling along my path, when in the distance I hear a great murmuring; it was so confused that I could not clearly make it out. I commended myself to my angel, that he would not permit those people to come near:

— Oh! my defender! cover me with your wings, so that, as they pass, they may not see me.

This said, they draw near with great strides; they did not see me; I began to run with all my strength and arrived at the foot of an altar, where my Good was. With what fervor I thanked him! and yet my angel. [?]

I wanted to tell him so many things, but an invincible force seized my mind and carried me away to reflect mysteriously upon a great event that was to happen to me; but, as if I had found myself at that very point, I felt all its pain; I would have liked to get out of it; I heard the words of the one who was treating me roughly though I was innocent, and I saw it as with open eyes, so clearly did my intellect reason upon it; my mind was so intent on listening to all the intrigues, calumnies and subterfuges that those creatures were making. Moreover, I saw how such actions passed within them with a satisfaction so little praiseworthy. In such pain as I was, I kept running, without reflecting where I was or where I was going. Without my noticing it, my foot no longer rested on the ground; the flight was most rapid, crossing a great number of fields; so it seemed to me.

In that new abode in which I found myself, beautiful beyond all telling, all the indescribable things that were there produced in me a perceptible joy; the angelic harmonies in varied ways inebriated my soul; my soul had a certainty of remaining there for ever; my poor spirit was nourished with much knowledge…

But, as if awakened from sleep, I found myself again in a valley where the very river that ran through it was frozen. I look to one side and the other: two very high mountains that held ice hanging down their great flanks. Only a gloomy silence could be breathed. Where am I? Who has led me to so dreadful a place? My path cannot even be found! Can it be that, while running along the way, I fell asleep and, dreaming, plunged down here? My soul holds too much strength; I feel that it was not sleep, but reality.

Thus numb with cold and utterly lost, I sat down and, gathering together all that stood within me as a hindrance, I rejoiced in it deeply; I cared very little about that frightful solitude. Having gathered together all the knowledge I had received, there appears before my mind a banner which passed from blue to black; on the blue was written: Joys; and on the black: Harrowing Struggles. I dwelt long on this consideration. A trembling begins to invade me and I burst into a flood of tears. Where am I? Is it I who came here through carelessness?» 71

A delightful Sion where all is love, while all is gloomy on the land of mortals.

I begin to hear a terrible noise of beasts of every kind and, finally, a horrible voice:

— It is I who deceived you, to bring you here!

The weeping, the sorrow, the terror were harrowing things; I commended my soul to my God; I asked his forgiveness, convinced that it had truly been I who was the cause of my being brought to that horrible place; my breast was reduced to wax, so much did it pain me. Mary, Mother of my God, help me! But all in vain. It was perfect darkness; and these dragons drew ever nearer to me and surrounded me with a thousand frightful snares: horrible sight! One of them, which for its size and ugliness was something horrible, had placed itself at some distance and seemed to be waiting for another. Here is one with a great unsheathed sword who wanted furiously to wound me.

From terror, and from the certainty that it was I who had put myself into that labyrinth by being negligent on my way, and that I had lost the road, my strength fails me; my weeping stops. And one of them is there; I feel it lay a cold paw, worse than ice, on my hand. I had nothing but the thought fixed on my God; silently I asked him for forgiveness, help and pity. These terrible dragons were preparing to seize me; I felt my soul separating from my body, because I was losing consciousness: it was a perfect agony!

A terrible uproar, and they all take to flight; but I no longer had the strength to manage to see who was frightening them, or rather, ordering them to withdraw, because I fainted. I felt only that a gentle hand took hold of me and leaned me on its arm. It was something comforting, but my eyes could not see, because they were closed.

When I came to myself, where did I find myself? In a delightful Sion! All was love. In the echo of those heavenly walls nothing was heard but love. A garland of beautiful and gracious young maidens, with angelic faces, gave forth a zephyr of purity such as to enamor and let sweetness itself penetrate. Oh! how you communicate of your beauty and beatitude — to whom?…

While I was saying this to him, they draw near me and, whispering in my ear, tell me that those struggles were permitted by God and that, by my abandonment in Him alone, my soul had gained much from them; that I should not doubt that what had happened did not depend on me, but was all a divine ordinance.

These disappeared, and a soul drew near me who congratulated me, telling me to be strong, not to let myself be cast down by faintheartedness, for the Lord is well pleased in the exercise of trials. If very few souls enter into these struggles, it is because they did not know how to advance at all toward the enemy, but at the first small skirmishes they fled, or rather preferred to remain in the lowest ranks of the militia; and they remain invalids; they nourish themselves just enough not to waste away.

— Oh! what can I do so that they may come out of so slothful a state? — I asked her.

— There is no remedy, because whatever is not pliable breaks when one tries to bend it.

And she left me. I saw nothing and heard nothing, but I relished much, without understanding where I was.

After a while I returned to the land of mortals: all is gloomy! Why, my Good, did you not leave me where you certainly were and were secretly filling me with bliss? Upright once more on my track, my foot must resume its material motion. I see it still long; not even its end can be seen. Only a painful climb! and where will it lead me? Will it be Carmel? or forests? or monsters?

Reflecting thus, I ran, so as to fulfill the will of my God. Halfway up the climb, I see that I must pass beneath a most frightful rock. My angel Saint Michael, come to my aid!

And yet I had to pass that way, because my track was so marked. As I drew near I heard loud noises; more than ever I asked my angel for help. When I was near, I felt a strong shock, as if that boulder had moved. What terror! The noise increased; no one could be seen, but everything seemed to me about to come crashing down. I was not mistaken: an upheaval took place, and my track too was thrown into disorder. With joined hands I prayed Saint Michael to come to my aid. Nothing! I began to hear something like the tramping of armed men, but I saw nothing. The noise alone distressed me. Turn back? No! this is my track, and on this path I must set out.

At last I come out from under that awesome rock. I stopped to look at it: how frightful you are! The noises ceased. With slow steps (walking), without noticing it, I remained absorbed in my God, and I do not know whether I walked in that way or remained still.

She finds mute children: she takes them with her to feed them and make God known to them. Only on coming to myself again did I find myself in a delightful garden, where there were a few children. I asked them who they were and to whom that beautiful place belonged. They did not answer me. Might they be mute? And I tried to make myself understood by signs. I was not mistaken: they were poor abandoned creatures who were seeking shelter. How much compassion they moved in me! I took them with me, because they had knocked much at that palace, but no one had listened to them. All joyful, they skipped around me. I thought at once that they were hungry. Turning to my God: what can I give these creatures, when I have nothing? what must I do? Taking off my cloak and going up to a woman who had much bread, I begged her to accept my cloak and give me bread for these creatures I had found along this way. The good woman looked at me and, taking the cloak, gave me plenty of bread. Having distributed this to the poor creatures, I was looking for where I could find a stream to give them something to drink; I see in the distance a little girl with an amphora coming toward us. Oh! what pleasure I felt, (and they) no less than I. I noticed that these poor creatures were burning with thirst and were rejoicing at being able to have water. Who has sent you, dear creature? As soon as she is near us, she sets down her amphora and invites us to drink. However many questions I put to her, I could never understand who had sent her or who she was. She took up her vessel again and, with an extraordinary swiftness, flew away, for rather than walking one may say (it was) flying.

These poor creatures were tired, and where was I to let them rest? My voice:

— A few steps more and you will find shelter for these creatures. And so it happened. I asked an old woman, seated on a stone, whether she would do me the charity of lodging these creatures. Grumbling, she looks at me:

— I have only one bed, and that is for me!

— Tell me, have you no straw?

Unwillingly she points me to a hayloft, which I accepted at once. And as best I could I put these creatures to sleep. But when they had fallen asleep, I began to pray and to weep: what shall I give these poor little ones tomorrow? My God, I feel myself torn apart!

As soon as (it was day), I went to the woman, who was already grumbling around the hearth. I begged her to be so kind as to give me bread for the poor little ones who were sleeping. What did I do? I took off my skirts and gave them to her, so that she would give me bread. She grew cheerful, accepted the skirts and gave me plenty of bread and fruit. How happy I was! I looked at the basket with great satisfaction; those poor creatures came skipping to meet me, and at once I put the basket at their disposal, and they ate their fill. The remainder I took with me, and we set out along the path.

How shall I be able to teach these mute creatures to love God and make him known to them? Thinking thus, I looked at them and felt great compassion. I heard a bell, and the more we ran, the nearer we came to it. It was a pretty little village with civilized people; I asked a young woman where the church was:

— I hear ringing and I do not understand where the temple is.

She told me that there are certain good souls who keep mute little girls. I cannot express what I felt! Having arrived at their house, I begged them to accept the poor little ones I had with me. They were not slow to grant my request; but the sorrow on both sides at having to part was something…! But they must learn to know God! My voice:

— One day you will see them again. On Calvary Jesus is found! 72.

And silent, I went along the way.

Refreshed by bread brought by an angel — The prayer of beginners.

Night overtook me, and also a great weakness. Where was I to go? My God, I feel that I am fainting! I sat down. A gentle boy comes before me, emerging from a bush; he comes near me, and I, almost enchanted, gazed at him. He asked me whether I wanted a little bread, which he had in a small but lovely little basket.

— Thank you! — I answered him.

And he:

— Why do you refuse it, when you are about to faint?

— How do you know?

— The one who sent me told me.

I remained so confused and could not account for it. A trembling seized me; and he pressed me ever more to accept that bread.

— Why so much fear? — he said to me.

I answered:

— Who has sent you? who are you? For charity’s sake, tell me!

— The one who sends me is God!

Oh! at this name I was shaken: Is it really true? might it not be the enemy? He is transformed and takes on his true appearance: an angel! Without heeding my hunger at all, I said to him:

— Speak to me of my God! Tell me what he told you to tell me!

— That you should eat what he sends you.

At once I took that bread, knelt down and ate it. 73. And he stayed close to me all the while; when I had finished, he disappeared. A giant’s strength came to me, and I resumed my way.

It was night, but the moon shone very brightly, and I saw the path clearly. Oh! how I reflected within myself! within my breast (I felt) a fire that was devouring me; I would have liked to find a pool of water to plunge into. I entered again into a colloquy with my God and earnestly set before him facts and doubts. I dwelt on aridity and on how many kinds of it there are; for beginners, the great vexations when that sensibility is lacking to them, when they feel in prayer the privation of relish; and then, when they begin to grow, now they meditate with some interior feeling and have a kind of recollection; they become attached to it, and woe if for some time it is lacking to them! they are disturbed and cannot find peace; they seek advice, and worse, because they leave their own guide and go in search of what they can find only in vain. In this case the finest remedy is to abandon oneself to one’s ordinary guide and in peace to do the obedience.

But it is very difficult to make them listen to reason. These are those souls that have a large dose of themselves, believing themselves to be what they are not; and with this encumbrance on the way they never manage to make a leap, and abandon themselves into the hands of Providence, and follow perfectly the voice of the one who guides them; but they always fear that they are not well understood, and they also fear that their guide is not the right one. Oh! for so little must you search so much? They keep everything to themselves and think they are — I repeat — what they are not. 74.

Having finished my reflection up to this point — which I cannot call mine, no, but rather that of someone who suggests it within me — I was tired; I would have liked to sit down: the night did not allow me.

The value of charity done for the love of God to anyone whatsoever.

Alone? no! I shall run on still, with the hope of finding farmhouses where I can stop. But, after I had gone a good stretch of road, a little boy all in rags comes before me; he tells me that he is hungry and cold; he shows me his little feet, which are pouring out blood. My God! a little while ago I was complaining that my feet hurt me very much, and his are covered with sores. I set about asking him where he came from, whether he had parents; but he answered me little; he only looked at me. Then he said to me:

— I am cold!

At once I took off my footwear and put it on him, trying to dry the blood and to clean his feet as best I could. And then I took off everything except my dress, and I put these garments on him.

— Do you feel warm? — (I said to him).

He thanked me.

— But I have no bread!

And he kept telling me that he was hungry.

Let us run, my child: who knows whether we may not find good people who will give us enough to eat our fill! Meanwhile you must tell me who you are and where you were born, how you come to be alone in these forests…

My God, who can he be? Meanwhile the stones were making my own feet stream with blood, and (I felt) such a cold that my teeth began to chatter; I could no longer bear to go forward; and there was no way of making him speak.

— Oh! listen, in the name of God, who are you?

And he begins to grunt. Oh! what fear seized me! so much so that I found myself between anguish and distress. Running, another one arrives, and from their appearance one could tell that they were two brothers. This one had a little basket of very beautiful bread and fruit; and skipping about, he offered me some. I told him at once to give some to this poor little one, who was so hungry. With a false smile he told me that I should buy it.

— Oh! how is this? you want to give it to me, and for that you want me to buy it? I have nothing left; see: barely a rag of a dress to cover myself. But how is it that you are here so early with so lovely a basket? are you not of the same house as this one?

He does not answer me; and both of them kept on coming with me.

— I am hungry! — the other was saying.

At last he said to me:

— If you eat some too, I will give you all of them, the basket as well.

I look at him and then, in a severe tone, I say to him:

— Do not tempt me, for you would do it in vain!

I hear a sound of bells. Oh! I am near my God! But meanwhile they were molesting me more than ever. Tired, cold, I felt myself fainting, when the one with the basket told me to take some of it to give to the other. I stopped (and said):

— Why must I give to him, when you can give to him yourself? You make me understand well enough who you are!

This said, they hurled themselves at me to seize me. They were two devils; I saw the things turned to ashes, and all terrified I began to weep. And they mocked me and kept trying to seize me.

— See what your charity has brought you to! What has it gained you? — the one I had covered was saying to me. — You have nothing left: you will die of cold and hunger. This is how you have always done your charities! see: they are reduced to ashes!

A great number of others like them come out, and all were telling the same story, adding that for my charities badly done I shall receive a great punishment; and they laid a thousand snares for me.

Tired, undone by weeping, at every step I took they tried to stop me, and they never succeeded. My God! reduced to this, without having done anything pleasing to you! Has the enemy alone, then, received charity from me? This terrible thought, that my Lord would be angry with me because I did not know how to give well to those in need…: but not to these ugly ones! I was about to faint, so many things were they doing to me. They begin to fight among themselves, I do not know why. And while they were saying: Let us take her! — I heard nothing more — a great personage took me, wrapped me in his cloak, and I felt myself perfectly changed. Rapt in sweet ecstasy, my God showed me what the charity I had always done had brought me, and even that which I had done to that ugly one shone most brightly. The blood shed from my feet was lovely rubies.

I found myself fully clothed again at the foot of the altar where my Good was. I fed on the Eucharistic Bread, and again (I remained) absorbed in my God. Nothing of my usual clothing was missing, and I did not understand how I would have gone on. In the ecstasy he showed me how charity done for the love of God to anyone whatsoever, even in the case that happened above, has a great value, provided one does not truly know that the poor person is not really poor, but does it either to hoard or to carouse; then it is not well done. And that ugly one came away from it in disgrace: how stupid he is! And this because he lacks light.

Never would I have torn myself away from the feet of my God; although recovered from the ecstasy, it was still a continual sweetness to recite prayers, to stay with my Master… But my voice:

— Enough! it is time to return to work and no longer to remain where you desire.

Without uttering a word, I kissed the ground and went away, strong as a giant, fortified by the Eucharistic food.

Demonic ill-treatment at the hands of a possessed woman. I found on my path a gracious young woman and asked her who she was, whether she too was traveling that way. (She answered me):

— For a little while, only long enough to tell you certain things that you need to know. I must instruct you.

— Thank you, good young woman: oh! how much I need it! I shall be grateful to you for ever.

And she looked at me:

— You believe that you are sowing good seed in your fields, but… — and she sighs.

How is it — I said to myself — that she speaks of what is mine, when I have nothing? Clearly she is mistaken, because I never had anything of my own. And promptly I told her that she was mistaken, that I had neither fields nor cottages, because I am very poor and possess nothing.

— And yet certain workers, who cultivate the land so well, told me that they were yours.

— Oh — I added — mine, never! They all belong to God; it is He himself who has instructed them very well.

She found herself confounded and, curtly, told me that I taught very badly how to cultivate, and that the Bride of Jesus, holy mother Church, was afflicted on this account.

— Oh! how is it you tell me this? who has sent you here?

— I came by heavenly inspiration to warn you, so that you may stop governing so badly. I, in a strong tone, answered her:

— I have never governed, nor do I even understand the word in its true meaning. You are mistaken; leave me, molest me no more!

It came into my mind: could it be a devil dressed in this way? I took out my rosary and recited its prayers aloud; but she kept on. She said to me:

— Enough! listen further!

— No!

— This path is for me and not for you, who do not know how to run it.

And I was silent. She comes before me to stop me.

— I beg you, let me go, for I must obey another and not you.

She grows angry and hurls an endless stream of abuse at me. I (go on) without turning round; seeing this, she hurls stones at me and never manages to hit me. Whoever can she be, on my path? could she be a demon? My voice:

— No!

So I turned toward her gently and said to her:

— Why so much rage against me, who feel nothing but the desire to be able to serve you?

Worse! it was something horrible: what came out of her mouth! And thus enraged she ran along with me; I did not cease to entreat her. At last, shrieking, she told me to get off the path and leave it to her. My God! must I do this? My voice:

— Never! she is possessed!

Then I stopped and in the severest tone commanded the dragon to come out of that body and return whence it had come. Horrible terror! She threw herself to the ground, she let out terrible howls, and how many things she hurled against me! It was something frightful. Seeing that it still did not leave her, I grasped my Crucifix and commanded it to come out. She gave so loud a shriek, and such an upheaval followed, that the unhappy woman very nearly fell headlong into a torrent. I caught hold of her and, having raised her up, wished to try to comfort her as much as I could. I invited her to come with me, but she answered curtly that she did not feel like it. I offered to accompany her: no! She remained seated:

— But tell me, please, do you feel unwell?

— No!

— Can I do anything to comfort you?

— No!

She sat there sulking, as though I had done her a wrong in praying God to free her from that dragon; and I kept asking her to tell me what she wanted. What was I to do? Leave her? it seemed to me a failure in charity. Poor thing! perhaps she will feel humiliated by what happened. Meanwhile I would have liked to find something to comfort her.

— Come, then! — I said to her — night is coming, and you are here alone. Come with me.

And I made her a thousand promises. Nothing! She turned to me and said:

— Go away, once and for all! I shall always persecute you. I looked at her:

— But have you still some ugly beast with you?

— No!

I turn round and see that loathsome creature, waiting for me to go away.

— Are you not glad to be freed from that dragon?

— No! go away!

My voice:

— Leave her! it is time lost. You will see her again. Now she wants back what she had.

Full of terror, in haste, more than ever I quickened my step to get away, and I did not dare to turn round. After a long way I began to hear the same howls and shrieks again. What fear! The night was dark, not a single cottage could be seen; weeping, I called upon my angel and told him to make me find quickly a temple where my God dwells.

The shrieks draw nearer. Oh! surely, surely it is that unhappy woman. In a flash, there she is beside me; furiously she seizes me by the arm and says to me:

— What you have done to me I shall do to you!

It would be easier to imagine than to describe what was happening within me. She strikes me, and at once my mind goes to my Crucified One at Pilate’s gate: oh! my Love, far heavier than these were the blows you received for love of me.

She, perceiving my prayer, said to me:

— Are they too few? I shall give you heavier ones.

So saying, she draws out a scourge and strikes. Alas! I was about to faint: my face bleeding, my hands, and I felt the blood running all over me. But I was always with my Crucified One; with the greatest delight I offered him the blows. So great was the desire to suffer ever more, so united was I to my God, that I did not think of what would become of me if she went on striking. I felt that I was fainting, but I did not care, nor was I even afraid. She gave me, one after another, such blows that I had to fall face down on the ground. But:

— Enough, thus far! — I heard said.

My Savior was not tended.

The woman vanished, and I found two gracious little old women beside me: one held me up and the other, with a vessel in her hand shaped like an amphora, gave me to drink. It was an exquisite cordial; it strengthened me. But they did not speak. The older one tried to tend my wounds and wipe my face. I thanked her and said to her:

— There is no need to tend me; my Savior was not tended.

She took an ointment out of her pocket and wanted to put it on my hands, begging me to let her tend my arms as well.

— No, thank you!

— Jesus — she replied — had his wounds anointed.

— But he was dead! — I replied — and I feel no need of ointment: no!

— I entrust it to you, and I tell you to make use of it.

And they vanished. I looked around and saw nothing. Alone, seated upon a stone, I looked at my track, and it was well marked: it seemed to invite me to follow it. I rose; I could barely stand. When will it be, my God, that I shall be able to find one of your dwellings and so receive you into this breast, which I feel so sorely afflicted! but more than this, (I am) panting to be able to possess you! With difficulty I moved my feet; every part of my body had its own pain. My voice:

— And yet Jesus, with all his pains, had the cross upon his shoulder.

Alas! I stopped and as best I could made one out of a thick piece of wood and laid it upon my shoulders. Having taken a few steps, it came into my mind that I was not worthy to carry it on my shoulders, but rather that I ought to lay it upon my breast. I was not slow to do so, when the pain increased to such a degree that I fainted, face down on the ground.

What was my confusion when I saw myself held up and raised by my God! Oh! my sweet Love! But I could utter nothing more. He signed me on the forehead and said to me:

— Leave this wood, anoint your wounds, regain your strength, for you must fight for my Work!

And he vanished. Full of strength, I opened the little jar of ointment given me by the gracious old woman and tended the deepest wounds with it. And I took up my way again, preparing myself for the struggle, which was not long in coming.

Two workers plot to kill her; she is freed by her angel.

They were armed men, whom I found after a long stretch of road. They were laying waste a strong and well-built edifice; I cried out with all the strength I had:

— Stop, in the name of God!

They, hearing such loud shouting, seemed like so many drunken men; they looked at me and stood still, waiting for me. When I arrived (I said to them):

— Why do you plan to do so much harm? who are you? who sent you? Do you perhaps think that this edifice has no one to defend it? Withdraw!

And they kept listening to me, astonished; they took their tools and went away. One who was their leader left me with these words:

— I shall return armed with powers!

My God! what will come of it? My voice:

— Take away the rottenness that is inside!

At once I made a search and found one of those workers who had worked so cunningly that everything might be destroyed, and who, together with another, had arranged it all. I seized the threads of their plotting, I intercepted their communications; and he who had said to me: I shall come with powers! was able to obtain nothing.

The edifice regained its former foundation; the tumults vanished and, as it ran swiftly in every work of charity, it was a delight. I took the two schemers with me and kept them well guarded, so that they should not escape me. I handed each of them over to whoever had given them to me.

When all was finished, I felt tired beyond all belief and sought to find a little corner to take some rest. A loud din startled me and I looked for its cause: nothing! Surely it must have been my imagination. And once again I lie down to rest. Worse than ever: I go round to see whether anyone had entered those cells: nothing! My God! what do you want? make it well understood by your slave, always ready for your orders! Lying down once again, worse than the other times! I hear a frightful upheaval. What do you want, my Lord, my Master? I do not understand: you called Samuel three times, but at the third time you made yourself understood (cf. 1 Sam 3:4-18). And I set about searching: what can it be? how and where must I go? So heavy was the sleep I had that it overtook me even standing. My voice:

— Go to the bottom of the garden and you will see!

For fear, I could not bring myself to go into that garden. Oh! what if this were the devil, who had sought to imitate my Voice so that I might go there? Then I overcame myself and went. What was my surprise at seeing the two whom I had taken away, who were scheming to see whether they could lead astray others who might give that disturber the means of achieving his aim! Full of courage, I went before them and ordered them to go away; but they were so enraged that, being able to do nothing else, they shrieked like two possessed women, threatening to beat me. Oh! how I pitied them! how ugly it is when a person is bewitched by a passion! A dreadful state! they become beasts (save for the soul). They stoop to commit very loathsome things, for they behave in so mean a way that they are pitiable.

Seeing that I in no way yielded to their threats, they resolved to seize me and reduce me to a sorry state. But no! I stood firm, knowing that I was doing my duty as a slave, for so my Lord willed, and I was afraid of nothing; when one of them, enraged, gives me so hard a slap; and I, so happy, turned the other cheek so that she might give me another. But in an instant they stop and, as though frightened, take to flight. Whoever was it? Having turned round, I saw a tall young man with a stern face; I stood for a moment looking at him, I too hesitant. He added:

— Do not be afraid!

And he took off his cloak. Oh! my angel!

— They will no longer be able to do anything here. Leave this place and go elsewhere in haste!

And he vanished. I began to run, and more than ever I felt within me so strong a fear…: surely those wretched women wanted to do great things. I pressed my dear Crucified One to my breast and, running, I came to a small village, where all the people seemed to look at me as if in surprise. Whatever can it be? A woman comes up to me, looks at me and says to me:

— How did you manage to escape?

— Why do you say this to me, good woman?

Another answers:

— It cannot be she!

This talk of theirs made me very suspicious; I asked them where the church was; they point me to a long ascent:

— At the top of this is our parish church.

I was happy, but troubled by what I saw and heard. Having arrived at that gracious church, at once I asked to be able to feed at the heavenly table: my Love, Lord! But even the man who kept it said to me:

— How did you manage to free yourself from death? Are you the one who drove those usurpers out of that dwelling? and how were you able to escape, when everyone was saying that those two had come armed to kill you?

I stood listening, and in a flash my mind understood everything: when the angel put them to flight, they were to kill me! And I thought how my God, so infinitely charitable, sent someone to free me. 75.

I answered nothing to this man, except:

— I beg you to ask whoever is in this church to give me my God.

And, throwing myself to the ground, I gave vent to a flood of tears. Strengthened by my God, my weeping went on; I could not restrain it. I stayed until evening at the foot of the altar, where, through the kindness of those Fathers, they let me remain. Everyone offered me refreshment.

— Thank you, no! I need nothing.

With my forehead on the ground I sobbed, not thinking that night would come, nor where I would go. I thought of nothing else but of thanking my God and of staying with Him. Then one of these Fathers bids me go out, because the temple had to be closed, it being night. I rose and, turning my gaze, saw one of them who was also praying. I approach him and, kneeling at his feet with joined hands, I beg him to let me stay that night at the foot of the altar, for he would be rewarded for it by my Lord. He looked at me and, with a heavy sigh, told me that I might stay. Oh! I kissed the ground and then the hem of his tunic: may God reward him!

I returned near the altar and, prostrate, I adored my God and poured out my soul to Him. My voice:

— As soon as you have received the Lord, make haste and leave this village, so that people may not see you.

Having heard this, I was put into great distress. How am I to do it, my God? when will these Fathers come to give me my treasure? This said, I remained absorbed in my God, and an angel gave me Communion. 76.

Abandoned in God upon a mountain — A most beautiful castle destined for the Work of God.

That keeper came grumbling with a bunch of keys; he opened the door for me. Alas!

I look: it is dark! My God, what am I to do? A violent trembling seized me and, weeping, prostrate on the ground, I asked for help. I feel an invisible hand take hold of me, and I remained without understanding anything more: how, I do not know! I found myself alone on the top of a mountain which was frightening merely to look at: all rocks, and so high… There was no trace of a road. It was a most beautiful day.

But who has brought me here? my Good, is it you or one of your angels? Explain to me why you have had me brought here! Nothing! I sat down and, praying, I remained in peace. I look toward one side, which seemed to me less forbidding, to see whether there was a path by which one might descend, but nothing! And yet a kind of tumult could be heard. Once again a perfect silence returns. I could not understand how I came to be on a mountain without being able to descend. Night too will come…

Meanwhile I was fainting with weakness; I took heart and searched among those stones to see whether I could find grass to feed on. And so it happened. Having gathered this grass, I began to eat it, blessing my God who gave it to me. Oh! how happy I was at that sumptuous meal of mine! When I had finished, I leaned against a large stone. How it happened I do not know, but I was once again rapt in God, and I learned from it one more eloquent lesson:

— Your abandonment in me gives me great satisfaction. Here — he continued — I brought you to take you away from a fierce struggle of which you would have been the victim.

Coming to myself, I found myself no longer on the mountain, but in a delightful garden of a most beautiful castle. Confused, I did not know what to do:

— This will one day belong to my Work — so I understood inwardly.

But now what must I do? I kept repeating to myself the words I had received inwardly: It must be yours, my God! I took courage and knocked. An ill-mannered woman did not want to let me in; she asked me a thousand questions. I begged her with such insistence that, for the love of God, she would take me to her lady, who, being so charitable, would have helped me. After a long discussion she makes up her mind and takes me with her; but, repenting, she stops me and did not want me to go any further; but while this was happening, behold the lady: at once she comes toward me and, taking me by the hand, leads me to her apartment. We spoke much of God, and (she asked me) how I came to be in her garden. I answered that my Lord had sent me, and that he would greatly have desired that her castle be given to Him, to put in it workers who would labor in his vineyard cultivating plants. She listened to me with pleasure:

— I understand everything: your Lord is God?

— He is indeed my God — I added.

— Did He tell you so? — so she added.

— I am good for nothing, either to say or to do, being a poor slave who knows nothing.

— Very well, you shall have the castle; indeed, I shall have it put in order, and you shall put the workers in it.

But that wretched maidservant, who was listening to everything, comes out like a madwoman and wanted to prevent the work; but Jesus put such firmness into that heart that all her chatter and shrieking were of no avail. And as soon as possible everything was handed over to me.

My Master and Lord, provide the workers, that they may be according to your desire!

I was thinking about it, when a gracious discourse occupies my mind and, without realizing it, I was unfolding in it all that had to be done, and what I would meet as stumbling blocks and vexations, although there would be many hardships and sufferings. I do not know: I felt within me a kind of sweetness.

When this was over, I found everything set in order as to how I was to proceed. My God! how this unhappy humanity always flees from sufferings! I feel that it already trembles at what is to come; but your slave will keep it in subjection and everything will be carried out to the letter.

I gave myself with all my power to fulfilling the work given me; and with this the controversies and sufferings were not slow to arrive. At last, the edifice being completed, I sought to rest for a moment, so as to regain strength.

My voice:

— It is not in this way that you must have strength!

Saved and guided by Saint Joseph. I understood that I was not to rest, but rather to run wherever my Lord would trace the road for me. What pains — I went thinking to myself — are those of seeing souls who outrage my God! and nothing can be done to make reparation. It is torment! — I reasoned on this with vehemence, but tired from running, and no end was ever in sight.

I was looking for a stone to sit on, when I see a poor old man approaching me, who tells me to quicken my step, because unknown people were about to arrive and it was not good that I should be found in those fields, for if they had found me, not only would they have done harm to me, but the field would have suffered from it. If I were not there, they would go straight on without doing any harm.

— Good man, tell me, who are you?

— Look at me! — so he answered me.

— But how? — I said to him — I have been deceived by others, who also made signs as you do.

He answered me:

— Have no doubt! Walk on, I beg you.

— I said to him:

— You are right to urge me to quicken my step, but I feel that my strength is failing.

— Do you want my staff?

— Oh! that shall never be! If it is true that you are a good and holy poor man, I would never dare to take away your support; on the contrary, if I had another, I would give it to you; but I too am poor, I have nothing.

Wherever my Master may direct me, I shall certainly not have where to lay my head. But, good man, know that at this thought I feel exceedingly happy, for I desire nothing, only one thing, which I feel so consumed with longing to possess: oh! my God!

And he looked at me; he was pleased to hear me speak thus; and meanwhile he walked with me. I added:

— And what if you were the enemy? Oh! I would never accept an object that had been in his hands!

He began to laugh. And, old as he was, he walked faster than I. I looked at him and marveled at it.

— Courage! — he said to me — for we have only a little way left! Oh! my Lord, give me strength to arrive where you desire!

But having said this, a fear came over me that this man, who had the appearance of an old and poor man, might truly be the infernal enemy. I stopped and in a stern tone (said to him):

— Where are you leading me?

— To a temple.

— I tell you frankly that I feel so frightened (thinking) that you are betraying me.

— No! — answered the old man.

I look at the path: it is mine and well marked! Oh! most holy Virgin, Mother of my God, help me!

And once again he laughed so graciously. But meanwhile I was very distressed; he noticed my disquiet and with heavenly manners exhorted me not to be afraid.

Well then, why will you not tell me who you are?

— You will know later.

Here we are at the door of the temple. He made me go in, and he vanished. How I was left! I could not be at peace: it was certainly the Spouse of the Virgin Mary, Saint Joseph! I kept repeating his words to myself: that I would know it, but might he mean them as this, namely that he vanished! But nothing! I threw myself at the foot of the altar and, with the greatest desire, I awaited the coming of my God into me. Having received my Good, behold me rapt in God! Where did I find myself? The poor man who had accompanied me was Saint Joseph: he was beside me, no longer with the staff, but most beautiful; and he showed me how he had saved me from so terrible a danger: I saw those evildoers, who were going about in search of me. He said to me:

— Do not be afraid, for neither now nor later will they be able to touch one of your hairs.

I thanked him, begging him not to leave me in dangers, but always to come to my help.

It is not a time of sweetness but of sufferings. [?]

She weeps bitterly over an act of curiosity — love, for you are loved.

Coming to myself, my God! I was no longer in the temple, but rather in an immense field, which was uncultivated and had to be set right and put in order. I called some good workers and as best we could it was set right. But there was another, all wheat, but in it there was much couch grass. Indeed, it was so intermingled that the wheat could not have strength even to hold up the small ear. Without thinking of the size of the field, I set to work with all the strength I had; I was rooting out that noxious weed and had already made a large heap of it. It passed through my mind: who will carry it away? My voice:

— There is one who sees to that: work!

And I rooted out ever more of it. Glancing at the wheat, I see it more luxuriant, and the more it grew and strengthened, the more my strength grew together with my courage. Then I see two young men of such gracious manners arrive with a little cart, and they carry away the couch grass, and as the heap grew large they took it from me; but I could not see where they were carrying it. Curiosity seized me to go up to them and ask them. Overcome by it, I left off rooting out the couch grass and went up to them; I asked them what they did with it and where they were carrying it. They answered me in a sorrowful tone:

— Your curiosity, scattered over the wheat you have worked, the very same — look at it: it is burning!

I forbear to describe the sorrow, the torment: it is better to consider it than to describe it. With my face to the ground, I implored them to ask my God’s forgiveness for me. I took hold of a trunk all covered with thorns and beat myself until I shed abundant blood. What am I to do? I am lost! I have displeased my God; I do not deserve, no, forgiveness! And they looked at me.

Such exhaustion came over me that I fell and was about to lose my senses, when one of them, taking me by the hand, (said to me):

— You are forgiven!

I look: he was a most beautiful angel. Full of shame, I went on weeping and thanking God, asking him to thank Him too, with earnest promises that I would never again commit acts of curiosity.

— Look! — he said to me — The wheat is once again beautiful and healthy, now that you have worked it.

The devil was whispering to me to ask him where the other had gone, who together with him had been carrying away the bad grass. Oh my Love! — I exclaimed aloud — that shall never be!

The angel, perceiving my fear and languor, for I was left exhausted, in order to test my obedience and to do something pleasing to my God, told me to make haste and go to remove the rest of the couch grass and to clean the field. I rose without uttering a word, all content to bring (the work) to completion. But I fell. With courage and a lively desire to go there, I rose; but once again I fell. My God! a little strength! I do not deserve it, but this body will not stand. And I tried to help myself as much as I could so as to manage to walk. My efforts were useless. My angel comes up to me and, taking me by the hand, (says to me):

— By your blind obedience, by your love in carrying out the orders of God, you have gained much, and the Lord grants you all the strength you desire.

It was a second! And I, strong as a giant, cleaned out the fields. And I set off along my path, running, full of ardor for the glory of God and to seek his will in all things.

I reasoned over what had happened and felt a keen and deep sorrow for it. My voice:

— Enough! you must forget: love, for you are loved!

Oh! sweet Love! how can I come to do something pleasing to your Being? This said, rapt, I do not know whether I was walking with my feet on the ground or rather, I should say, as I believe, flying. In an Eden of Paradise I came to myself: everything spoke to me of love! It was enchantment, my Love! my bones, the very marrow of them, were being consumed: Love! I heard a sweet and melodious song, which also added to my undoing. Every now and then I could say nothing else: my Love! I am dying! But sweet it would be to be consumed by love and to die of love! come! continue, O sweet sounds! your echo undoes me. My Love, let me stay here until my last breath! 77.

From Tabor to Calvary.

My voice:

— From Tabor one must climb to Calvary!

And everything vanished. I returned — where? to my yoke! Poor slave! So it is for you, O wretched humanity! Angry with it, I beat it with all the strength I had. My voice:

— Enough! it is not this that God wants, but sacrifice. My God, what must I do? And weeping I fell asleep with my head upon a stone. An invisible hand:

— Wake up and walk!

I opened my eyes and, having looked around, saw nothing. Who woke me? In this way I spent the night. I resumed the way: it was very harsh, for it was a mountain so steep that I often slipped. Oh! how rough it is, my God! And at once it came into my mind that my God had climbed it with the cross on his shoulder. What did I do? I contrived to take two pieces of dry tree and (making a cross) I wanted to carry it on my breast, but every now and then I fell; at each fall my bones received terrible jolts. So great was the consolation I had from it that every fall was a great joy to me.

— How happy I am — I went saying — at the thought that my Good also fell, and hurt himself far more than I, and for me he fell so heavily!

Here I am on the ground again! Laughing I rose and saw that I had hurt myself badly. My Love! blood also came forth from your veins, and it was the blood of a God! Mine is rottenness, not even worthy to be offered in expiation of my sins. Oh! if at the end of this ascent, my Love, I had the good fortune to find you and tell you that I love you so much! Oh my sweet treasure, Being of my life!

Saying this, it was always the same story: now on my feet, two steps, and then on the ground once again! We never arrived. I began to faint, and I commended my soul to God, that he might hold it close to his breast. And on the ground again! Exhausted, I could no longer rise.

Thus, among the stones, I was overcome by a sweetness beyond compare. My mind was occupied with most absorbing reasonings; I was explaining to myself something that was to happen to me; and, as though my intellect saw everything, I was seeking the way to conquer and so to gain fields for God. Absorbed in this way, I was resting sweetly. When I roused myself, I no longer found the cross. I looked round and round again: nothing! Where have you gone, my treasure? As I moved, my bones seemed out of joint.

With the help of generous benefactors she is able to increase the Work of God.

A gracious peasant woman arrived and told me that in the valley of the mountain there were people waiting for me, and she urged me to hurry and run.

— But what is the matter with you? — that creature began to say to me — Do you want to lean on my arm? I feel sorry for you.

She said it with a heavy sigh. At this way of hers I became troubled:

— Why do you say this to me, and why have you so much pity for me, you who do not know me? Who are you? And those people who are waiting for me, who are they?

I stopped: I no longer wanted to go forward. My voice:

— Obey!

I set out together with her, and she told me many things. One moment I listened to her and the next I was preoccupied with what those people would want of me. When I arrived, there were people of every sort. They welcomed me very kindly and wanted me to enter their dwelling. My God, where am I?

One of them, the eldest, began to say that they had heard of the Work of God and would like to know how to entrust a portion of their possessions to it, to enlarge the vineyard. I gladly accepted and many things were concluded; but on seeing such abundance, and having in my mind certain fields of the Lord where the poor workers have so little to live on, a sadness came over me which my Jesus permitted to be seen outwardly. One of them, who spoke little but kept his eyes fixed upon me, while the others moved away, stopped me and asked me where my sadness came from, for he perceived that I had a deep sorrow. When he had said this, I would have liked to excuse myself, but without realizing it I gave a deep sigh: My God! When this was said, he wanted more and more to know the cause.

— I am thinking that here those workers whom I shall bring into your field will have such abundance, while I have large fields where they live with hardship.

— So you are in need of help?

— Very much — (I answered), ashamed.

He said nothing more to me, and withdrew. The others take me to see the very beautiful preparations made to receive the workers, to whom were to be entrusted the creatures whom they were to cultivate and make into good Christians.

That gentleman returned. I do not know how, but I had regained a certain serenity within: a gentle consolation had entered there. He came up to me and asked the others for permission to speak to me. As soon as they had all gone, he put into my hand so large a sum that I was left speechless and amazed.

Thank you! — I said to him — May God reward you by returning it to you a hundredfold. And I shall tell my Lord to place you at the head of the benefactors and to pour his abundant graces upon your head.

He took his leave and I returned to the others; but so great was my eagerness to go away, so as to reach the place where they had such need…!

Having taken my leave, I ran with all the strength I had, heedless of hunger, cold and sleep. I arrived at that large field and at once the one who directed it ran to meet me; and full of joy I handed over to him what my Master had had given to me by that good Catholic gentleman. Amid tears and amazement he received it, and at once the workers took heart again, and moreover a greater increase could be given to the Work of the Lord. And I returned, bringing a portion of the good workers to begin the new and beautiful edifice. They set to work with eagerness and, with the help of the Lord, it turned out most beautiful.

The hypocritical worker: a moral portrait.

I set out on my path and, along it, I went thinking of the greatness of God and of his infinite mercy. Meanwhile I stop for a moment and, kneeling on the ground, with my forehead upon a stone (I pray):

— From your mercy I want love! I am exhausted, but I desire nothing but love!

My voice:

— It is not a time for sweetness, but for sufferings! Go along this road.

I rose and, running, I went on:

— My Love, in suffering there is love!

And, out of breath, I regained strength:

— But from your love, my Master, I receive it!

A spectacle! As I drew near to where I heard shrieks and laments, I felt my breast torn apart. Whatever can be there? There was still a considerable distance, but the keeper of that field saw me from afar and ran to meet me. We were so breathless and panting, the one to hear and the other to tell, that we stopped without being able to exchange a word.

— Oh! — she began again — Blessed be God who has led you here! There are a great many dissensions, to the point that there are some who want to abandon our field. The very owners who gave it to us are also angry with us. Come and help us, for pity’s sake!

— Do not be afraid, for the Lord will set everything right.

I ran. When we had set out for the place, behold a crowd of people, but the worst were the workers who, imprudently, without realizing it, were doing great harm. These having withdrawn, and the owner having been heard, my voice:

— The damage is all on account of that worker who keeps silently apart: see to it.

When I had finished setting everything in order, without the owner and the others noticing, I took her away. My God! how terrible hypocrisy is, and how slyly it knows how to act! She was one of the most zealous and silent, so much so that the keeper confided in her: she was good for her, because she made bad use of it for her own ends; and she would have utterly destroyed that field.

But along the way she broke her silence and, with insulting words, threatened me if I did not take her back there. With all the strength I had, I exhorted her to calm herself and come with me, for God would see to settling every affair of hers which she said she had left in that field. Seeing herself now far away and no longer able to hope to return there, oh! how she went out of all reason! With all the gentleness I could find (I tried) to persuade her: nothing! She threw her garments to the ground and, dressed again in some rag or other, went back to where she had no more peace.

So, broken-hearted, I threw myself at the feet of my Crucified One and, pressing him to my breast, I commended that soul to him, and with tears of deep sorrow I made my lament:

— Why did this happen? Along the way I begged you to give strength to my words, so that she might be converted: why let her go astray?

I could obtain no answer. Tired, I fell asleep at the foot of the cross. In a dream I saw a creature on whom God had bestowed so many benefits; she took no account at all of what she received, but attributed to herself all that she had. I said to my God: This soul cannot know what she is doing. Poor thing, it grieves me; surely, inwardly, she is innocent. Another person comes forward, whom I could not make out, and says: Anything but innocent! look! And vanished.

As though it were in a painted picture, her evil inclinations could be seen, and everything derived from pride; her heart, greedy for a return to its affections of flattery, was so black and ill-formed…; only the swollen valve could be seen; smoke came out of her nostrils; her ears had a horn on each side; on her forehead she wore a band as black as coal; from her mouth came forth certain flames of fire. Alas! at such a sight, all terrified, I threw myself to the ground: Miserere mei, Deus! Have pity, my God! To what state that poor soul is reduced! Ah! grant me, I implore you, my God, to suffer as much as you will, provided I obtain that she leave sin and return to humility and acknowledge her fault.

She obtains the conversion of the worker at the cost of her own sufferings.

I implored him so much that I obtained it. I was given over to certain loathsome devils, who every minute offered me new treasures and with such cunning tried so subtly to assail me, and then, by means of holy things, (suggested to me) the good I would have gained if I had done this. At last, with a thousand terrors, laying out in detail (certain) deeds which, by the mercy of God, did not exist, they made me see that I was a labyrinth of infamy; that my soul was so chained by false ideas of my own that there was no longer any escape.

Alas! already my strength to fight was failing; fear was gaining ground, the anxiety that such grim combats might leave bad impressions in me. How painful it was! all woods, the mountain was barren: they alone were working with all their might. As soon as fear entered into me, they devised the most terrible things.

At last the mountain splits open halfway: an abyss of fire! A horrible spectacle of every sort of torment. Alas!

— Look! — one of them says to me — you see there is a place for you too!

And indeed there was an empty one. (My) shrieks and torment were indescribable.

I took hold of certain thorns and with all my strength pressed them to my breast, so that their points might enter into this wretched flesh. From trembling I felt myself fainting. I call upon the most holy Virgin, my angel, Saint Michael… My Jesus! ah, destroy me as it pleases you, do with this nothing of yours what you will, but not in that abyss. If you will that I feel those pains, so be it, but together with you, my God, in that… 78. And I stopped. What were those ferocious dragons doing? they whispered all kinds of things to me; but, exhausted, I hardly understood any more than a little.

All of a sudden that horrible mouth closed. They vanished. And, as I was fainting, my angel caught me swiftly; and I, leaning on his arm, had no strength to utter a word. He said to me:

— The soul you desired is already saved, converted and contrite. Within me I rejoiced at it, but I had no strength. I tried to thank him with my gaze. He comforted me; he took a little flask and gave me to drink. As soon as I had drunk that exquisite cordial, I revived and (said to him) a great thank you. I would have liked to tell him so many things, but above all I asked him about my God:

— Where is he? Tell him never to allow me to see and hear such terrible things. And I wept over it.

— Is he angry with me? Perhaps I have not suffered as he would have liked? Oh! assure me that he loves me and will not abandon me any more.

— He was always with you in those struggles and was much pleased. Had He not been there, you would not have held out.

— So, he loves me? Oh! surely my poor and miserable humanity, at such terrible assaults of those dragons… Oh!

And once again I wept and trembled:

— How shall I manage to forget them?

— And yet you must forget. Woe to you if these thoughts should occupy your mind.

— Ah! for pity’s sake, find me a remedy so that they may never again present themselves to me.

He signed me on the forehead with the sign of the holy cross, and vanished. I realized that I was no longer on that terrible mountain, but in a gracious valley, where a varied song of birds could be heard; a pretty stream of water flowed, almost hidden by a little hedge; it was very beautiful; I went near and gathered in my hands enough water to refresh my face. I did not dare to touch my forehead, thinking that that sign must have remained imprinted on me; but in my hands, which were still wounded, I felt relief from that water. My breast still pained me from the pricks I had received. I sat down and stayed listening to those little creatures singing so well.

— How well you know, with your gracious song, how to give praise to my Lord! Oh! my Love! how I too would like to know how to praise you and make you praised, to love you and make you loved. 79! But how? I am so wretched that I have nothing to offer you. I had a miserable will and this, as soon as I knew it, I gave you at once: there remains to me only this miserable humanity, to drag wherever you command me to go. No longer mine, I only drag it where it pleases you, and it will always be, with your help, an instrument of your divine will. 80.

While I was reasoning thus: whoever is it? That blessed soul, which my angel had told me was saved, thanks me, promising to pray for me. Oh! thank me? No, thank God; it is through Him alone that you are saved, but this poor slave is in need of compassion. She looks at me, and I repeat to her: Pray for me, that I may be reduced to ashes for God! She vanished.

My Love, I feel that my breast is being consumed by the great desire to love you. When shall I know how to love you and be able to possess your love?

Penances for a soul in purgatory, whose debt can be paid only with blood.

I fell asleep in that thicket where I found myself seated, so drained of strength. Was I dreaming or awake?

I saw a soul that was in purgatory, and with joined hands she begged me to tell a certain person that she was suffering much, because that person had not given what was in a piece of furniture in her house. A voice, whose I could not see, told me to pray for her and that she needed to satisfy a debt, but it could be canceled for her only with blood. I roused myself and looked around. Oh! — I said to myself — it was a dream: exhaustion, the unhappy position in which I found myself, caused such a sleep. I tried to rise to set out on my way, but it was still dark night, all silence, nothing could be seen: with difficulty I saw my path. I was so cold and hungry that I could not stand on my feet… Thus, pondering over the decision to be taken, I sat down and thought that, as soon as it was light, I would find herbs or wild fruits and would feed on them.

Before I had even finished my reasoning, the sound of a bell is heard. Oh! my God is here nearby! Without further thought, I run to where the sound (was coming from). In the midst of a lovely wood there was a little church; I entered and threw myself at the feet of my God, beating my breast: I am not worthy, my Love, to receive you, but my breast is panting to possess you, my heart throbs to have you within it.

Behold, the candles are lit: in a moment I shall possess you! So it happened. Oh! bread of heaven, what strength you give to the one who is weak! My Love! This said, I remained absorbed in Him. A voice said to me:

— I, for you, so much charity, and you, for those two souls who suffer so much, have you no charity?

— Oh! how, my Love? Then it was not a dream, but reality, what happened to me in that thicket. I shall do all that they have asked of me.

After a long while, having come to myself, I went to my path to set out to perform the act of charity for which blood was needed, for the one and for the other. Thus thoughtful and in haste to arrive, having entered the cottage, I at once set about fulfilling what I had promised, offering to my God my blood to ransom that soul in purgatory together with the other.

And, ever full of strength, I came back to go on my path; and I kept recalling the grace I had received that morning; it occupied me so much that I thanked my God fervently for it.

My voice:

— Think of collecting something to take to a flock that is truly lacking food.

In search of food for a flock — A great help from an elderly lady.

I look about me: there is no one here. Where shall I be able to find charity?

On that stony road there are not even any inhabitants. I quicken my step as much as I can; in the distance I seem to see a farmhouse: I shall ask for bread. Meanwhile I feel my strength failing. Poor me! how shall I get there, for it is still very far? But with your help, my God, I shall accomplish the mission.

Having reached those people, as soon as I asked them, for the love of God, to give me bread and whatever they wished, because certain creatures were hungry, they drove me away roughly and sent me off with rather ungracious names.

Once more on my way, (I come) to another cottage and ask for something for the love of God.

After grumbling, they give me a little piece of bread, all gnawed, and order me to eat it in their presence. I would have liked to take it to those creatures, but I was thinking that they certainly would not eat it, because they would be disgusted by it. While I was reflecting thus, these people thought that I did not want it, and what things they said to me! They would almost have liked to beat me; but I calmed them, telling them that I feared to fail in charity by feeding myself instead of taking it to those creatures.

They made me sit down and I ate that little piece of bread with singular relish; but one after another they came to look at me. An older woman stops and asks me many questions; I answered courteously all that I could. When I had finished eating the bread, I rose and with joined hands thanked God and the people who had given it to me.

A woman comes running and tells me to stop, for it was not advisable for me to go on, because night would overtake me, and she begged me insistently.

— Infinite thanks for your charity; God will count it to your merit just as if I had accepted it, but I cannot: those poor things are waiting for me and I must go and seek alms for them.

— But at night? and besides, the people of the village near here are exceedingly miserly.

— Poor things! — I answered her — God will see to it.

And I go away. Having gone some way along the road, I find the maidservant of that older lady, who hands me a purse with a great deal of money and says to me:

— Since she cannot give alms in front of her sons and daughters, she sends it to you secretly by means of me, and she desires that you remember her much to God.

And she gives me a note:

— You will make use of this in your great necessities.

How much I sent her my thanks can be imagined. I ran in haste, taking all the shortest ways, and I had no need to toil, because my track always showed me where I was to go. At last it becomes dark night. My fright was something horrible; the more I walked, the less I ever managed to see the end. A trembling begins to prevent me from running. My God! have pity: I am afraid; I feel myself failing on every side. In my imagination I saw men who would have taken from me what I had and was guarding so as not to lose any of that great providence. I began to weep: For charity’s sake, my God, help me!

Oh, surprise! who comes to meet me? The two souls who had gone to paradise, those who had asked me to do (penance) for them. They said to me:

— Do not be afraid!

With them there was a beautiful light which let the countryside be seen very well.

— Oh! dear souls, infinite thanks! Tell me something of my God. Tell him that I love him so much; but…!

Thus I stop, weeping. They comfort me and did not want me to weep. They assured me that I was much loved by God, and that they, for the charity received, would always help me in my necessities and accompany me in dangers.

As soon as I had arrived near the cottage, my dear companions vanished; but before this happened they told me that this office had been given them by God: that whenever I found myself in such circumstances they would come to keep me company. I thanked them with all my soul and they departed.

When I reached those creatures, they received me with open arms, and at once I handed over to the eldest, who acted as the first among them, all that I had, and told them to pray for the one who had given it to me with such charity: that God might multiply it a hundredfold for her. How happy I felt to have been able to sustain those creatures and relieve them from want!

A field of young virgins who sing to Mary and wish to become brides of Jesus. I was invited to stay, and I felt every desire to consent; but my voice:

— It is not the time!

I understood everything, and courteously took my leave. Nourished by the bread of angels, I set out on my way, to where my Master willed that I should go.

A field of young virgins, all seated, who were singing praises to the most holy Virgin. I went near and asked them to whom they belonged. One answers:

— To no one!

— How is it you are gathered here? who are you?

— Daughters of Mary.

— Oh! dear creatures, do you love this great Sovereign?

— We love her very much.

I stop, and the poor things gather round me.

— How do you belong to this Queen? what habit do you wear?

— None.

And they told me how they gathered in that valley so as not to be seen or heard. And they prayed much to the most holy Virgin that she would open for them a way to be able to abandon the riches of the earth and put on the rough wool of the brides of her Son Jesus.
