Having heard this, I stood silent, and they began again:

— Who are you?

— I am a poor slave of the Lord, who goes about gathering bread and providence to maintain his brides.

One, the boldest, (said):

— But whoever is this woman who calls herself a slave?

— Oh! yes, I am the slave of my dear Jesus, my Savior! You will surely desire to be loved by my Master, and I do not doubt it, since you desire to be his brides.

— Oh! — exclaims one — Are you then one of them? And she stops. Another said to me:

— Where are these brides for whom you say you procure sustenance?

One said:

— I feel that I love them, and already (I feel) a lively desire to be among them, to live poorly.

This said, all of them take off everything precious and of value that they had, begging me to accept it and use it for those to whom they already feel attached. And for fear of being surprised, they leave me, begging me to return the next day at the same hour, for they were resolved to follow me. We parted. Who can they be?

X

To suffer, love.

Having arrived at a shore, she finds the workers’ ship broken to pieces: she sets everything in order.

Although the night was advancing, I kept running: (I felt) a strong impulse to walk, without fear or anything else ever coming into my mind. I arrived: where? on a shore. What darkness! how rough the sea was! No one could be heard. Where am I going, my God? what must I do?

I look around me: I no longer see any track: wherever am I? And yet, although it was dark, I always saw my track up to here: now (it can be seen) no longer. The sea was making a terrible noise. Poor me! My God, come to help me! why did you make me come here?

Little lights rose here and there in the sea: what fear! Alas! they are not lights, but fires; I strive to make out what they were: all devils, who seemed in great merriment; while I was looking at them, they were increasing. With as loud a voice as I could, I cried out:

— What are you doing, you ugly loathsome things? Go back to where you came from!

The sea grows calm and I no longer see them. I kneel down and, clasping the rosary of the most holy Virgin, I recited it very loudly, (exclaiming) every now and then: Mary, my Mother, Mother of my Jesus, I am afraid!

All being calm, behold, the beautiful moon begins to rise, and already the sea could be clearly made out; reflecting it, it seemed crystal clear; (how) calm (it was)! The shore was beautiful and not far from me there were fishermen’s boats. I felt so drawn to go and see; but no, my God: here the path ends! This said, behold, the path too, which was marked, led to that place where the boats were.

In haste I ran there. Oh, what a spectacle! A ship all broken to pieces; the creatures were inside another and were sleeping. Meanwhile I hear a whispering; I look: I see nothing; but it had stayed in my ear where it had come from. I go near: what a spectacle! It was the two commanders of the ship, who were busying themselves with all their might and were trying to flee and abandon those poor creatures, and moreover without the ship, which was all in a bad state.

— Stop! — I (cried) to them — This is not your property, but God’s!

They wanted to slip away from me.

— Never! Stop, for we have accounts to settle! Where have you put all the workers you had? The ship that was entrusted to you, where is it? What are these colors, different from those in which you were clothed?

They seemed dumb. Then I realized that they were not alone. More than ever I held them fast. In a stern tone (I said to them):

— Speak!

One answered:

— We have been shipwrecked: the ship is broken to pieces and the workers are sleeping.

— How does it come to be on the sand in pieces?

— Until we reached the shore itself, there were certain people out of the sea who helped us. As soon as they went away, the ship broke apart.

One, in a low voice:

— They had promised us a great deal.

In a flash I understood everything.

— You are not alone!

A thousand protests that they were alone. With the strength of my God I leaped into that little boat: who was there? two shepherds who were hiding! I began to say to them:

— Why hidden here? What is done for God wears no mask. Is this (perhaps) his will: to take creatures and workers away in a ship so as to give the ship itself another course, and to teach them to trample on what the Lord had given them, through a diabolical illusion of making themselves independent of their guide and of building an edifice upon the sand?

They listened to me in silence. What happened was a most ridiculous scene. They had all lost their bearings; those two looked at each other; after a long silence one said:

— We have nothing to do with it. The ship is all in pieces. No one knows how to make anything out, because the stormy sea that came carried everything away.

These two women, hearing such reasoning, began to shriek like two possessed women:

— What? you have led us this far, and now that we have nothing left you treat us like this?

The men get up and flee. The women wanted to go after them; but then, with ferocious rage, shrieking, they threw all their belongings to the ground and began to weep. I went up to them and with the help of my God tried to persuade them and to restore them to peace, for everything would be set right. They looked at me; and I said to them:

— What? after doing you so much harm, they still treat you like this?

They threw themselves to the ground asking God’s forgiveness, and I together with them, prostrate on the ground, (prayed):

— Mercy, my God: have pity on us!

I begged them not to weep any more, but to come with me to see what had become of the poor Ship. Surprise! It had risen up again and nothing was lacking. My God! Did your angels work so well? They gave a cry of wonder. Those who were sleeping, having woken, learned in a flash what had happened. How moved they were! These workers too went aboard the little ship, which had graciously returned to the sea. Having taken the helm, I sought to give thanks to my Lord. Meanwhile I saw that every now and then he was steering the helm with me. Oh! my Love! your slave cuts the figure of a pilot, and she is but a shadow! He sat down beside me — oh! what joy! I remained in ecstasy; meanwhile he spoke to me of what I was to do on arriving at the port: that one would turn back and all the others would pursue their way and one day would enter the heavenly homeland.

The port was drawing near. Oh! my Love, put this ship far off again! let us go out to the open sea once more! do not leave me!

— Much suffering still remains for you.

And he vanished. I held the helm tight: here was my Good! I had not even noticed that we had stopped in port and were already at anchor. I did what I had been ordered, and the one who had been marked went back away, and all the others set to work. Oh! how many they gathered, and how far they advanced in the navigation of their mission, and they assembled many others, so that they put together not one little ship, but a fleet!

Alone, in the little ship, she sails up the Tiber and arrives at the feet of the Vicar of Christ.

How this consoled me! But my voice:

— Take the smallest one and put a sail on it; and then do not worry about where you will go!

Having at once carried out what I was ordered, I took the smallest and, having put the sail on it, at once sought to go to the helm. I hoped to find my God, but not only was He not there, there was not even a helm. Without giving it a thought, I saw myself carried by the wind out to the open sea; every moment I seemed about to be swallowed by the waves, but I feared nothing. I prayed when I saw myself almost lost: My God, if the boat sinks, you will make me walk upon the water as you did with Peter; would you give me your hand too? (cf. Mt 14:28-31). And I kept on.

At last, tossed this way and that, I see that it takes the course of a very large river. Having entered it, there were many fine ships and small boats: and I in that battered ship! As I passed near them, all the owners mocked me, and I laughed at it. One gives me a shout, seeing me advance like this and make my way all by myself:

— Where are you going?

What was I to say?

— Where my Master sends me!

— This said, he loads me with insults:

— Insolent woman, go back!

— I cannot: my Lord sends me here!

Worse! he grows angry:

— She comes from far away with nothing, and then she will want bread. We shall give you none: we help only our own, not foreigners.

— Have pity! I ask nothing of you, nor shall I ask. This very poor little boat will give you no trouble: I shall tie it to one of those rocks.

Grumbling, he was persuaded. Another, kinder but very curious, wanted to know how I had managed to arrive in that manner, in so ruined a boat, without a helm, with a sail all in tatters. He looks inside and sees nothing in the way of provisions.

— How can it be? She says she asks for nothing: how will she manage? — this he said in a low voice, but clearly enough to be heard.

Having tied up the boat well, as best I knew how, I sought to go to my Good in the great temple, to his Vicar. Oh! what a surprise! So ill-clad, ragged as I was, a poor slave of the Lord kisses the foot and the hand of his Vicar. Oh! most humble Sovereign! Oh mercy of God! He asks her about the little ship, desires it near Him and prophesies its future. Oh my Savior!

She returns with the beautiful ship flying the flag: TO SUFFER — LOVE, to incorporate it into the Roman Church.

With all the strength I had, I ran to fetch the little ship to bring it to where the Vicar is; but a stormy sea rises, a contrary wind dashes me against a rock. The weeping and the prayers were beyond compare. I had almost lost hope of being able to put it back to sea; so damaged by that blow, it would certainly fill with water as soon as it is at sea. I wept much, but I was sure that my Master would give me another, or else would make this one beautiful for me. Each of those from the ships said something, and one was so insistent that I do not know what he would have done to me.

After a great struggle, my little ship came out of it far more beautiful, and it was elegant: it had its gilded helm, a most beautiful compass; no longer the tattered sail, but an elegant flag which bore written on it: To Suffer and Love!

To two dear creatures who joined me I gave an oar each, and I was busy entering the port straight and then (going) to the feet of the great Vicar. What a surprise for the commanders of the large ships! They did not speak at all, but, full of wonder, they looked at me.

One, who could not restrain himself, comes up and wants to know how the thing had gone, and that I should take good care not to do this or that any more. I turned to him:

— I beg you to leave me, for your argument is hardly logical: in the Work of the Lord philosophy, theology, calculation have no place; all empty chairs!

— What sort of reasoning is this? — he said to me.

— Poor slave that I am, I never studied and I understand nothing: one thing alone have I sought to study and perfect myself in, in this matter: the will of God! to seek to do it blindly, in perfect abandonment in Him, like a slave faithful to her beloved Master.

He looks at me and then, with a gesture of contempt:

— She is an enthusiast! She has little judgment: let us leave it! And he addresses words to my workers to seduce them, but they, in a commanding tone, answer him that he should withdraw, that he has nothing to do with them.

He had guessed to a nicety what he said of me: a slave who knows nothing, truly unlearned in the sciences:

— And it is for this that Jesus took you, to work you in his own way, so that no one may say this is the work of man, but that divine wisdom alone has cooperated — so my voice said.

Having brought myself, together with my two companions, to the feet of Peter, the great apostle, I could say nothing else to him but that he should say many things for me to my God: that I was bringing the little boat to the feet of his Vicar, so that it might be incorporated into his Church. 81.

The ship, grown very large, ploughs the sea under full sail — New diabolical snares.

As soon as I had done this, I returned to my two creatures and, in silence, set out toward a farmhouse to have shelter for that night. Having withdrawn alone into a little room and seized by a heavy melancholy, I wept over it all night long. Before my eyes stood the great sufferings that still awaited me and, weeping, I said to my God:

— I do not weep, no, my Lord, for the suffering I see prepared for me. No, my God! I hold myself tightly to your cross, I love it with your love; but I do not know why I cannot restrain my tears. I love you! and if you wish to add still other torments, yes! increase them as much as you please! Your slave knows she can bear everything, provided that she bears the weight in you and with you.

But the weeping was choking me. When day came, I resolved to go to my God and to feed on Him, and to put an end to this human weakness. So, running, I made my way to my Beloved and asked to be strengthened. So it came about. Peaceful, resting in my God, I gave myself no thought about anything.

My voice:

— It is time to go away: to work!

Along the way I met good people who gave me many gifts, and I received them all with great indifference; I was able to relish nothing: my God alone made up everything in me. Tired, I sat down near a tree and fell asleep.

I saw in a dream the whole of hell, which was in turmoil; and those devils were plotting together how to seize the little boat of the Lord, and they made themselves sure of succeeding. One here and another there, they went about whispering that it should be taken from the land and thrown into the waves of a stormy sea, and so, swallowed by the ocean, should exist no longer. They were mistaken! Poor blind ones, used to seeing nothing but fire, their sight cannot see the light!

The ship was making great progress, the sea was favorable to her, she ran under full sail. From the little one she had been, she had become a very large ship and well fitted out, with strong armor to be able to defend herself from the enemy. She keeps gaining ground, she conquers many cities and towns. The enemy roars and every now and then manages to butt her with his horns: but nothing! she drives them back, because she is bound with iron. Ever victorious, she makes for great harbors and flies her flags: Suffering and Love! 82.

In certain harbors (the devil) makes an uproar, gets in among the workers and manages to steal one or another; but she never goes away with him: no! Poor creature, she remains an orphan, she drags out her life; but he does not trouble himself, because she cannot return to the gracious work of the Lord.

The snares they laid for me to catch me were something tremendous; but nothing frightened me; it was not my affair but my Master’s, from whom I also had all power over these ferocious devils. While I was going from one town to another and was half asleep from great weariness, enraged, they leap upon me, seize me and roughly throw me onto a rock, and there I remain alone. There was only a multitude of these beasts in front of me, mocking me. Oh! how loathsome they were! But I cared little or nothing about it; only I felt much pain from the blows I had received; but I did not want to let it be noticed that I was hurt. Wearied, I grew angry with them and (said to them):

— Go back to your chains, take yourselves out of my sight!

It was a spectacle. The sea was all in turmoil, it seemed a seaquake; the rocks were moving. It lasted minutes: something horrible happened. As if nothing had occurred, I remained on the rock. My God! I am cold and hungry, but I am happy to do your sweet will. As best I could I tried to pray; but every now and then: My Lord, are you still leaving me here?

Night was drawing near, nothing could be seen, a darkness…; only the murmur of the sea could be heard. I shall stay awake, for if I fall asleep, my God! I shall surely fall into the sea. Peaceful in my God. What mercy of my Master! as in a gentle ecstasy he carries me away. I felt that I was rising from the rock: two graceful angels had interlaced their wings and they carried me to dry land. I found myself near a cloister of his brides; at the first ring they came to open to me, and what a surprise! seeing me at that hour, they thought I had come on foot, and at once what charity they showed me! How grateful I felt! I asked them whether there was still long to wait before I could have Jesus.

— Oh! there is still too long.

— I beg you, take me there for a little while and then I will consent to rest.

This done, as soon as I was left alone, as I thought over what had happened to me, I felt an extreme need to thank God. Very softly I went back to the foot of the altar and with all I knew and with all the strength of my words I thanked God. Oh, surprise! who was there? a little friar of Paola, with a curl of black hair, and yet he was praying. I felt a great urge to observe him and to look at who he was.

— Oh! my Father, thank God for me and tell him to fill me soon with his love.

But as soon as I had said these words, he disappeared. 83.

Again among the young virgins who await her

— In search of sustenance for the brides of the Lord.

The emotion, the consolation was great, at the thought that that dwelling of the brides was surely pleasing to God; more than ever I felt I must thank the Most High for so great a mercy received in having admitted even me into the number of his handmaids. Having fed on the bread of angels: to work! But where?

In a brawl, some women without faith wanted to snatch away one of these creatures consecrated to God, to lead her back once more to where nothing but worldly scenes exist. I fought, but Jesus conquered! Those human hearts feel nothing but carnal affection: unhappy women!

Having set out on my way, where did I find myself? in that valley where I had promised to return the next day, for those dear creatures were waiting for me. Oh! on seeing me, what rejoicing! and with it a gentle reproach, because I had failed to keep my word. I calmed them, telling them that it was indeed true that I had promised them to come, but there was the clause: always provided it pleased God:

— I am not mistress, but slave of my Lord and, to tell you the truth, I am here because He himself sends me here.

— Then will it please him that we come together with you? Every evening we waited for you with terrible anxiety; we have suffered.

And they told me many things. I exclaimed:

— Well then, in the name of the Lord let us go, and let us hurry our steps so that no one may catch us.

So we did. Having arrived at the house of the Lord, I handed them over to the portress and happily left them.

Having gone back out to find human creatures who might help me to carry sustenance here and there, that going of mine was hard, because most of them shut the door in my face, hurling a storm of insults at me. But still I went to another: nothing! One woman was so enraged that she threw at me a big piece of wood she was holding in her hand. To all I said:

— Thank you, all the same! May God reward you.

How much walking, and nothing! The day was ending, night was drawing near, and I had found nothing. I took courage and went to the pastor. Alas, what a reproach! He would not even see me; he had me rebuked by the servant and then driven away. Going down the stairs I began to feel so happy, and I said:

— My Love! why did that servant not give me a slap? I would have been happier still.

Laughing, I went down the stairs; the doorkeeper, seeing me laugh like that, thought I had received some providence; he comes up to me:

— Give me something for my children.

— I have nothing!

Then he called me a bigot and a hypocrite, and began to shout. I tried to persuade him that I really had nothing:

— In the name of the Lord let me go, for I have received nothing and I have nothing. I entreated him so much that he was about to let me pass, but unfortunately his wife came out, and worse: how much she said to me! she would have liked to beat me, but I persuaded her by telling her to have pity on me and that, if she wanted my skirt, I would give it to her: I had nothing else. She stops and, moved with compassion, turning to her husband, says to him:

— You can see he gave her nothing.

She added further:

— But since it is late, surely during the day you will have collected something.

— Nothing, not even a crust of bread! Let me go, I beg you in the name of God.

— Go! — and with contempt they open for me.

Oh! may you be ever blessed, my Lord, who drew me out of so ugly a combat! I went round still a few dwellings where these lords of the world live, but nothing! Away! They called me a witch, they threw after me whatever they had in their hands. Seeing that it was night, I approached a convent of nuns, but they too had me sent away by their portress, although I had begged them to let me spend the night in a corner of that porter’s lodge.

— It is not possible!

Patience! I set off to reach a church and beg the sacristan to lock me inside, so that I might spend the whole night there. There was no chance. Jangling the keys loudly in my ear, he said to me:

— We are closing: away!

Without giving it a thought I went out. Jesus! will you leave me in the middle of one of these streets? I was sure that He would see to it.

A poor woman comes up to me and says to me:

— Whatever are you looking for at this hour?

— I am looking for a charitable soul who would be willing to lodge me, even in the stable with the animals.

— Where do you come from?

— From very distant roads I have come to find charity to bring to certain poor brides of the Lord, who live on the bread of alms.

— Who are you? — she added

— Oh! — I answered with a long sigh — a poor slave of the Lord!

She looked at me and then said to me:

— Come with me: I have only one room and one bed.

— Oh! be blessed a thousand times! Your charity will be rewarded.

We set off toward her poor dwelling. Oh! how many prayers I said along the road for this poor creature! Having arrived at the house, wonder! there was a table sumptuously laid, with exquisite refreshments. At the sight of them she cries out, both from joy and from surprise:

— Who, who has laid it out like this? Oh! how happy I am to have you!

— Whatever are you saying, good woman? It is I who see myself brought in by one with whom I do not deserve to be. Take me where you put the rubbish; that is enough for me.

This poor woman begins to weep:

— Either you come and eat with me or you will make me die of grief!

My voice:

— Satisfy her!

And so I did. I took only a little bread, because weariness prevented me from eating. And I thanked her. She wanted to leave me her room.

— Oh! that shall never be! God, good woman, will reward you just the same as if this wretch had accepted.

And I placed myself at the entrance of her room, where there was a small dark passage; and there I stayed praying all night: I prayed for my benefactress and for those who had made me suffer so much that day; and I thanked God for the great grace he had done me in sending me so good a creature who sheltered me.

While doing this, I remained in ecstasy; I felt a something in my soul, which was resting sweetly. Oh! what a soft bed! it was something delightful. So I passed the night without noticing it.

Returned to the world of miseries, full of strength and vigor, I would have fought against an army: so full did I feel of the strength of my God! I heard that the woman too was awake; I thanked her and went off to the church to receive my God early. So it came about. My voice, while I was making my thanksgiving:

— Go once more round the same way you went yesterday and ask alms for love of me.

So I did. What a wonder! those whom the day before I had found so haughty that they would have beaten me received me with such kindness, and I gathered great providence. After going round for two hours I had collected a great deal; and the voice of nature, which always feared meeting with blows, prompted me to go away; but my voice, which had sovereign dominion over all my faculties, (was against it):

— No! — I answered — My voice told me to go again all the way round that I went yesterday.

And so, running, I went all the way round again, and what I gathered was extraordinary, and I no longer knew where to put (the proceeds). I finished at nightfall. Some wanted to give me food, some lodging; I thanked them all very much, but I accepted nothing.

On the way, it was the last door left for me to ask at. It was already dark, and how afraid I was! But these too gave me alms. I was thinking how I should ever manage: and there, at the end of the street, was the good woman who was waiting for me. I thanked her and accepted the lodging as the night before, resting in the same way, except that she had me find in that corner a straw mattress and a pillow. I accepted a little bread; and then I was pained at having found that bed, because I feared I would no longer have the rest of the previous night. Having finished taking that refreshment, I went close to that bed; it was my intention not to lie down on it, but my voice (said to me):

— Lie down, for it is I who had it prepared. Patience! I said within myself, and I lay down. My voice:

— Why so unwillingly?

— My God, no!

I lay down, and I asked pardon and forgiveness of my God, after he had had such charity as to inspire that woman to prepare this for me. My sweet Love! Oh! you know why: I would have wished to spend this night like the last. This said, I remained absorbed in my God, and so I received great instructions.

She miraculously heals a sick woman; the voice: «Flee!» — She puts to flight the evildoers who had entered the church.

As soon as day broke, my longing was to have my Jesus and then to return to the workers to bring them the providence I had gathered; but a servant of a most distinguished noble lady (told me) that, before leaving, I should go to his mistress. What can she want? After being strengthened with the bread of angels, I went.

What a wonder! she was gravely ill. She embraced me and said to me:

— Do not let me die!

My God! if I were a good creature, I would say that I would have hoped in my prayers; but at once I blushed.

— What can I do, poor slave! only serve you as best I can.

— That is what I desire — she answered me.

With how rough a manner I tried to make myself refined in order to serve her delicately! I sought every means. I remembered that the workers are always directed by Saint Anne, and I proposed to her that she should make a great promise to this Mother, for I had much hope in it. This done, I took her blessed water. Oh! prodigy of the great Mother Saint Anne: she was healed instantly! The promise of a vow was made: her daughters had other fields to cultivate.

But this event spread at once, and many would have wanted some of the water. I began to tremble, all dismayed, because I did not know where I was. My God had compassion on me; my voice:

— Flee! (61).

So I did. No one noticed it and, running, I went off to the poor workers. I went into the poor hovel where I used to withdraw when I came back from begging and where my voice sent me. So it happened. In the middle of the night, my voice:

— Get up, and very quietly go and see what is happening. The evildoers have got in and are trying to get into my temple.

At once I hurried there and found it was true; but on hearing that there were people about, they fled and could do nothing to that temple, nor to the brides of the Lord.

What weariness! how I felt myself fainting! I stayed at the feet of my God, waiting for the hour to come when I could possess him; and meanwhile I told him that I felt very unwell and that he should make haste to come, because I felt my strength failing. Inwardly I had a great longing to rest. Having my Love with me, forgetful of everything and even of myself, I told him all that I had done. I would offer you my sufferings, but I am ashamed, because compared with yours, which you suffered for me, I feel myself all full of shame. Oh my angel Saint Michael! adorn a little what I suffer and what I have suffered and done, and then you, if you think fit, carry it to the feet of the Lord. Oh! how happy I would be if he laid it upon his most holy feet! But I do not find myself worthy enough to be offered to the Majesty of a God.

I was attending to some business when unknown people came to torment me. Taken unawares, I was frightened and cried aloud: Help! without reflecting on what I was doing. Thus troubled, I grew agitated and did not know what course to take. After reflecting for an instant, I began to defend myself boldly: how they took to flight! And I was left free, with only the thought that my God had given me the strength of a giant and a convincing word. Oh! my Love! — I began to say, in the midst of the work I went on doing — as you made Balaam’s ass speak, so you are pleased to make your slave speak (cf. Num 22:28).

Accused before a most severe judge, who treats her harshly, on account of a worker.

While I was reasoning thus, my voice interrupts me, commanding me to go where certain unknown people were molesting a flock of good and innocent ewe-lambs and wanted to steal several of them. Without further thought I leave everything and set out where I saw the way traced out for me. Having arrived where these wretched people truly were, as if I had come from a sumptuous banquet, I set about driving away those ugly ones and putting the flock back in order, by changing its guard and giving it again a faithful keeper.

While I was standing still, leaning against a stone, I was severely rebuked by very eminent persons; and one of these sent me to a most severe judge who, badly informed, abused me horribly over certain accusations which, truly, I do not know where they could have got them from. For a few moments I remained speechless, and then I begged him to have patience and listen to me; but it was something curious: all because they were defending a worker who had barbarously withdrawn from the field and was strongly protected by the pastors.

This finished, I went to another, and yet from him, rudely, I received certain answers…! My God! — I kept saying — it is nothing compared with what you suffered!

At last, tired, I went back to my poor cottage and, throwing myself on the ground weeping, I begged mercy of my God. Everything was dark bronze for me; I walked in perfect darkness and found new stumbling-blocks, oppressed by a thousand sorrows.

A summons from another pastor, that I should go to that trial. And so, running, I set out. But what a surprise! The unhappy woman was coming out from the judge victorious, and was strutting about in the midst of her protectors. I huddled under a portico and stood there all trembling. I forced myself and prayed my Crucified One to help me, because I felt myself fainting.

Having reached the judge with difficulty, oh! how I trembled! The calumnies, the horrible inventions I heard! My God! how will this so cruel persecution end? I no longer even knew how to answer, because they were of a curious entanglement. And he let me go free, telling me that he would come together with others to defend that unhappy woman. It was not long in coming true; and first a pastor came with a world of pretences; he wanted to make me believe certain invented lies, so that the very gestures he made were of an exaggeration without equal; he would abase himself to nothing with the protestations he made; he would have liked to persuade me that for me he would have sacrificed anything whatever.

On the following day, what was my surprise! he was together with the other judges and, his character entirely changed, but ferocious, he insulted me more than ever in a quite singular way; he had the support of the others and made himself very strong. Having had the unhappy woman brought before me, crowning her with laurels and completely absolving her, satisfying her in all she desired, they condemned me. Oh! my sweet Love! Then indeed I was glad, thinking that you too, my God, were set below Barabbas! And with cheerfulness I stood before the judges, full of consolation, offering them my wretched service in the small refreshment they took. Within myself I was happy. My dear Crucified One! they only condemned me to give what they thought fit, but I was not condemned to death like you. They insulted me, and I tried to imitate you in doing good to her.

One of these, after several days, came back to my poor cottage and asked my pardon, telling me to forget what he had done to me. Oh! whatever is this, my God! No one came to ask your pardon, neither Annas nor Caiaphas nor Pilate, and why do you allow them to ask it of me?

But the struggle was not yet over, because the others still sought to oppress me, especially one who was very ferocious. At last his turn came, and he was able to vent himself to his satisfaction, and he left me in a very bad way with his ill treatment. He took to flight, shouting all the while. I was left spellbound; the people who saw him so furious were left spellbound too, and they asked one another: whatever is this man doing? for what reason? Other workers were weeping over it, and I tried to raise their spirits with jokes and laughter, thinking that he must have needed to vent himself and that, if it was a good for him, it was good too that it had happened. My voice: A day will come when you will have to do good to this man who persecutes you so much; but he will always remain with a hardened heart. He believes that no one does better than he; he is persuaded of it and lives convinced of it.

I suffered much in seeing how he treated the poor workers, and still more the vineyard of the Lord: he always despised it as if nothing but weeds had grown there; he saw its fruits and I can say that he relished them, judging them excellent, and yet he would never have given it any help. If this happened, it was entirely the work of his master who, grateful, wished at least to bless some of those large fields; but this man always dragged him out and sought every invention to keep him away. What a terrible aversion! One can never manage to believe that in this land of labor there can be creatures so ungrateful for the good received; and yet, in the vast field of the Lord, unfortunately there are some. My voice, while I was reasoning:

— And how many of them I had when I preached to my ungrateful people!

I stopped to think and to weigh well these holy words and, after a long while, I answered:

— Oh! how I must always complain!

I almost felt in me a something of displeasure because I could not manage to obtain that all should correspond to the great benefits of the Lord. I began to say:

— My God, how am I to conduct myself?

My voice:

— Always do as much good as possible to your neighbor, without caring whether they will correspond or not. Never judge and accuse your brother of ingratitude: always seek to excuse all the actions of others. 84. Take with you a good worker and go into that field, where there is need to straighten some plant that is bending badly.

A dream about the number of persons who think only of themselves.

Without delay, I went into that field and at once set myself to straightening the plants. My voice:

— Remove the one that stands near that wall: it holds a poison within, which is deadly to anyone who should unhappily taste it.

I was not slow to obey. Tired, I sat down on a heap of earth, without heeding that night was drawing near. I fell asleep and, in my sleep, I was reasoning keenly on how there can be creatures who make their good consist in themselves alone. A great personage presents himself to me and shows me how such beings are the majority, and that even among his handmaids there are some of these. I asked him who he was and whom he meant by his handmaids. He was silent.

— Why do you not let me see your face clearly? — I, still in my dream — Handmaids? This name is given to the brides of the Lord, to his handmaids, but I cannot believe that you are my Lord, because your voice is new to me and does not satisfy me at all.

— I said that among the sisters too there are such beings!

I gave a shriek and said:

— I understand you well! I tell you to go away from me, for you have nothing to do here: those you seek are not here.

Oh! how he was taken aback! In an ugly and angry tone he said to me:

— You will find out whether I am telling the truth.

— And how? — I answered him, still in my dream — you never tell the truth, because you are a liar (cf. Jn 8:44).

Oh! he flew into a rage and gave me a hard blow of the fist on the forehead, which shook me, and I woke up in much pain. It did not seem to me that I had slept, no, but rather that I had struggled with that dragon which was tormenting me so ferociously. I set myself to ponder who he could be and what he had told me, that is: that such persons were with me too and that I would find out. I thought about it seriously: can it really be true? He is a liar, but many times he is also forced to tell the truth. So it seems to me good to make a thorough review of it. And without heeding anything else I set myself to investigate.

What a surprise! I found not one, but rather a number large enough that I had to teach them with care to change course, because their path was entirely wrong. With great agitation I sought to remove this real damage and to clear out thoroughly what was most spoiled, leaving the threshing-floor clean.

Order to go to the harbor, where she will know the will of God.

My voice:

— Do not heed your weariness, but go near that harbor: there you will know the will of God.

Tired, exhausted, without provisions of any kind, I set out toward that harbor of which my voice had told me; but when I was a third of the way there my strength failed me and I had to take refuge in a cottage. Having arrived with difficulty, I fell seriously ill. My God! might it be that that voice was not mine, which always guides me? I was hesitating thus, when to this perplexity of mine another fact was added: a holy soul, who had much light and whom I had found by experience never to have been wrong in anything she had foretold me at other times, 85, came close to me and told me that in that place through which I had to pass there were people waiting for me to kill me.

— How? — I said to her — In that harbor I know no one; I do not see how there can be persons concerning themselves with me.

She answered:

— And yet I assure you that there are, and they are waiting for you, because they know to a nicety the hour of your arrival.

I was greatly shaken and felt myself urged to turn back. Meanwhile the illness increased and the agitation of the fever grew ever greater.

— Do I go or not? — I kept repeating to myself — No, I am not going! Surely this is a trick of the enemy.

I spent days so painful and agitated that I never managed to gain calm and strength. At last, having recovered from the illness, I called the holy creature to me and frankly asked her what I ought to do. She looked at me and in a resolute tone said to me:

— Either you resolve to go, or all the workers who are on the other side of the harbor will be forced to come away, all of them. You think about it!

Sadly I answer her:

— But if they kill me, it seems to me that it will be worse.

She:

— No! God will see to it!

— Do you assure me?

— Yes!

Without heeding anything further, strengthened by the eucharistic food, I undertook the journey together with her. When we drew near, behold a storm with rain and wind. I look at her and say to her:

— What shall we do?

Oh! my Love! What does she answer me?

— What God inspires you to do.

— Let us go!

Here we are at the harbor. The sea was rough, the rain (continued). Again I asked her what I ought to do. For answer I received:

— What you feel inspired to do.

Without knowing what I was doing, I find myself with my foot on the boat and, as soon as we had both got in, the boat casts off and swiftly carries us to the other harbor. Never did my mind have the thought that I must meet those people who, she had told me, would kill me: nothing! The holy soul stayed as close to me as one who guards something precious. I begged her to let me go for a moment, for I would come back at once. She, with entreaties, begged me to be patient, for I would get off at another stop, as at that one it was not advisable. And it never came into my mind that there was the fatal point for me: nothing! As soon as we had moved away, this holy soul said to me:

— We are out of it!

And with a great sigh she rejoiced at it. Then there came back into my mind what she had told me and all that I had gone through. Oh! how I blessed God for it! And I admired his ordering and how much he had done in me. I could have wept bitterly at the thought of how a God orders and makes one act without one’s knowing what one is doing. He, by an act of his divine will, removes from the mind the most important things, calms one in dangers, gives action to the person, making her go where his will is to be fulfilled.

Very peacefully I arrived at a cottage, in a very poor state, because I had suffered much and felt that I was about to faint. This truly happened. I let myself go and spent the whole night between spasms and failing of life. I commended myself earnestly to my Crucified One that he might give me strength. There was a moment when I felt my soul detaching itself, and I thought I was taking refuge in the side of my Savior, weeping:

— My God! do not leave me: I feel that I am dying!

For a good while I understood nothing; I was only in a sweetness of paradise. When I was roused: Where am I? My Crucified One:

— You are with me! You have suffered much, and this was needed. Recover yourself and work, for there is much to be done!

XI

To work with renewed vigor; but the weight of humanity must be felt.

Full of vigor, all cheerful and as if nothing had happened to me, I set myself to work. The workers I had with me looked at me and did not understand how it could be and where I could have taken so much strength and vigor. While working, every now and then I thought to myself about what had happened to me, and I looked at what strength I had. Oh! how your power gives life to the dead!

Meanwhile my mind (was) enlightened about all that I had to do. I accomplished great things with swiftness, and it was curious: when the poor workers saw me so well, they were amazed. Within myself I said: they are right, because I too feel that I am living another life, so strong.

I put fields and cottages in order. I found much to struggle with pastors who had nested themselves in certain farmhouses, so that strength was needed to make them come out. Their power was great, but the arm of the Lord rendered them powerless to revolt; rather, they went away taciturn, contenting themselves only with grumbling. What work in the Majesty of a God! He makes lions become sheep, he subjects them to the judgment of one of his slaves, giving force to her word. The poor men, confounded, come out and go elsewhere to pitch their tents.

Such was the work I did that no creature could keep up with me. With the strength of my God, oh! certainly no human creature could compete with me, it could not! In this way I made haste to put the workers in order and to receive other fields to cultivate.

This strength lasted me a long time, when one fine day, while I was putting some work in order, I feel my strength failing. I had to sit down on some tangles of grass, and so, silent, I looked at the work. My voice:

— It is time to take up the work again with human strength alone!

Whatever can it mean?

— Speak to me more clearly!

As soon as I had uttered this, I understood everything: that human nature had to act, and so it behoved me to submit to taking food and rest. I leaned against a wall and began to weep: My God, why have you withdrawn your grace from me and abandoned me? Perhaps I have not corresponded as was pleasing to you? So great was my sorrow that, getting up, I ran to throw myself, where? into a heap of thornbushes! And I fainted. The sharp thorns pierced my whole body; several remained inside, because they had broken while going in. But I felt nothing, because I had lost my senses.

My angel Saint Michael took me by the hand and pulled me out of that bramble-bush. Once I was out, I came to, exhausted. I looked at him. He sat me down and told me not to doubt, that I had done everything well and that my God was most pleased with the fulfillment of his will. If he had so ordained, it was nothing other than his good pleasure that I should return to feeling the weight of humanity.

She washes her wounds in the water and makes it wholesome.

Meanwhile the thorn-pricks gave me most acute pains. I told him that I was suffering greatly from the wounds inflicted on me. He looked at me with a glance of compassion and, taking me by the hand, in a flight he carries me near a great stream of crystal-clear water, and said to me:

— Refresh your wounds in this water and you will be healed. He disappeared. I felt so ill! At once I went near the stream and bathed the wounds, which, as soon as they were bathed, healed. And those thorns that had remained inside the flesh came out, and the hole remained healed.

I still had to bathe my right arm, when I hear a tramping of feet. I turn round: it was a pastor running toward me. I covered my arm and, without letting it be noticed what I was doing, I began to drink. He, in a loud voice, said to me what was I doing, that I should not drink, that that was bad water. I answered nothing and went on drinking. Then he grows angry, comes up to me and asks me whether I was doing this out of despair, wishing to bring death on myself.

— Oh! — I answered him then — quite the contrary: if I drank of this sweet water, it is to have life and health.

He stopped and said to me:

— Who are you?

I answered him:

— A poor slave of the Lord.

And he:

— From which direction do you come?

— I do not know!

— How do you come to be here?

Seeing that he was asking me so many questions, I got up to go away, although I had an ardent desire and need to bathe my arm, which hurt me so much. But he began to say that if he had told me this, not to drink, it was because all those who drank of that water died; since I was a stranger, charity required that he should warn me. He added further whether I had drunk much of it. I answered him resolutely:

— As much as I needed.

And he looked at me. Poor man! he was waiting for the effect. I wanted to move away to see whether this man would go away, and then to return to heal my arm. But he gets up too and comes to accompany me. Then I told him frankly that I had no need of his company. And I looked to see whether I had set my foot properly on my path. I noticed that there was no path at all; and I stopped, turned toward where the torrent was, and what a surprise! Nothing could be seen any more: it had dried up. My arm! I thought at once. And he, grumbling all the while, stood near me. Oh! what astonishment, when he too noticed that the torrent had dried up! He gave a cry:

— Oh! how can it be? For so many years there was this terrible scourge for our village, where so many souls were lost, which has always brought such terror: now it exists no longer!

— Oh! — I went on — why so much uproar? Rather let us seek to thank God for so great a mercy that he willed to show you.

He looked at me, begging me to tell him who I am, where I came from… Then he showed me his desire that I too should go to the foot of the altar to thank the Lord.

— Yes! — I answered him — How happy I am to be able to come where my Master is!

In haste we reached the church, and all together we thanked God. The hour was late and this pastor wanted me to stay at his house; but I refused and went to take refuge with a poor woman.

Meanwhile I desired nothing but the moment when I could at least take the thorns out of my arm. I was thinking how I would do it; the pain was growing. At last, alone in that little corner, as best I could I tried to see the thorns and remove them. But a good number had gone in so deeply that there was no way. The weariness, the exhaustion, the acute pain I felt were such that I fainted.

A good vocation: the treasure of Poverty.

After a long while I came to and heard knocking. Who was it? the poor woman bringing me something to eat.

— How is it — I said to her — that you are here? who sends you?

— What? was it not you yourself who came to my bed and begged me to give you a little to eat, saying that you were coming with me?

— Oh! thanks be given you for it, good woman! God will repay you this charity of yours.

While I was eating, she was looking at me. Within myself I was thinking how my Lord had acted thus toward that woman so that she might come to my help; and I thanked him with all my soul. And I desired nothing but the moment when she would go away, so that I could speak freely to my God and thank him; but she did not move. I begged her to withdraw and go to rest, thanking her infinitely; but no. She told me that her heart could not go away, because she saw me too ill; that she could not leave me. And she began to weep. I tried to comfort her and said many things to her so that she would tell me the cause of her weeping. She revealed to me all that she had never said, and I obtained that she should abandon everything and follow me, giving all her possessions to the poor and to the Lord.

Oh goodness of a God! what mercy! With resolute spirit she told me she wished to follow me. And at once, heeding nothing, she set out on the way with me. When we arrived at a poor cottage, what was my distress, because I feared greatly, thinking that at the sight of so much poverty she would be dismayed. I was mistaken, because she fell so much in love with this treasure of poverty that she rejoiced to possess it.

Oh! how you know how to change hearts, my God, from riches to want, and you give them such relish for it that they cannot help loving it! Oh yes! I find no word more fitting for this Poverty than to call it a treasure. One must taste it to be able to say something of its exquisiteness. Oh! all riches and grandeurs cannot be compared with the beauty and exquisiteness of this dear Poverty: only one who knows how to taste it can say how pleasing it is.

A short time after she had been bound by vows to the dear Crucified One, she became a good worker, a handmaid of the Lord; she went through many fields, and fine cultivations have come of it under her supervision.

She saves a cottage from ruin — A comforting dream.

I left that part so well ordered and went where there were certain risings of workers, which only the hand of a God could curb. But my voice said to me:

— Run with all the strength you have, so as to arrive in time to stop people who have made up their minds to go in there, to put every creature to flight and, in the end, to take possession of everything.

While I walked I was thinking: whatever can it be? how? and what will come of it? In short my mind was traveling a thousand miles. Having arrived at the cottage, I found people there who at my arrival grew agitated and fled this way and that. For fear that they would carry off the workers from me, I stopped at the door and was able to stop these wretched women, who were about to be carried away.

I locked it with a thousand bolts and began to say to them: whatever were they doing? had they forgotten that there was a God, to whom they had to give account of all they had laid waste; and would they still have had the boldness to commit the final crime of abandoning his walls? And where would they go? And the grace that God had done them in leading them into his dwelling and placing them truly in a state of such loftiness? is it thus that you correspond to it? Oh my God! forgive them, for pity’s sake: they do not understand what they are doing!

They looked at me with a certain manner so contemptuous, as if they wanted to tell me that I was wearying them. One could see an agitation in them, and it clearly appeared that their minds were thinking of joining others, with whom they had not been able to go together when I arrived. What sorrow! what blindness! poor creatures, how wrapped they are in cloths of little lasting! I commended myself to God that he might give my words the power to persuade them.

I stopped, and so I stood in silence; but these women were plotting among themselves in low voices. I grew angry and in a loud voice ordered them to stop it, otherwise I would find the means to bring them to their duty. They were frightened and did not even dare to move. Seeing this, I took heart and more forcefully than ever made them see their blindness.

When I noticed that they were beginning to be convinced, I sweetened my words again and sought to make them penetrate into their hearts, and so to remove the things that had been put there, which had reduced the hearts of these wretched women to so bad a state.

They surrendered and, with great consolation, I saw them once more given, with sincere and repentant spirit, all to God in his Work. Oh mercy of my God! with what goodness and patience he waits for the sinner! What would man have done had he seen so ugly a betrayal? Without doubt they would have been condemned immediately.

Having finished the reordering, I lay down to rest on a little straw, because my limbs could no longer stand. Weaker than ever, I fell asleep, dreaming that in that hovel where I was there were holy souls who were guarding that flock. Roused, I looked all around: I saw nothing. Without thinking that they might be in other cells, I fell asleep once more. The same dream; awake again, I never felt the strength to go and look. I made a movement of my head, looking around. Fallen asleep once more, more than the other times the same dream seized me strongly: that in this cottage there are good souls who keep watch and pray.

At this word, «pray», I got up and at once went to the little church. Oh! what a surprise! a servant of God, who had been dead for several years, was kneeling near an altar with joined hands, and was praying. Oh! — I said to myself — I have understood how those women surrendered and how this cottage has been saved! He disappeared after a few minutes, and I was left so consoled, thinking that it was well guarded and sure that it would lack no help in anything.

On the bed of suffering we are all equal: the great and the poor.

Having set myself to pray with great fervor, I thanked my God and waited anxiously for the hour soon to come when I could receive him within this breast of his, for I possessed nothing of my own. After remaining a long time with my God, my voice makes me understand that it was no longer time to stay, but that I should go to one who was very ill.

I obeyed and in a flight went to help those who were moaning. I found poor creatures all numb with cold, who aroused compassion; moreover they were very grave, because lacking assistance. It was heartbreaking to see them. Having made them as comfortable as I could, given them comforts, raised their spirits, they all seemed reborn to a new life.

For those sick for whom there was no longer any remedy, it only remained first to seek the comfort of the soul and then to save them and exhort them to resignation, encouraging them that soon they would enjoy the fruit of their resignation and of the sufferings that my God sent them. How I tried to make them see this passage as sweet and beautiful, like one who undertakes a journey to go and see a delightful city!

And so I succeeded in raising up those spirits made fearful by the approach of death. They conversed with me about how they would carry out the errands I gave them: that they should ask my God for pity and mercy for me, that they should greet my holy protectors for me.

— Oh! when you see the majestic sovereign Queen of heaven, pray to her for me!

They were so enthusiastic that they no longer thought of fearful death, but only of making acts of love and of repentance, so as to be able, with these, to pass quickly from the antechamber of purgatory to the beautiful heavenly homeland.

A pastor comes up to me and says to me:

— Oh! is this the gracious way of preparing these unfortunates, who deserve it so little?

— Oh! — with a proud look I say to him — What? are these not creatures of my God? If they are rough and ignorant and sinners, they too have a soul, which must be united to its center. Is it perhaps necessary to comfort only the rich? and do they alone have a humanity that deserves to be relieved? and will they not have sinned too, as unfortunately I too have sinned, poor slave? Oh! how badly these words sound to me! On the bed of suffering, which is preparing us for the great journey, we are all equal: the great, the poor, we all need succor and help. For these poor creatures it is harder than for the rich man to find succor and relief.

He fell silent, and looked at me with surprise because I was carrying out all that had been given me to do so that (a poor sick man), joyful and contrite, might fly to eternal rest. And my two good creatures entrusted to him I kept with me; there were too many of these unfortunates. Having tidied up, we tried to find a small bed where we could lie down; none was found, and these creatures were tired. I found one and thought it right to give it up to these creatures.

At last, exhausted, I lay down where a woman had died a little before. Oh! it suited me well, for I had so great a desire to lie down. I stayed on this loathsome bed two hours. When I was in deep sleep, a moan wakes me: it was a poor woman seeking help, having a terrible disease: leprosy!

Without looking further at what it was, I ran to help her and embraced her, to relieve her from the throes of the disease; and I called the good chaplain, so that he might give her the last comforts of Holy Church.

This good religious came and, on seeing that I was holding her in my arms to relieve her, cried out that I should withdraw from so fierce a disease. But what! I answered him not to fear. Meanwhile she expired, comforted by the Lord, for she carried him with her in her breast.

But what the charitable priest had said came true to a nicety: the disease showed itself in me and I fell ill. I was dying, when an angel, or better a soul of the Lord, came to heal me. I regained my strength, and my voice ordered me to leave and go to a field, where there were flowers and laurel to be woven». 86.

Refreshed and guided by Saint Michael the Archangel.

Without caring for myself at all, I went searching to find what my voice had told me. Night falls and still nothing is to be seen. What, have I been mistaken? I was weak and felt a fierce need to take food; neither farmhouses nor churches could be seen. Alone! From exhaustion I began to weep:

— My angel Saint Michael, ah! come and help me! Leaning against a big tree, I stood weeping. In this position I fell asleep. A gentle voice wakes me. Who was it? A heavenly messenger who was bringing me bread in a basket.

— Oh! dear angel! tell me, who has sent you?

— God.

— But I — I said with a great sigh — how gladly I would long to be nourished by Him alone!

And I did not dare to take the bread. He, peacefully, exhorts me to eat. I took the bread, kissed it and then, kneeling, set myself to eat it. Oh my Love! from you comes this treasure! And then, turning to the messenger, I said to him: When he sent me this bread, did he bless it? Tell me: what did he tell you to say to me? nothing?

He answered:

— That you should eat!

— But — I answered — I am not at all satisfied: I want Him! And I began to weep, and he comforted me.

When I had finished eating, he gave me some water to drink: it was a most exquisite liqueur. I did not notice that it was night: nothing! The moon was most resplendent. He began to say: — It is necessary to set out on the way.

— Well then, will you do me the charity of accompanying me?

He answered:

— Certainly, that is my charge.

I gave a great sigh: Oh my God! I want you, I want you!

He answered:

— Let us hasten our steps, for in a few hours you will find him.

So it was. As soon as dawn came, the sound of bells was heard. But on this journey he instructed me with sweet discourses, giving me so much knowledge: how the soul in union with God is blissful, is nourished… Oh! how those hours passed for me! I felt no weariness at all. Oh! if only day had never come!

As soon as the church came into sight, he disappeared. I went into the temple of my God and found myself wholly in Him. I asked him whether the voice that sent me on this journey was his ordinance. He answered me:

— Yes! and today you will find the field.

Difference between the love of God and that of creatures.

I would never have departed from this temple; but it was his will that I should go away from it. So, without further remark, I set out. After walking two hours and more, behold what the voice had told me. Oh magnificence! it was something delightful. I went on into fields of various and varied flowers; many graceful young women vied with one another to offer me some. I accepted many; but I always kept in mind the word: «You will find flowers and laurel to weave». What am I to do? — I kept saying to myself. And these women brought me more and more. There was laurel. One of them, older and more courageous, said to me:

— See all these fields, how beautiful they are and so full of flowers!

— Yes — I answered her.

— Well, for not knowing how to weave them, once gathered they wither and become foul-smelling.

— Oh! — I added — Why do you not try to give them to Jesus?

— You tell us how we must do it.

— Let us make a weaving and give it to that church which has a field attached, but a poor one; the farmhouse where the poor workers are is in so bad a state that those poor women live there wretchedly.

These creatures stood listening to me.

— Very well! — they said to me — weave as many as you like, take them to those creatures, and likewise for the church you speak of.

I was not slow to set to work. And they helped me with great pleasure. How happy I felt, because I was making great things with those bunches. I took a quantity of laurel.

— This — I said — is for you, who with such generosity help the poor and the brides of the Lord, as well as his church. You will be crowned with laurel for an eternity. And I shall study to weave it very well, putting into it all the skill that my Master will give me.

One of these, who more than the others kept silent, comes up to me and says to me:

— Could I not also learn together with you the same lessons that your Master gives you?

— Oh! yes, certainly! He — I began to say — is all to all, and he rejoices greatly when a creature shows herself desirous to learn. Yes, come with me and you will see how you will learn to weave roses and lilies… I was forgetting the laurel: more than anything my Jesus cares for this, and how graceful is its weaving!

Without thinking, carried away with joy, I exclaimed: My Love! My Love! Spellbound, she said to me:

— But how is this, when just now you told us that you are alone and a slave of the Lord?

— And what you say is true — I answered her — Is he not my God, my Love?

— What? — she went on, as though I had blasphemed — you speak of love?

— Yes, my God is all love for his creatures.

I noticed that she was entirely unversed in this matter, and I begged her to listen to me. Meanwhile all the others gathered around me, and I instructed them on all the points of our holy Religion, going on to make known to them the difference between the love of God and that of creatures; that the heart of the creature has need of love and how, for not knowing the sublimity of the love of God, they love creatures. In the love of God lies the whole divine essence, and it has neither limits nor end; that of creatures is deceitful and soon vanishes, it withers like the rose plucked from the plant and set in the sun: one sees in the open the disillusionment of the perishable things of the earth; but the love of my God, Master and Lord, blazes ever more in the heart of the creature and at last, with its rays, carries it away and consumes it in his most sweet divine ether. Oh yes, Love!

I cannot describe the effects these words of mine produced in the hearts of these poor creatures. The one who more than all was touched by grace said to me:

— I am coming with you! Let us gather all my share of this field and take it with us.

The others gave me a great deal, entreating me to return as soon as possible. Having taken my leave together with that dear creature, we brought those treasures to the farmhouse and to the church. Oh Love! She learned so well to love, and she came to be loved by my Good! She was a rose just blossomed into a graceful white lily, which under the shade of purity had been kept for the most pure heart of Jesus. She was not slow to taste the delicacies of the Bridegroom, and by deeds she could better teach what she experienced of them. She did great works with all those varied treasures, and she kept the fields of the Lord very well for me. The workers increased, to the astonishment of all. Who was working? My Master! in appearance there was the creature, but in reality it was the Creator who gave the direction and beautified the work.

«It is I who guide your steps» — My Good: your words are unchangeable!

My voice:

— Leave her in charge of the field and go elsewhere: there you will find a good and zealous pastor who will hand over his flock to you.

I set out on my way, and kept repeating to myself: wherever can it be? why, dear voice, do you not tell me where this pastor is? while you have such goodness as to teach me, do you send me thus groping? What distress I feel for fear of going wrong! My voice:

— This cannot be, because it is I who guide your steps!

At this answer I prostrated myself on the ground and, with arms open in the sign of the cross, I gave thanks to the Most High. I began to recite the prayer of the most holy Virgin and, swifter than ever, quickened my pace. Having arrived at the foot of a cliff, there was no longer any way of going forward. I would have climbed up had I been able to clamber, but I had to stop without moving. I did not complain, nor did I think of where I was: nothing! I sat down and, all joyful, (said):

— My Good, your words are unchangeable!

I was full of faith that my God would, even in an instant, have turned that mountain into a royal and delightful plain. Night comes; the torrent that divides the road from the mountain swells: and nothing! I begin to feel a commotion.

Still motionless, I took a few stones and made a seat of them as best I could. It grew darker and darker. With my Crucified One pressed to my breast, I peacefully fell asleep.

A loud rumble woke me. They were black figures, which I could see precisely because of their blackness, although it was late at night without a moon; but in that brightness of the clear sky objects could be fairly well distinguished. One of these shadows, the tallest, came close to me and told me to go with him, for he would lead me to a pleasant cottage where there were gracious people waiting for me.

— Who are you? — I said to him calmly.

— I am a man of that house, which came to know that you are here alone and, through the charity of those persons, I was sent here.

— Liar! go away!

— No! — he answered me — You are deceived. The voice that told you it was with you is I; I will give you proofs of it: if you do not come with me I will make you see the truth!

I answered him in a severe tone:

— Buffoon! go away! for in the name of my God I will make you see what faith works.

He began to sneer, mocking me:

— Faith! — he kept repeating to me — Split this mountain, then!

— I shall certainly do it! — I said to him. And he:

— Before you can do that, I with all my followers will undo you and carry you off with us.

— I tell you — I said to him — to withdraw!

Meanwhile, I hear a troop of others arriving. I got up and said to him:

— Now you will see!

I commanded the mountain, in the name of God, to level a road for me to climb. And behold, the road appears, broad and beautiful, from the bottom to the top. These, terrified, looked at me; turning to them, I said: — All of you who wanted to be rid of me! You are not permitted to touch a single hair of mine. Go back to your chains.

A group of creatures guided by a pastor of good zeal, but inept.

They hurled themselves down and I saw them no more. The waters of the river too made way for me. On a delightful day I was gently climbing the mountain. When I was halfway up I met certain creatures all dressed in uniform. They were alone. I stopped them and asked them where they were going. Arrogantly they answer me:

— Where we please!

— Very well, dear creatures. Forgive me if I have been too bold; but I know that on these roads there are evildoers and that, being so alone, you will be afraid and could have real troubles.

They stop and say to me:

— Who are you?

— Dear creatures — I answered — I am a poor slave.

— Oh! what? — they said — in these parts of ours we have no slaves.

— What are you saying? — I answered them — I do not believe it! A small altercation followed, curious in its way. Vexed, one of them said: — Whose slave are you?

— My God’s.

— Ah! we understand: she must be a pious bigot, a companion of our pastor!

— What are you saying! — I added — Where do you have this pastor? And they paint me a picture of him in their own way: they call him a cretin, ignorant, capable of nothing but praying.

— Oh! how fine! — I added — what? does he not give you instruction? does he not make you sociable creatures? From what I see in you, your spirit would tend toward family and society. What a pity!

And here I made myself appear wholly of their party. Meanwhile, with indifference, I wished to continue on my way; but these, eager to hear me speak and seeing themselves humored, begged me to allow them to accompany me.

— Yes — I answered them — very willingly, so we shall be able to speak of something beautiful. Meanwhile, would you kindly tell me whether your dwelling is far.

They answered me that it was near.

But are you alone?

— Oh! we were many, but because of that great sanctimonious fellow!… If you knew what has happened…

— Oh! tell me, and if I can be of service to you in anything I will do it with pleasure.

My God, help me! I kept repeating within myself. What horrid things did they not do! and these too were setting out in search of finding another shelter that might please them more. That poor shepherd was truly a good soul, but what he wished to do was not called for by God; he acted only out of zeal; he lacked the compass to be able to navigate. And they went on telling me. Every so often I interrupted them in order to know what lay in their souls.

— Here — they tell me — we are almost there.

And they beg me to sit down, because they wish to tell me everything. I consent. When they had finished their sorrowful and unseemly story, I began to say to them:

— Tell me frankly: if that shelter took another form and came to be furnished with good persons who would impart to you learning and doctrine, would you be content to remain there?

— Certainly, we would be most happy, oh! — they all went on saying — and we would believe that there is a God.

— Oh! poor me! whatever are you saying? — I added.

— You must know — so they said — that it is despair that forces us to speak in this way.

I rise and say to them:

— Well then: promise to follow me and to behave well, and I will put you in a position to be good and instructed, so that you may earn your bread and live honestly.

They all kneel down and make protestations of obedience and submission.

— Tell us, — they say to me — and what will you do about that shepherd?

— Leave the thinking and the acting to me, and the firmness to yourselves. And we set out toward that house.

I found that shepherd weeping, because they had all fled from him and only an old warden (had remained), who grumbled about it with all her might. This poor man, on seeing me together with these little runaway sheep of his, blessed me and left everything in my power to do and undo. I sent the old woman away and kept the promise I had made to these runaways, who were not slow to leave off thinking of the fine world and, trampling upon each and every thing, learned to love God and to live and die for Him alone.

The God of mercies is a most severe judge.

20 January 1892.

Absorbed in deep meditation on the Passion of my Lord, I passed swiftly to the mercy of God toward man. I found myself plunged into an abyss and felt wholly pressed together, as though in that abyss every fault were to be scattered: I rejoiced at it! When all of a sudden the vision changed into the justice of God. How can I describe this? The smallest imperfections are written and portrayed before one. The God of mercies is a most severe judge! I trembled from head to foot; a strong inner agitation made me incapable of recovering myself in the thought of mercy. No! wretched me! Forgetful of every created thing and of myself, I thought of one thing alone, and this occupied all my mental faculties: my Love as Judge! I felt myself shuddering all over and I wept bitterly. My voice:

— Why do you let yourself be carried away so meanly?

Full of shame, I asked God’s forgiveness for it, and I kept thinking how mercy, for one who loves, triumphs over justice (cf. Jas 2:13). Weary, I fell asleep; but it was so brief, because as soon as I had fallen asleep a voice woke me, telling me that it was time to pray, since certain souls were very fiercely tempted. What can it be? Throwing myself to the ground, I prayed to God with all the strength of my soul and made ardent vows that the Lord might free those creatures from the snares of the devil and command those ugly ones to depart. And, to prevent them from consenting, I began to scourge myself so that, by my mortifying the flesh, they might remain free and not be left the prey of those terrible dragons.

This done, I fell into a prostration of strength and had to let myself lie on the ground. In those sufferings I enjoyed a great consolation: it was union with my God. 87.

Meanwhile, one of these poor creatures — who was surely her angel — said to me:

— Thank you! through you we are set free; from God you will have the reward for it.

And she added that she was already the possessor of so immense a treasure.

A «mystical dream» on the pains of purgatory.

I fell asleep and was taken by a mystical dream: there were certain cliffs that seemed to be uninhabited, but I was accompanied by a gracious angel to the bottom of these cliffs, and there one heard creatures groaning who, in the manner of beggars, were asking for help. I turned to that angel and said to him:

— Where are these poor creatures? Take me to them.

He answered me:

— I will not take you to all of them, only to some.

I added: — Why will you not take me to all of them? I hear an infinite number of these creatures. Oh! take me to all of them, for I want to relieve them, since they are immensely afflicted; they are suffering cruel torments.

He, ever firm, answered me nothing. After I had implored him a great deal, he answered me:

— I cannot: I will take you only to those for whom I was sent.

He led me to these. The torment that each one suffered was terrible: one for want of modesty, another for not having fulfilled her office well. The most terrible was that of murmuring. Such was the fright I felt that I fainted. It seemed to me that I myself felt all those pains.

From the mouth of one there came forth a flame that seemed as though it must destroy and annihilate her; for those were figures just as if they had been living and real. I could look but little at them all, because I fainted; but I knew them well. Their voice repeated: Pray! pray! Alas! When I came to myself, I found myself at the foot of the altar and burst into a flood of tears: Oh my Love! your mercy! And then again I swooned. The torment was terrible.

In that lethargy I remained a long time; a good custodian, thinking me dead, shook me, knocking hard on me, and already several pious women had also come near me to shake me; when the whispering began among them, my God gave me life again and I, on seeing these people all around me, was very ashamed and tried to withdraw elsewhere. The warden, grumbling, scolded me roughly, telling me that this was no way to behave, that the women had been frightened. I answered nothing; I withdrew into a chapel of the Crucifix, where I began to weep and to plead:

— My sweet Love! I suffer greatly, I have no more strength! Be moved to pity, my God: set those souls free!

My angel, coming near me, said to me:

— They are free! your suffering has brought them to be purified. Now, without torments, they pray for you, thanking you.

Oh! how I rejoiced at it! He disappeared. And I, so enfeebled, could not stand. I gazed at my dear Crucified One and could say nothing to him but: Thank you! But my gaze was accompanied by the voice of nature, which was asking for help.

In that position I stayed a long while, when all of a sudden I felt myself strengthened and, rising full of vigor, I went where charity was awaiting me. I ran swiftly, hungry to give myself wholly to relieving those poor sick people. But where was my goal? where was my spirit dwelling? what did I have within me? Drunk with love, I ran through those wards, I worked without knowing that I was working; they spoke to me, but I understood little of what they said to me; my eyes still kept imprinted what they had seen, seconded by the sweet thought that held my attention enchained: wherever I looked it seemed to me (that I saw) those sweet objects that had so quickly vanished from my eyes. My mind passed swiftly to that abyss of sorrows, where so many cruel torments were heard. Oh poor little ones! I went saying to myself.

A strong fear seized me that one day I too might go there: what torment! Where and how to lessen it? I wept, and in the solitude of a cottage I was consumed with grief.

Here, my God, in this land of thorns, make me pay for my infamies! hard is my slavery, but it will always be nothing in comparison with what I heard and saw.

Having made this prayer, I fell asleep on the ground. A strong shake woke me: who could it be? my angel Michael!

— Your prayer has been heard (cf. Lk 1:13).

— Oh! — I exclaimed loudly, and kneeling down with joined hands I thanked him, begging him to tell his divine Majesty to consume me soon with love.

— Only you, oh my angel, can thank God.

Having said this, he disappeared.

Anguished inner desolation; the tempter: «Your love is a chimera!».

In that attitude I remained a long time, ever thanking the Most High. When a band of monsters placed themselves all around me, whispering horrid things to me, and moreover that I would not only go to that terrible place of pains, but worse still. I turned to them and answered, mocking them:

— Go away, filthy ones!

One answered:

— Away? — and in an affirmative tone he repeated: Away!

I said to them with assurance:

— Go, I tell you!

They answered me:

— When you come with us, we will go.

— Oh loathsome monsters! with what boldness do you say these words to me?
