They made an obscene gesture of mockery at me, and did not dare to speak.

— Go, I tell you!

They began to dance and to do certain filthy things. Then I rose and commanded them, in the name of God, to go back to where they had come out from. They stammered, but went away.

The thought of a sad future invaded my mind. I would have wished to reason about why I felt this sadness, and an abyss of turbulent things was to draw near to me. I understood nothing. The suffering of this state was something terrible. Here alone! At this consideration I began to weep and called loudly upon my God. The heaven was of bronze; the earth was a burden to me, because everything it contained gave me pain.

A dark and seductive voice displayed before me the delights of creation, so that I might settle back into peace and think no more of the melancholy of the life I had led until today.

— Those caresses, that love which you believe to be blazing, is nothing but a chimera, a natural feeling. The voices have always been ours. Oh! — at last it exclaimed — you grieve me greatly, your weeping pains me. No more sufferings for you, but delights I wish to give you. Do you see?

A picture of something beautiful opened before my eyes, and the same voice continued:

— Your seat in the heavenly homeland is of a magnificence without equal. Oh yes! you are right to rest; it would be better if you could abandon this painful way.

The buffoon, seeing me silent as I listened to his lies, believed that I was consenting, when at this last invitation I grew angry and:

— Away, be gone, infernal whisperer! — I said to him.

And I wept bitterly and redoubled my protestations that I would consume myself on the battlefield of my God. Amid sobs I let myself fall to the ground. An invisible hand raises me and, without saying anything to me, strengthens me. What to do? — I kept repeating to myself — Nature would have rebelled and I had to struggle. But at last a restlessness assailed me so fiercely that the combat was something terrible. The fear of not being able to win was already troubling me, and I felt a strong trembling from it. My angel! come and help me! The night was dark; I did not know what course to take.

Seated near a large stone, weary and weakened, I fell asleep. I was enjoying a gracious dream: all the delightful landscapes that unfolded one after another were most beautiful; plains with most exquisite fruits; beautiful and graceful young girls on high hills were gathering provisions for the winter.

A magnificent tree of immense girth spread out its branches, so beautiful, with most beautiful fruits, so far-reaching, that I could not see the end of them. Oh! beautiful and graceful you are! — I said to it in the dream — This tree, as though it wished to answer me, with a certain movement bends its first great branches so as to greet me, and they rise up again. At last the tree itself, so enormous, bends, as if it had been of wax, in an act of submission. I was confused, I was frightened:

— Rise up, for pity’s sake!

In a flash, there it is once more in its former attitude. From that tree there descends a gracious Matron and, having come near me, she said to me:

— Why are you so disheartened?

— Oh Lady! do not come near, for I am a poor slave abandoned by my Lord.

She took me by the hand and made me a sign to look near the tree. Oh! who was there! my Savior, my Love, my Master! I said with a loud cry: — It is my God, he is the Master!

And he disappeared. The Lady, pressing my hand, said to me:

— Your tears, your sufferings are well gathered up. Wake up and feed on the bread of angels, since you must go where I would wish for the fruits of another date palm [?]; see to it that they are not bitten by vipers that would poison them: they would no longer be good for your Master.

When I awoke, where did I find myself? At the foot of an altar, where shortly afterwards a minister of God came. Having fed on his most holy Body, I went to gather those fruits: oh! how short was that time for me, in which alone I could unfold properly the dream I had had: the sight of the Matron, but (above all) that, that of my Savior!

Drunk with love, I flew through those fields, eager to gather those fruits and to guard them with all diligence so that they might not spoil on me. I besought my Master to pour upon them the dew of his divine grace.

XII

Here is the learned Shepherd I had longed for!

Meanwhile an elegant shepherd approaches me, but a very humble one, and asks me for news of the field. With a charity worthy of a true servant of my God, he introduces various subjects of conversation. Within myself I said: but will this one too be pretending? My voice repeated to me: No! With immense pleasure I listened to him; the time I had spent with him seemed to me a minute.

When I had gone away and was alone, I began to reason, commending myself to my God not to permit me to be deceived. Once I was assured that he was a true worker and that he cultivated the vineyard of the Lord very well, that his work was upright and that he had the orders carried out exactly by those who found themselves working under him: oh! how I longed to see him again! My God was not slow to let me find him. I implored him to be willing to cast a glance over the fields that I had been set to work as a slave. I told him that I had always made that journey alone and had met many shepherds; but from them I had had only frights and great fears and terrors.

Oh! how he listened to me! In his immense charity and goodness he made that path easy for me to run; at every great rock that lay in the way I found myself lifted up by his grace because, as though it had been a little pebble, I passed over it without feeling grave pain. My God! you have sent me this servant of yours to take from me those anxieties which, for want of strength, I could perhaps no longer bear, and I would succumb.

Once assured that it was so, with energy and without fear I set out every subject, however tangled it might be. I entrusted the working out of it to him. In my want of manners I was borne with by him; the roughness of my ways was tolerated by his kindness. He was so reserved in his manners that his modesty was enviable. Oh! true Shepherd of the Church of Christ our Lord, firmly bound to the successor of the great Pius, most tender admirer of the Immaculate Virgin! Oh! what thanksgiving must I ever render for having found so holy a Shepherd!

But still, every now and then as the days and nights went by, I continually felt the disturbance of that famous shepherd who had made me suffer so much and who kept renewing certain stratagems, so that I might find sharp stones to make me feel their hardness. Even now unpleasant things happen that trouble me. Oh! they are a real affliction to me. But as soon as I have told the matter to the good shepherd, he cuts the struggle short, levels the path and gives back peace. The workers too are happy to have a shepherd so powerful and charitable; they love him greatly; and their whole way of acting has changed: they try to be observant of their duty.

Oh! my Love! I see a new way opening: I am looking at it, and I am fearful as I travel along it; and yet I find it strange for me and, if I must say so, it seems that I am continually dreaming. How far will this so sweet path lead me? Meanwhile, the persecutors and people who have received so much good molest me and try to commit every sort of injustice and insult, thus molesting the Work of the Lord. How many Judases betray (you, my God)! The evildoers apply themselves to stealing what is yours; they go roaming all around your fields to see whether they can bring about their devastation.

— No! — my voice says to me — Do not fear, and work in tranquillity!

I feel that I enjoy a peace that is yours, my Love! I feel a strength…, surely it is yours: yes!

The upright shepherd smiles at the account, wishing to lighten my pains, believing and fearing that I may suffer from them. No! His thought is always turned to the Work: he watches over its fields, he wants it respected and wisely consolidates its foundations. He wants the workers humble and submissive.

While I was working together with my chief workers, a small and delightful dispute arose about the new Shepherd. One let slip an expression as though she were afraid of him. The infernal enemy violently invades my mind: and what if he deceives me? What if he should grow weary and, not wishing to have other pains and troubles and crosses, abandon me? This reflection was so strong upon my soul that it was unbearable to me. I withdrew to pray and to weep, telling my Lord that, for pity’s sake, he should not let this happen, because his fields would suffer much from it; that he should rather accept me in sacrifice, but not permit his fields to suffer. I was thus prostrate on the ground; my voice: — Be at peace! he has been placed by me; he will grow in affection for my Work and you will do great things with it.

My God! — I kept repeating to myself — you will do! For joy I could no longer think straight. Exhausted, in that position I fell asleep.

Oh! it was not a dream. I found myself in a delightful field: the grapes were of extraordinary beauty; all the trees were laden with fruit; the flowers and the other small plants were so well cultivated that it was an immense delight. My gaze was not able to reach the end of it. There was a meadow with a large fountain in the middle; I set off to see it: it was full of water; this flowed out beautiful and crystalline, to water this immense field, from large channels jutting out at the top of the fountain. I took delight in seeing so beautiful a work; I could not move: I felt strongly (drawn) to observe that work more carefully. What could it be? Outside this fountain, on the ground, there were very tiny pipes which every so often sent forth no longer water but drops of blood, and this mingled with the water that was flowing. Oh, what a surprise! My angel Saint Michael comes before me and says to me: — This blood is all yours: it was gathered when you shed it from the blows you received for this beautiful field.

And he disappeared. What I felt! who could describe it? What I said to my God, my Love! I would never have moved from so delightful a position. My voice orders me to rise and travel along a path. I do not hesitate an instant.

I had gone a long way and could never understand anything. Sometimes I found the holy and charitable shepherd, who with charity and zeal helped me to surmount those obstacles that lay along the path. But what was my surprise at seeing so much benevolence, and I nothing! I felt an immense indifference, always in the persuasion that what he did, he did out of duty toward the Work of God, but not to relieve this slave of the Lord from the oppression of so many pains. Thinking thus, a deep melancholy seized me and this, advancing rapidly, made me of a sour humor; but that is not all: it passed into turmoil. Then I realized that it was the work of the devil, that whispering put into my mind: that it was not to relieve me from my pains, but only to sustain the Work better. I began to say to myself: What did you desire, O useless slave of the Lord? Was not this your only satisfaction: to find a learned shepherd who would steer my ship well? My voice: — He will be a great relief to you in the care of the fields.

Oh! how I feel that I am resting in peace! I place all my trust in him. How I thank my God!

Weary, I fell asleep. A loud rumble woke me: it was a monster circling all around me.

Oh! Away, infernal monster! But no: standing still, he explained to me what he was doing in a field of workers. He had succeeded in seducing more than one and had sown among them a great cockle that had entirely taken away their peace. And he showed me that he would continue until he had undone that flock.

What a sorrowful life! I felt such anguish that I would have flown to that field. But when I mentioned what had happened to the good shepherd, he at once restrains the workers with his authority, puts to flight whoever was serving that monster as an instrument for wreaking havoc and, having raised up the spirits of the workers, great good is hoped for in the harvest.

Is this a dream? Yet I tremble lest this holy treasure be lost to me. I go saying to myself: this is a fact, not a fantasy. One could say: the upright and just shepherd walks on a sure road, his castle is unshakeable! 88.

He resumes with new eagerness the cultivation of the fields, at the head of the workers.

My voice: It is time to sow my fields well.

Procure good seed for yourself, and first let the couch grass be removed from the soil.

How shall I go about carrying out such a command? I was very thoughtful, when a seller comes before me, shows me some good seed and offers me a great uncultivated field to cultivate. I accepted everything and had to provide the workers. Not finding them, I fell into distress; my voice taught me where I was to take them from and I was not slow to carry out what was suggested to me; with great activity we worked that field and, after sowing an excellent wheat, we drew from it a fine and abundant harvest.

We entered other neighboring farms, and there was a celebration at the arrival of the workers. But that dragon had carried off some of those who had remained there; they were so grieved that no reasoning availed to calm them. After a long reasoning they were persuaded and thought no more of what had happened; but they were all intent on repairing the damage that those had left, and set to work hard so that the cockle should not come to occupy a better place than the wheat.

I tried to help them with all the strength I had and they, seeing me so wearied, abandoned their laziness and worked with eagerness. Oh! it is useless for a good captain to command his army to face the enemy and take possession of the ground, if he does not himself go first, exposing his breast to the grapeshot hurled by the enemy: so too an overseer who truly wants her workers to be zealous and wholly intent on their work, and to keep their mind and heart always turned to their Lord and Master, must be the first who from dawn to sunset holds the spade in hand to furrow well all the plots of the land, so that in good order the water of the grace of the dear Master may flow and water those souls well.

But certain shepherds were so little capable of giving true and sound direction to those dear workers that they gave me much pain and, what is more, they believed they could manage to put me out of the field, so as to overturn once more that beautiful cultivation which my Father and Teacher had made. With every sort of invention they tried to slander, so as to attain their purpose; but it availed nothing. In all that they contrived, when they believed they were at last victorious, they were left put to shame: my Master sent a ray of light upon the truth of the facts and their snares were left overthrown. How many times I felt great compassion at this, knowing that they were not striking the slave, but were touching the Work of God, which is the apple of his eye!

The gift of the Cardinal Protector: at last, a true shepherd!

When I got back to my cottage, oh! what did I find! two shepherds who, together with one of the chief workers, had come to an agreement, and she had put together a sackful of inventions.

The poor men were surely incapable even of suspecting that on this miserable earth there were creatures who could so well distort the truth, while there was nothing in it that was plausible. Oh! what a weaving! One, poor man, was surely so persuaded of its truth that he grew indignant with me and would no longer even see me. Oh! what deeds spring from the hardened stones of hearts. It seemed to me (impossible) that such a creature should have a heart so insensible or, to put it better, panting to be able to relish another’s harm, that with such ease she seeks every means to manage to deal secretly certain stabs that leave an incurable wound, and she goes on, after having received so much good. Oh! what a wound, my Good! I keep thinking of the horrible betrayal of Judas! Oh! my Lord, what torment you suffered from it!

In this description of mine (in which it appears how) all the ways I had traveled were so well (pointed out) to me, since my Master sent me a shepherd so excellent and charitable, truly a worthy prince of the Church, I feel that I have great veneration for him. He is the only one, my dear Teacher, who knows how to work so holily well in your Work, pre-eminently. He carries out a perfect work and greatly loves that the fields be well cultivated; he demands good seed so as to have white and spotless wheat in the harvest; in good time he has the cockle removed, so that it does not spoil the ear of the grain. He relieves me greatly in the struggles and keeps the workers in their place; indeed certain tumults are no longer heard and they are all holily fearful.

A curious effect it produces in my soul: I notice that I no longer have any wish to describe certain things that happened in the woods, in the fields and on those arid mountains, or in my poor cottage. Already advanced in years, (it is given to me) to find a Shepherd who bears the rod only in his surname, Verga, but surely such a rod sprang up in a bed of sugar cane. Oh! I always pray my God to preserve him a good century for the good of his fields and of the workers. How sweet it is, my Lord, to think that, after 25 years of great suffering, without ever having found a true shepherd, suited to his immense vineyard…! Your vineyard has had learned and holy men, but they were not for your fields. 89.

Having returned to my cottage, weary, I threw myself at the feet of my dear Crucified One and, without further thought, I let my humanity pour itself out with its Master and be relieved for an instant from an apprehension that was distressing it greatly. With my forehead resting on the most holy feet of my Savior, I began to say forcefully that the ingratitudes I receive every day from his ungrateful workers break my heart, and moreover their inventions hurt me so much that they leave me so exhausted that it is worse to me than a scourge. And I told him various things that had happened. He answered me:

— Why do you weep? Did I weep when Judas betrayed me?

— Oh my Love! have pity on me! bear with my outpouring!

And I fell silent. Every now and then tears and sobs escaped me.

— Oh! — thus I broke the silence — I am a wretch of a slave, full of every sort of infamy! I deserve nothing, only punishments, because I am worthy of nothing else.

And my grief grew all the more at seeing myself deprived of my Good. A thousand thoughts (assailed me) that I had displeased him, because I was not working according to his divine will; thoughts of certain workers, whom I clearly saw to be so little gentle and who, instead of drawing the beginners to themselves, frightened them, and these sought more and more to flee if they were given the chance. Distressed by a thousand thoughts I set myself to pray and weep, without complaining of anything. At last, weary, I fell asleep amid sobs.

«The time will come when this pumpkin will stretch its branches from one pole to the other».

A gentle touch upon one arm roused me and I saw a personage near me. He said to me: — Why do you weep? Do not lose heart; set out and go to the end of this road; there you will find great ones of the world who are trying to seduce my workers.

My God! I exclaimed, and threw myself to the ground. But he disappeared in a flash. Who can it have been? My workers! no one could say that but my Lord: so it was he himself, my Beloved! And so, on the ground as I was, I kept looking at the place where he had been and would never have got up. It no longer came into my mind to do what he had ordered me; but my voice:

— Why delay any longer?

Oh! as though these words had been a jolt, I flew and, running along so long a road, I never reached its end. My God, how long it is! Night is falling, and what shall I do? Meanwhile I was walking, when I see a crowd of people; but I could not make them out well. At last I was able to make them out and saw that they were workers and, together with them, several shepherds who were heatedly discussing. I drew near and they were surprised. One of these said to me:

— What, here?

— And you — I answered him — are you here too?

— Certainly! — he said to me in an irritated tone — and I tell you that your way of proceeding has little foundation.

I added:

— Pray, I beg you to tell me where and how you find this disorder?

— In the work you are doing — he said to me — you run too much. A brake is needed, otherwise these workers will do nothing good.

I began to laugh and said to him:

— Have you anything else to tell me? Who sent you here? — Kindly tell me who is the superior who is so concerned with our fields.

The others were silent, but with glances they spoke a great deal with the workers. In an ironic manner the shepherd went on to say:

— Know that I liken these fields to the pumpkin plant, which runs and is all leaves: in the end its fruit is a pumpkin!

Then I answered him:

— The time will come when this pumpkin will harden and give you indigestion. It will rise above all the plants and, at last, will stretch its branches from one pole to the other; its roots will suffer no harm, the woodworm will never manage to nest in it. Its fruits will be pleasing to the Bride of my Lord and its flowers will have a fragrance all their own.

He stood looking at me, because I said this resolutely and in a rather severe tone. Turning to the workers I said to them: — Oh! how faithless you are! From morning to evening you touch with your hand the wonders of my Almighty Lord and Master, and you are disturbed over so little and do not know how to answer? and what grieves me most is that you were almost letting yourselves be convinced.

The one who wished to play the orator fell silent; the others blushed and they all went away together. 90.

A worker’s account of the plots woven against the fields of the Lord.

From what I had heard, I did not stop making further enquiries, persuaded that they would have spoiled some of these workers, especially one who, like a leaf in the wind, kept her affection in the fields of the Lord. And I was not slow to guess who it was. I went near her and begged her to stop digging and, if she had doubts that the cultivation she was doing was going to yield pumpkins and not good wheat, to stop the work by all means, for the Lord had no need of her at all, but another would come in her place.

She gave a long sigh.

— Certainly — she answered me — that shepherd was right.

— Well then, why do you not think of going where he will put you, in a field that yields only wheat, and so you will not have to mix with the pumpkin heads, since the one you have is enough?

She looks at me, and then begins to weep.

— My God! — she exclaims — how that shepherd turned my head upside down!

I begged her to tell me what he had said to her. At first she would not at all, and grew more and more vexed. But I tried to convince her and, with the help of God, I succeeded. Oh poor thing! how many things she had heard brought forth as true, so that while I heard them (I wondered) whether they had happened? But what am I saying? Never! Where and how do I find myself? Am I not the whole subject of so many calumnies? And where can they have contrived them? How that ugly dragon knew how to weave so much stuff!?!

And a most profound thought about the shepherd seized me; I was so taken up with it that I understood little of what she was relating. This halt of mine made such an impression on her that she stopped her account; she looked at me, she would have liked to guess what thought was binding my mind and preoccupying me so seriously. After a good while she shook me, asking me what was the matter with me and why I was not attending to her account; whether perhaps I was suffering because that shepherd had come to know so many things that were perhaps hidden. Hearing this, I roused myself: — Whatever can this suspicion of yours be? As I see it, it seems impossible to me, but if you admit it, it may happen in others, certainly not in me, who know little of this language, which I understand may be caused by a mind much infected with rash suspicions.

She looked at me and, asking my pardon, fell silent. I resumed:

— Then why do you not continue your account to me?

And she:

— Must I really tell you how I feel and why I would not want to go on any further? On seeing you so little attentive to what I was telling you with such frankness, you have put within me an anger, joined to such an aversion, that I would almost hate you if it were not a sin!

I looked at her fixedly and then said to her:

— I realize that I have been at fault, but I must confess to you that it is my very bad character, on account of which, many times, while people are telling something, my mind goes to a very important matter and I no longer notice what they are telling me, and so it seems that I care little for what they tell me with such kindness; and on the contrary my desire to listen is great, in order to set right things that damage the Work of my Master. What would you have, dear worker? (I acknowledge) that this way of mine is not good at all; I always resolve to amend it; it is for this that I have great trust in the mercy of God to obtain pardon for it. And will you not forgive me? Yes, I hope so. Come now! tell me, and be persuaded that at the end of your account I shall be able to tell you everything.

She looks at me and resumes her account, keeping her eyes well fixed on my face to see what effect those terrible words had on me; but they produced no effect on me at all. They only awakened in me a lively compassion for those unhappy ones who tried to do so much harm to the fields of the Lord. When she had finished, I resumed, laughing:

— Well then! now, after such sad things as you have told me, and so well plotted, I see that they had fiercely woven a plan of war against the fields of the Lord. But may my Lord ever be blessed, who freed his fields from the enemies. And tell me: who could have overthrown these fierce plots if not a God, who in an instant undid a work of a long time, which must also have cost no small labors and anxieties? Behold, everything is overthrown, nothing remains standing any longer! the wind has swept everything away with it, because, having no substance, it had to be scattered with the air and in the air.

Having said this, she remained so deeply moved that she no longer dared to say anything.

But the worker does not manage to identify herself with her vocation.

I resumed:

— Now let us take a look at the beautiful work that my Master did. Not only did he dispel everything, but he made use of the evil to draw from it a manure for his fields, and we see them beautiful and vigorous. The trees put forth their foliage, the vines their delightful leaves, the pines and the oaks are full of graceful birds’ nests, and the birds with their song weave graceful melodies. Whoever has the good fortune to rest in the shade of these delightful trees enjoys peace and consolation there.

She looks at me and, smiling, thanks me, and tries to work well and willingly. I set her to work and see to it that it is the lightest and least burdensome. Thus we were working together, when night came upon us without our noticing it. She, almost frightened, said to me:

— What are we doing here in the middle of this field? Only work is spoken of and no one ever thinks of feeding themselves. I answered her:

— Have no doubt, for my Master is that God who feeds the birds, and who can fear not to have what he needs? (cf. Mt 6:26).

I look around me and see nothing. The field was without trees; not even a farmhouse could be seen. My God! what will become of this poor creature if she is not provided with what she needs? Teach me what I must do.

— Trust, and nothing else — my voice says to me.

Now it grows dark. She was no longer speaking, but from her face one could see that she was saying a great deal. A most fierce struggle arose in me, but I held firmly to the word: Only trust!

At last I hear a noise and look anxiously: it was a peasant with a cart and two oxen, which he was urging on so that they would go. As soon as he sees us, he lets out a loud: Oh!

— Come!

But I was afraid; she was looking at me as though she wanted to say to me: do you see where you have brought me? what will become of us! The cart draws near and the good man invites us to get in, telling us that he had orders from his master to come and fetch us to take us to his farmhouse, which was awaiting us with a good supper prepared. I turned to that frightened one and begged her to follow me by getting into the cart. With little goodwill she got in, and the good man drove us along the road from which, after a short climb, a large cottage could be seen.

— There — the good man began to say — is where we must go. See how beautiful our farmhouse is!

She looked at me with two big eyes as though she wanted to reproach me for having got into the cart; seeing her like this, I said to her:

— Why so much fear? Oh! how small a heart you have, filled only with mistrust! Oh! you are too human. The fields are God’s; what is being cultivated in them is for Him: how can you doubt that He Himself is thinking of us? Oh! I am happy! I feel it: the cart that is carrying me is his, the man will be according to his desire; where he takes us we shall surely find our Master…

And I felt within me an indescribable joy. The unhappy woman, who knew nothing of the beauty of the divine ordering, began to weep. What to do? I felt no compassion for it at all and laughed at it heartily. After a long stretch of road, when it was already quite night, this unhappy woman began to shout.

What? — said the good driver — your complaints, which you have made until now, I am tired of hearing by this time. I assure you that your little faith, your attachment to yourself, will reduce you to utter misery.

Oh! what an impression these words made on me!

She fell silent, and I remained confused and hopeful that the unhappy woman might draw profit from it for her soul. I saw her still dominated by a strong combat, and she gave no thought at all to putting away those ill-founded ideas of hers. She began to grow impatient and would have liked to get down. The good driver, seeing her so, addressed other words to her, and ended by telling her that by now her behavior was too indelicate, and that he was persuaded we could hope for nothing from her.

More than ever I drew close to her and tried, with exhortations, to persuade her; but I perceived that her obstinacy was growing more and more, and that this could only be a diabolical artifice. Without further heed, in a loud voice I declared to her that it was by now a black wickedness, produced by none other than an evil spirit. She remained motionless. Then I gave a command: that the dragon should depart. What happened? The cart very nearly went to pieces, but the good young man seized the horse and, smiling, said:

— He has gone!

What? this young man laughs and says: He has gone? Little by little I draw near him and say to him:

— Pray, tell me: who are you?

He answers me nothing; he only looks at me and says:

— Here we are!

Fearing that he had not understood me, I ask again who he is. He points out the church to me, while the horse stops. By the light of a small lantern one could see that we had arrived near a church. He made us get down and, while we were turned round to see properly where and how one could enter, the man and the cart went away, and nothing more was seen. 91.

I knocked at the door of the church, but nothing was heard. Where are we? That man who brought us here did not even wait for a thank you. Here near you, my God! but I cannot go in and throw myself at your feet and tell you many things. At last, after I had knocked a great deal, a poor and very old priest came to open for us, grumbling at me because it was too early, and I had no business going to cause him so much bother.

I knelt down at the foot of the altar and thanked my God for it. As I lay there prostrate, he thought that I was asleep and gave me a hard blow with his fist on one shoulder to rouse me. My God! what my fright was is better guessed than written. I got up, but did not utter a word, because I thought it had been someone from outside who wanted to strike me, but I saw only him, and he told me that it was not right for me to have stayed in that position, still believing that I was asleep. I obeyed promptly and leaned on the chair. I could not understand what that good old man had against me.

Having received my God, I went to work together with that poor creature. But what was my surprise! She told me frankly that she wanted to leave me. Oh! how I suffered from it! but even so, without losing my composure, I accompanied her to her native cottage.

«Your ignorance is made up for by my wisdom».

Alone, with slow steps, I set out toward a field where I knew there was great work to be done. While I was walking so thoughtfully, halfway along the road I met a good shepherd, and on drawing near him I felt something supernatural.

Oh! I am not mistaken, this is a servant of yours, my God! And at once I asked him how he was and where he was going. With all courtesy and charity he answered me that he was going in search of a person from whom he expected much good for a small flock of his.

I accompanied him, speaking much of my God. When I came near a cottage, which was inhabited by my workers, I tried to take my leave in order to go in; but he stops me, telling me that the one he was looking for was I.

— Oh! can it be? I am a poor slave of the Lord who knows nothing but how to dig the ground and go wherever my Master commands me.

But he insisted. My voice:

— Listen to him and give him lodging, for he will join a fine farm to my others.

I received him and, having given him as best I could a little room to lie down in, we parted with the word:

— Tomorrow everything will be arranged.

And he was all enthusiastic; it would take too long to relate his protestations and how much he blessed the Lord for having at last let him find the one he had been seeking for many years.

When he had withdrawn, I went to my God and prayed him earnestly to give me clear knowledge so as to handle so important a matter well:

— Oh my Love! your slave is very ignorant.

My voice:

— Your ignorance is made up for by my wisdom!

I fell silent, and without further ado I set to work, without caring what I shall say, what I shall do and what will happen. How well the work turned out for me! The arrangements and the interweavings were magnificent things. When it was finished, I did nothing but gaze at the divine ordering; I took delight in what I saw so beautiful and so magnificently ordered.

My voice commands me to run, and everyone persecutes me because I run too much My voice:

— It is time to advance into the fields and sow with courage!

— My God, your slave is ready!

Running thus, at every moment I found people, and shepherds who molested me, telling me that I was running too much in sowing, that the harvest would not be fine at all. At last to these were added some great shepherds too, who grumbled a great deal. A certain panic seized me and I was almost about to slow down the work.

My voice:

— Oh! what are you doing?

Without further heed I began to run faster still. Oh! what befell me! A superior of the shepherds stops me, scolds me roughly and with far from gentle insults says that I am a proud woman and that I see nothing but the satisfaction of having fields so as to give vent to my pride, that I attend only to having farms and fields.

Oh! how I felt my breast tighten: I felt it being crushed as between two very large stones. I went saying to myself: how am I to conduct myself? my voice does not err, and yet it is always the one that commands me to run; and everyone persecutes me because I run more than anything; with these are joined even the workers, my companions, who grumble and complain because I make them work too much; not only that, but they are pained by my continual walking without giving myself respite, that I rush too much. They do not at all accept this way of mine. And many times they say to me:

— It is time to stop and put things in order, and not to scourge yourself so much in this way.

My God! what to do? Is not the voice that commands me to run yours? Perhaps that ugly one is trying to deceive me?

How much I had to struggle! My humanity joined in with what these people were saying: it took their side entirely and associated itself perfectly with them, and would willingly have put into practice what these were saying, that is, to stop. Thus assailed, I prayed God to take me out of so painful a state. Was I mistaken? Weeping, I lay with my face to the ground.

My voice:

— These people speak in a human way. Forward, follow me!

Oh my Love! your slave wants nothing else but to carry out your orders perfectly! 92.

A mystical dream, foretelling new labors and new storms.

Weary, I fell asleep upon a piece of wood. I was overtaken by a mystical dream. A gracious angel took me by the hand and said to me:

— Rise, look!

He showed me a most extensive and very beautiful field; it was so vast that my eye could not manage to see its end. Turning to this angel I asked him whether all that I saw was my Master’s, and said that I could not see how far it reached. Laughing, he answered me:

— Such is its extent that you will never be able to see it. The more you run, the more great and beautiful fields you will find; among these there will be some that have only thorn-thickets: you must not stop, but try to uproot them and work the ground well, manuring it to make it fit to receive a good seed. The workers whom you will set to cultivate this arid field will have to suffer great prickings, but those who resist and persevere with pleasure and love in working this thorn-thicket will have a double reward from the Lord; and those faint-hearted ones who will urge you to stop and go more slowly are placed among the number of the slothful, because they have little love for suffering; they want nothing but the comforts of their body, they fear every pricking and are frightened of everything.

— Look! — he said to me.

Oh! I gave a loud exclamation and clung to him; I held him tightly with both hands. It was an abyss in which nothing was to be seen but every sort of pain: lions with open mouths, which would have torn anyone to pieces; giants, who went about seeking to destroy works of the Lord; a torrent, which devastated and carried along with it boulders of stone and living beings; a creature in the midst of those foaming waters that were flowing from every side! already many of the trees of the mountain were falling into this river, and this creature could be seen lost from moment to moment, because she was wrapped in those great billows of water. I cried out loudly:

— My angel, save her! I feel I am dying of grief. Oh poor thing!

And he, laughing:

— That creature is only figurative: shortly you will be its reality.

— Must I perish in that abyss?

— No: you will suffer all of those pains, but you will never have to perish. Do not fear: with your heel all those wild beasts will be held in check; the waters will wrap you in their waves, but you will find yourself victorious on the mountain.

— Oh! for pity’s sake, do not leave me.

He goes on to say:

— Once you have reached the mountain, you will have great consolations.

— Tell me! — I said to him hastily — I want no other consolation than that of seeing my Lord.

He signs me on the forehead, and leaves me.

When I awoke, where am I? Alas! from afar I see that immense fortress-rock. I was trying to find a way not to approach it, when I see a crowd of dragons about to hurl themselves upon me. Where to flee? I ran, and they came after me. A loud rumble: the rock breaks away and such an upheaval follows in that land, and I found myself: where? among the agitated waves or, to put it better, in the swollen current of that immense river. Alas! I am lost! I remembered nothing of my dream; I only felt a great terror. I called at the top of my voice upon my Crucified One. Those ugly ones called to me from the bank of the river and, every time I called upon my dear Crucified One, they mocked me, saying:

— We alone can save you: in a moment you are finished!

— No! Away, buffoons, liars!

To the biggest one, who promised to make me happy, saying that if I only stretched out my hand to him I would be saved, I said:

— Away, ugly loathsome one!

And he:

— Meanwhile you will perish!

— If I perish, it will be with my God!

But by now the current became so strong that it overwhelmed me and dashed me among stones and rocks. At every moment I believed I was being undone. That ugly one — although I no longer saw him, yet I heard his voice — shouted to me:

— Do you want me? I am coming!

— No, no!

But I had neither voice nor strength any longer, and I commended myself to my God that he might succor me and have pity on me, but nothing! At last the river rises greatly and I am carried by the current onto that rugged mountain. Broken, alone, I began to weep: My God! I feel I am fainting! And I let myself fall among those stones and remained completely deprived of my senses. Oh! how I felt a real agony beforehand! Once I had lost my senses, I felt nothing; I was like a dead body.

Coming to myself through a most perceptible shake, I open my eyes: Oh! whom did I have near me: my Good! Oh my Love! Thrown on the ground, I wanted to tell him so many things, but my strength did not allow me. Taking me by the hand:

— Rise! — he said to me — you have suffered much and in this you have gained much. He signed me and disappeared.

Hard struggle with the infernal enemies: she gains the victory by the power of her Crucifix.

I remained so fortified and full of strength, beside myself with the consolation I had felt. Oh! my Good, my sweet Love! And I was inebriated with it; I would never have moved from so beautiful and delightful a mountain. But no! I reflected that my Teacher had given me much strength so that I might be in the struggle much better than before, and that this had some meaning.

Well then, while I kept my gaze fixed where my Good had been, behold a loud rumble: whatever is it? A large band of brigands, for so they appeared, were coming toward me. Alas! I am lost! Where can I save myself? There is no more escape! I threw myself to the ground and with all my strength called upon my Lord to come to my aid: nothing! They approach at a great gallop and already I see them near me. I was about to faint from fright, when I recognized one of them, and it was the most seductive devil. Coming to myself and gathering all my strength, standing upright:

— Stop! — I shouted.

A few more steps and they were near me.

— Who are you?

They did not answer me.

— Away, buffoons!

As soon as I had said this, behold them all in motion; each one played his own trick on me.

— Away, I tell you!

One, the seducer, answers me:

— No!

— Why not? — I said to him.

— You must accept great sums from us, and these are much greater than those provided for you by the one you call your Master and Lord. We want to give you far more.

In a jesting manner I said to him:

— Buffoon, withdraw together with your band!

— I will never withdraw!

I thought of giving them a serious command:

— In the name of God, go back to where you came from!

They do not move and almost spurn me. Seeing this, I feel a something!… for an instant I remain without words. They took heart and were almost near enough to seize me.

— No! — I shout loudly at the top of my voice — No! Away in the name of God! They stop, but do not go away. Already I felt great fright at this, when one leaps out and says:

— Over us you have no power: either surrender to our wishes or else we will hurl you down from the mountain. Here you have riches of every kind, and one day we will make you better off than a queen.

— Oh! away in the name of my Lord and Master!

— Oh! — they answer — Buffoon! Do you think you can have power over us? No! you are deceived!

I did not want to let them notice my pain, but they noticed it.

— Oh! at last we have caught you!

— No! I do not want your riches: I love my dear poverty!

Having said this, they come to a halt, muttering among themselves so that one could not understand. One takes a branch from a tree and, enraged, beats me.

— Surrender!

— No! — I answered; and meanwhile I called loudly upon my God.

The mountain seemed to be collapsing; I saw myself lost. Oh most holy Immaculate Virgin! I cried: nothing! One, so ugly, said:

— Oh! at last you have no power over us; that is why we have come.

Horrible event! They multiply; in a word, there were some of every kind. Beaten as I was, they still intended to give me more. I took my Crucifix, grasped it and, full of ardor, said:

— Stop! in the name of my dear Crucified One, hurl yourselves all down to the bottom of this mountain!

They wanted to resist, but I proudly held my Crucifix on high. Fearing that, when they were at the bottom, they would get up to their tricks, I commanded them to return to their chains. They disappeared.

A mysterious dog succors her and then defends her.

What am I to do, my God, my Master, here alone? All aching from the blows, I felt such a prostration of strength that I could no longer stand on my feet. There was nothing to feed myself with; I had no strength to climb; I kept thinking that night would come and I felt great fright at it. I curled up to pray that he might have pity on me and give me strength to climb that mountain, where I might find a farmhouse in which to take refuge: nothing!

I fell asleep, and in my sleep I felt that I was fainting. I believe it was not sleep, but a drowsiness from great weakness. A pretty dog wakes me with its paw, tapping it on my shoulder. Opening my eyes, I saw this animal holding a little basket in its mouth; inside were three most beautiful fruits and a piece of bread:

— Oh dear little creature! who sent you up here?

It fawned on me lovingly and invited me to eat. I began thus to say:

— Oh my Love, my sweet and charitable Lord and Master! I give you thanks for such charity!

I blessed the basket; as I did so, the dog bent its legs as if it wished to kneel. As soon as it saw that I was eating, it gave me two caresses and then lay down quietly nearby. Every now and then I looked at it.

— Are you not eating, poor little one?

With its tail it made me a sign of no.

— Have you eaten?

And it signals yes to me. The fear comes over me that this may be a demon; I stop eating, take my Crucifix and sign the bread. But this creature does not move. Oh my Love! must I eat?

My voice:

— Yes: it is I who sent it.

And I ate everything. Then I wanted to get up; I looked around me to see whether there was some spring of water, because I was parched with thirst. This little creature takes me by the hem of my dress and leads me near a rock, where a trickle of water was flowing. I drank of that water and felt myself wholly reinvigorated. I saw my track and at once set my foot upon it.

I set out over that mountain. When I had gone a good way, I see in the distance two evildoers with guns, and they too had dogs. They were coming toward me: where to flee? I wanted to run back, but the creature stopped me by my dress. Oh my Crucified One! I cried. As soon as these were near me, they were about to seize me: the creature, like a lion, leaps upon them and puts them to flight.

— Oh good creature! you have been sent for my defense, and what can I do for you, I who have not even anything to feed you with: for so long now you have eaten nothing.

Saying this to it, I kept a hand on its head and felt compassion for it. It looks at me, and with its mouth takes hold of my dress again, pulling me, and I followed it. It stopped and began to bark loudly. Whatever is it? I turned in every direction and saw nothing. After some ten minutes’ halt we began the journey again. Night was approaching and I was frightened, not knowing where I was. At last a house could be seen from afar or, to put it better, a farmhouse; I quickened my step so as to reach those people and ask them for lodging; meanwhile the thought came to me that my Lord, in the arms of the most holy Virgin, also went to stop in a hut. The dog, my companion, as though it had read my mind, looks at me and caresses me. Oh! how can this be? The thought comes to me that it is a demon. I signed myself and then made the sign of the cross over it. I was confirmed that it was not a demon, because at that sign it almost bent its legs. Oh! who is this creature, my Love? Is it you who sent it to me? I asked it so many questions, but it only looked at me and then, wagging its tail, welcomed me joyfully.

When little was wanting to reach the farmhouse, it stops me; standing upright in front of me, it rests its two paws on my arm and holds me still. I wanted to scream, but my throat was closed; I pushed the creature and tried to free myself: no! I gave a loud cry: nothing! In the distance I see two tall men approaching: I am lost! I was almost fainting. The creature let go of my arm and, taking firm hold of my dress, dragged me into a cave.

These men passed, and the creature leaps up at me again in sign of victory and shows me the path, and I, running, tried to find a dwelling. I no longer see the cottage. Where are we? The dog, as though it wanted to say to me: I have saved you (was rejoicing), and I, caressing it, said to it: thank you!

The two souls, saved through her, encourage her on God’s behalf.

The night was already far advanced, without a moon: where are we going? I hear two women’s voices saying to me:

— Do not be afraid: we are with you!

— Who are you, souls of God or monsters?

No; the dog kept silent and every now and then tugged at my dress. I could see two shadows, and they seemed to me two workers, but however hard I strove to look at them I could not make them out clearly. My fear kept growing and I trembled from head to foot.

One of them comes near me:

— Why such terror? Do not be afraid, be at peace. We are in the midst of a barbarous people, and where you are is a field of evildoers; and those from whom the good dog has hidden you, had they seen you, would surely have done you harm in a thousand ways.

— But who are you?

— Soon you will know. The moon will rise and you will recognize us.

— For pity’s sake, tell me! This is a very cruel suffering.

— We cannot. These sufferings of yours make firm the fields of the Lord.

— Then you are workers?

They remained silent.

— Then, if you are good souls sent by my God, tell me something of my Love! And if you are able to return to Him, I would like to give you a prayer, so that you might bring it to Him in person.

I felt a calm, something sweet; my fear vanished and I walked gladly in that darkness. Every now and then I stretched out my hand to feel whether the dog was near me.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — If only the light of the moon would come soon! Then I could see you.

One of them added:

— Tell us what you want us to bring to the Lord.

— Oh! only one prayer: that I am dying of grief because I can no longer find Him!

One of them answered me:

— Soon you shall possess Him.

— Thank you! — I said to her — but that is still not enough for me.

— What more do you want?

— Oh! — I sighed deeply, and fell silent.

— Ah! we understand you well; but for that there is still a long time: the fields need to be cultivated — they said to me, pointing out to me a field of which more than half was untilled.

My voice was a balm to me; I kept questioning her, asking whether my work was according to the will of my God; and (I asked) whether they knew of anything that did not please my Lord.

— All is well — they answered me —; He is pleased with it.

— But I — I added — am very much afraid, because I am so wretched and of such little understanding; I am always afraid of spoiling things.

— No! — they both answered me — God is not pleased with your excessive timidity, which so many times is the cause of not a few of your sufferings.

My God! — I said within myself — they are right! See, the moon sends forth a thread of light and I can make out their garments; they were white, spotless. I tried to draw near them, but it was not possible.

Oh, what a surprise! They were the two good souls who once had promised to accompany me. I stopped to kneel and thank them; but they would not have it, and said to me:

— In this forest where we are walking, only the grace of the Lord can save you from terrible misfortunes. We shall accompany you as far as the door of a church, and then your faithful dog will stay with you until you have entered the temple. He too is the one who at other times was sent for your defense.

I stood listening as if in ecstasy; I felt great consolation from it. I stretched out my hand and stroked this poor faithful creature.

— My God! Why do you tell me nothing of my Lord? Ah! at least promise me to tell Him that I thank Him, but that I am dying of love: it is too long since I have seen Him! Oh! I walk so far amid torments of every kind, and Him I never find!

They gathered round me and, pointing out the church to me, vanished.

In a church, the Lord repays her sufferings with great consolations

I threw myself to the ground on the steps to pray, but the dog does not allow me, and drags me by my dress into a corner behind a column that stood as an ornament at the door together with other smaller ones: he signals to me to hide, and so does he. After a little while, behold, men’s footsteps and voices saying: We’ll get her! Oh, what terror! I stayed there huddled and trembling; the poor animal, having seen them pass, caressed me as if he wished to say to me: Do not be afraid! But the trembling was very strong. Here come still others: I thought I would faint from terror. At last I hear a loud rattling of keys and someone comes to open the church.

At once I wanted to go in, but the grumbling keeper stops me:

— Who are you? and what do you want? At this hour no one may enter. Weeping, I begged him, for the love of God, to let me in.

— No! why did you make such a knocking? I thought it was a sick person who needed us: instead it is you and the dog!

— Have pity, do not shut me out!

Having said this, he was moved to pity; and the dog vanished. The good sacristan, fearing he had shut the little animal outside, said to me:

— He has gone away, or else he is waiting for you outside.

I, who had seen him disappear, said to him:

— No, he has gone.

He closes the door securely and then leaves me in that vast temple, where the only light was the little lamp burning at the high altar. I broke into a flood of tears; I threw myself to the ground at the foot of the altar and begged my God to give me strength to withstand such terror. It seemed to me that all the skeletons had come out of the tombs: as soon as I raised my head, behold, a dead man’s skull!

At last that good sacristan returned, and I was very much afraid, because in the dark he was watching me in silence, and I saw him only after I had heard a muffled tread. I felt exhausted; at last he took his little lamp and came near me:

— Poor creature! are you tired?

— Oh! — I answered — will it still be long before I may receive my God?

— No! — he answered me — I feel sorry for you: the first Father who comes down will give you Communion. But may I know who you are?

With a great sigh I answered him:

— I am a poor slave of my Lord!

But the good keeper wanted to know how I came to be in those parts, and at night; in short, he did nothing but ask me now one thing, now another. Seeing that I did not answer him, I moved him to compassion:

— Are you a hermit who lives in some cave?

— No! — I answered him — Have pity on me and let me receive my God soon!

He looks at me with compassion and leaves me. And I prayed my God to come into me soon, because I felt exhausted. He will nourish me and be able to restore me, for I feel myself fainting.

That good shepherd came and gave me my Good. Oh! as soon as I had Him within me, oh my sweet Love! I told Him all that I had suffered. And I told Him that I felt great consolation, because I had suffered so much. My feet were all torn and gave me sharp pains… But with my Good I no longer felt anything. And I told Him of all the fears I had had, and that the two good souls whom He had sent me had greatly consoled me; I spoke to Him also of the faithful dog…

While I was so breathlessly telling my story, my Savior stretches out His hand upon my head as if to caress me, and smiles at me. I remained in ecstasy, so much so that all the services in the church came to an end, and the Father who had given me my Good came and tapped me on the shoulder, saying to me:

— What are you doing?

Roused, I looked at him. He began to say:

— Come with me, and I will give you something to refresh you.

— Thank you! — I answered him — I have need of nothing. May God reward you for the charity you wish to show me. Then he said to me:

— But we must close the church: you must withdraw.

I looked at him and said to him in a pleading way:

— Would you do me the charity of letting me stay a little longer?

— Very well, but after my dinner I intend that you go away — so he said to me.

— Very well, I will do so.

«See to it that the seed you sow is good».

Meanwhile it seemed that they had gone away, but I kept hearing movement now here, now there. My God! I began to say: what must I do? Must I again find myself in the midst of such wicked people? My voice:

— Go out, for good people are waiting for you; for several days they have been looking for you, because they need workers.

I kiss the ground and rise to go out. The door was closed, but the keeper was not long in coming. He opened it for me and I thanked him, and he, so good, asked of me the promise to commend him to the most holy Virgin. I promised him to do so, being greatly obliged to him.

After a few steps, behold, two good men stop me and ask me for workers for a large field, which they wished to entrust entirely to my companions. They take me to see the field, and it was very vast, but untilled. I was so surprised to see very lovely valleys and immense fields, all for us. Within myself I thought: but what of the dark night in which I find myself? My voice:

— This is the fruit of your great sufferings. See to it that the seed you sow is good: so beautiful and lovely will the harvest be.

Those good people accompanied me as far as my old cottage, leaving me with (the request) to return soon to those lovely fields.

The thought of the good seed gave me great anxiety and, placing myself at the feet of my dear Crucified One, I asked Him to tell me what seed I was to send there, for I did not trust my own choice. Oh! how soon I had the answer: This (seed) shall be the workers, and you shall not leave them until you have seen that the fields are in good order.

I was not slow to carry out what I had understood. But hard and painful was the toil. The fields were untilled. My God! what was I to do? The more I toiled, the less I could ever manage to see the field clean. At last I threw myself to the ground and, weeping, asked the eternal Father to tell me what was there that brought so much harm: what could it be? A shepherd who was not after the heart of God! I was not slow to offer fervent prayers that he might be removed. My God! The workers, instead of being all fervent and intent on giving glory to their Lord by working well in His vineyard and rooting out the couch grass, what were they doing? Through their bad cultivation it came about that this weed was doubled.

Oh, what mercy of my God! He sent me three good workers; two of them truly full of love and zeal for the work of the Lord, who found the means of removing him.

Oh! how many blessings from the height of heaven will He not have poured in great abundance upon their heads! Oh! how my Lord protects them for me, upholding them in all their steps, so that they themselves do not even notice it; but I so many times see clearly what my God works in them! And woe if they knew it! But I, who hold them dear and close to me, guard them as beloved workers of my Good. Oh my sweet Teacher! You who pour Your treasures into such little hearts, without those who possess them knowing it! And now He has placed this worthy and holy shepherd, who makes the workers run so well, and they render that task which the Master requires.

A prophetic dream: a high mountain to be leveled only by suffering. Truly exhausted, I fell asleep sitting on the ground, my head resting on a stone. I found myself immersed in the sweetest colloquies, and it seemed to me that I had my Lord with me who, taking me by the hand, showed me delightful works of creation: a most vast field, whose end one could not manage to see. He said to me:

— Look! this Work of Mine shall be without end. He made me turn round, and on the right there was a great and high mountain:

— This must be leveled entirely! there is no remedy, because it was built by barbarous people, and I let them do it, because these great stones you must remove, all of them, yourself. There will be some of them that will make you sweat blood: this will serve so that it may not grow up again, but the field will become beautiful and many lilies will spring up in it. My Father will be greatly pleased with it.

I listened to Him with a love that filled me with bliss. At last we reached the depths of a cave, which was as dark as could be:

— Do you see this darkness? Well then, you must give it light. The inhabitants all live in the dark.

— Oh! my Teacher! do not leave me here, for pity’s sake! — and I trembled at it.

— Not now, but alas you will enter it and will have to give light to those who live in darkness.

What I was feeling was such that I hardly even gave a thought to what was to happen to me. At last a great brightness opens: there were great things there that I can no longer describe, and He says to me:

— Only charity and humility enter this dwelling. And He vanished. I awoke and looked all around me: where am I, my Love? But was I awake or asleep? Ah! what a simpleton! Of course: a dream produced by weariness! I fell asleep with the desire to have my Good, and I dreamed of Him. But the mountain? And I went over again all that I had dreamed.

And I fell asleep again. Behold once more my Savior and Teacher and my Beloved!

— It is time to go where you believe you have dreamed. But it is not a dream, but rather reality! Take care to suffer with relish and resignation. This is My will!

I roused myself and, prostrate on the ground, thanked my Lord for it.

— Here I am, ready at Your bidding!

At once I set myself to work, and the dream unfolded to the letter. Only that, when I found myself at the place where that mountain stood, I did not know how I could succeed in bringing it down. I looked all around, and yet I asked the workers to suggest something to me; they all looked at one another in astonishment and begged me to give up the thought.

What is to be done? — I kept repeating within myself — How can I abandon this mountain, which my Savior told me must be brought down and at last turned into a field? I felt myself crushed. What did I do? I asked to be given a large pickaxe and, with all the strength I had, I set to work. No one came to help me.

Faith governed me, and I was sure I would succeed in removing that mountain and making it as my Teacher had told me. The workers, intimidated and fearing that I would order them to help me, asked me to go and work elsewhere, because they felt that that work would bring them to the ground and they would not withstand it. I looked at them and — patience! So exclaiming, I gave them leave to go where the earth was prepared for sowing.

Seeing myself alone working on that mountain, the more I labored to bring it down, the more I saw that I had done nothing. What pain I felt at it! Thus disheartened, my mind was already troubled by the thought that it had been an illusion and that there was some diabolical art in it. I stopped to think: My God! how am I to carry away all this material?

Tired, exhausted, I rested and laid my head upon a stone. I fell asleep amid sobs. Behold once more my Savior who, taking me by the hand, made me climb to the top of this mountain, and in the midst of its veins blood was flowing. It frightened me, and I asked Him what this was: — It is your blood! and only with this will this mountain become a beautiful and delightful plain. Many people will come to drink the water that will gush forth from a spring. Many zealous workers will come to help you. But first, you must form all those streams you have seen.

And He goes away! Awakened: where am I? where is my Good? Yes, it was He, because I feel that He has left His grace in me. What mystery is this? Foolish that I am: it is not that this mountain must be brought down by toil, but now I understand well: by suffering! My God, those streams of blood, how am I to shed them? 93.

«This mountain of sufferings and sorrows will one day be changed into a delightful garden»

I was all pensive. Meanwhile night was drawing on and I felt frightened. Where was I to go? I had nothing but a stone on which to rest my exhausted head.

Behold, from afar I see my faithful one (the dog) coming, holding in his mouth a little basket in which there was a lovely loaf; he gave it to me and went away; I called him with such insistence, but nothing. I saw him no more. I knelt down to eat that bread and wept over it.

Meanwhile I hear footsteps. What trembling seized me! I did not dare raise my eyes to look, fearing from one moment to the next to see men before me. But I hear that, as he drew near, (someone) calls me by the name of Servant of my Lord. Oh! what a surprise! I turned round, and it was an old man asking me for a little bread.

— Yes! my good man: here it is! And I gave it to him; I had eaten little of it. He looked at me and said to me:

— Why are you giving me all of it?

— Yes — I answered him —; I no longer need it.

Why do you not want it? Eat it yourself: I assure you that I take far more pleasure in it than if I had to eat it myself.

I gave a sigh: Ah! He looks at me and says to me:

— Why such affliction?

In a resolute manner (I say to him):

— I have nothing to say to you. Go, good man, for night is falling and you will no longer see the path. I felt so oppressed! I desired nothing but that he should go away, so that I might give vent to my tears. But he sits down. My God! who is this man?

I say to him again:

— Go, for it is much better that you make your way to your farmstead.

He does not answer me.

— Ah! I beg you, in the name of my Lord, leave me! He does not move. What fear! He began to say:

— Do not be afraid, for I have been sent expressly to remain here this night. This mountain, for you a mountain of most bitter sufferings and sorrows, will one day be changed into a delightful garden; its flowers will have a fragrance so sweet and delightful that every wayfarer will stop to look at them and will desire some for his own country. Meanwhile, I pray you, eat a little more bread.

I took a small piece, and then I gazed at him, for I felt a certain something! I fell silent, and meanwhile my mind was thinking: who can he be? He, seeing me thus, resumes:

— What do you fear? Your anguish is most pleasing to your Master.

— Yes? then you know Him and know Him well? Speak to me of Him: tell me whether He loves me. Ah! tell me many things about Him, tell me where He is! Will you see Him again? Ah! speak to Him of me and tell Him that I suffer greatly, but my greatest suffering is because I am always afraid of displeasing Him, and so that He may have abandoned me!

No longer able to hold back my tears, I wept bitterly; such violent sobs seized me that the bones of my chest seemed to break. He tried to persuade me: nothing! What pain I felt! The old man, having risen, in a rather severe tone ordered me to stop, telling me not to doubt that my Love loved me greatly and that He was always close beside me. I fell silent. Meanwhile the sky grows dark; he says to me:

— Here is your faithful one.

And he vanished. Oh! crying aloud (I said):

— Who can he have been? Faithful, where have you come from? And he wagged his tail and greeted me joyfully. He took me by the hem of my dress and led me into a little grove where, from the way the trees were interwoven, one would have said there was a farmstead. And he signaled to me to sit down. I knelt and prayed; this animal bent his two paws, as if he too were in an attitude of prayer, and looked at me. When the night was far advanced, he circled round me many times and made signs for me to get up. I was so exhausted that I could not stand. He led me near some fine trees. I sat down and, resting my head against a tree, fell asleep.

In a dream I saw all that I was to go through on this mountain: it was as if someone had given me an account of everything that was to come.

Many terrible figures. In short, it was a spectacle of the most terrible kind. There was also that shepherd who, with his terrible snares, would make me undergo horrible and most cruel torments.

I awoke screaming and weeping. There was a brightness from the beautiful moon: it seemed like day, so much so that, at first, I believed it was. My faithful one was no longer there. Now and then the screech of a large bird could be heard. And I went on weeping and calling loudly on the Savior: Ah! do not abandon me! I am lost! I feel myself growing faint, here alone!… Most holy Virgin! My Love, my beloved Master! come! I am lost!

A great eagle, with its immense wings, comes before me, beating its long feathers, and with that ugly beak wide open it was about to come near. It was so happy to be able to reach me, and I no longer had any strength, nor was I even capable any longer of receiving a frightening impression. I looked at it, and already it seemed to me that I was being devoured; I only managed to say:

— My God, have pity on Your slave!

The eagle stops, looks at me, lowers its wings and keeps looking at me; and I kept my gaze fixed upon it to see every movement it made. It settles on the ground near me:

— Oh! poor creature! fierce as you are, you have become my friend.

I began to stroke it. It strutted proudly at this, for it gave sign of it by ruffling its feathers.

— Oh! if only I could give you something! I have nothing: only tears…

Here is another noise. I look all around: they were two horrible griffins. They struck a horrible terror into me; screaming, I called upon my God. What does the eagle do? It opens its wings and covers me. But these were not beasts, but devils; and the wings of the dear creature were not enough. Furiously they drove it away and, seizing me by one hand, gave me such lashes that I was on the point of fainting; when all of a sudden they took to flight. And I let myself fall — where? into the arms of my angel who, holding me up, roused me and made me smell a little phial; and I came back to life.

— Oh! why did you not come before such ferocious devils beat me?

I wanted to tell him all that I had gone through. He looked at me and I, sitting near the tree, said to him:

— Ah! do not go away! lead me to some cottage; do not leave me here alone any more! ah! I shall die if you leave me!

— Shortly the shepherd is to arrive, who has many things to say to you.

— Oh no! What shepherd is to come? — I say to him.

He looks at me, and then, with compassion, says to me:

— The usual one!

I screamed:

— No! no! I feel myself fainting!

He comes close to me:

— You will not faint, because the strength of the Lord will sustain you. I leave you this cordial: you will make use of it when you feel yourself failing.

And he vanished.

Under the contempt and the harsh treatment of the «usual» shepherd.

A strong agitation seized me. And behold, the shepherd arrives. Full of fury, he throws down his hat and sits down. With two eyes that frightened me, he gives me his first greeting with a severe dressing-down, telling me that I was a donkey and not capable of anything; that he pitied certain workers who were in a field.

I tried to keep silent, but he grew ever more savage and frightened me. I prayed my God to send some good worker. I asked him where he came from, and he tells me brusquely that he comes from a field where the workers have not directed their work well, because I gave them a guide who is not capable. I look at him:

— What am I to do about it? — I say to him.

He flies into a rage and begins to ill-treat me and hurls some insults at me. I took fright and stayed silent. Then he came out with praise of one worker, lauding her greatly to me. I remained silent all the while.

— Oh! you do not like this! It is quite clear that only your little affected ones are pleasing to you!

Oh! how ill I felt! but I did not think it right to answer; he was too much in a fury. So, little by little, he went digging up new ones. At last his aforementioned worker arrives, and they exchange many courtesies, when he turns to me and, with a certain sneer, says to me:

— This one is innocent: she has the right to be defended and did not deserve to suffer such humiliation!

I look at them and say firmly that their way of acting is in no way edifying to me; and that if I do not suit them, they know what to do.

Oh! then indeed (they became) two volcanoes, with an eruption of words of every kind. I fell silent and, moving off, went away.

After a few days they left and ended up in a field where the guide of the workers paid no heed at all to what they were doing. It was a chaos of continual intrigues. How could that field hold out with such creatures? But for urgent business of his own he had to go away; and what did I do? I called the worker in order to drive her out of her nest; and it was a delightful thing: she believed it was the shepherd calling her and, instead, found herself face to face with two workers, stern and holy, who enjoined her to stop making a fuss and to set herself sensibly to work, and to think no more of the past, but to begin a true way, which will be the only one that will lead her to our God for an eternity.

No! she weaves every kind of quibble against us, and the shepherd, when he came to know of it, my God! broke loose against me, and I had to go through every kind of thing. There were moments when my blood stopped and I had no life left in me; fear and trembling were my faithful companions; I felt a strange movement in my nerves: they all stretched like so many little cords.

There was something that was (happening) in the fields at that time, because he, when one arrived who came from afar and was the overseer of the field, once she had had a report of it, laid everything upon the poor worker, and then grew agitated because, with his magical fancy, he went where the possible does not reach [?]. How was I to save myself? He goes away and I remain alone, because all the others also returned to their cottages. I was strongly tempted to go along with them, because, as night was falling on this mountain, nothing was being accomplished; but I feared to transgress what my God had commanded me. I was sure that this mountain will be leveled and will become a delightful garden.

Hard is the road of my exile, which divides me from my Good!

Everyone abandoned me. And I, having calmly set myself to pray, made a little bundle of wood to serve me as a pillow and, so as not to sleep on the ground, I took other pieces of trees and made of them a large cross, on which I lay down to sleep, tired and exhausted, at a late hour and in the dark. I heard a great uproar from afar: alas! what can it be? Get up — and do what?

My voice:

— Hide!

And where? A most vivid light lets me see a very thick thornbush and, without further thought, I throw myself into it and stayed huddled there. Fear and trembling did not let me feel those very sharp thorns; I wept and prayed. Behold, certain individuals draw near; there were women and men, and they were saying:

— She is not to be found; one can see that she was on that cross but, since it is night, her witches must have warned her to get down, and so she has left this mountain.

And they had stopped right near me, who was inside the thornbush.

— Tomorrow, if she comes back, we will kill her.

The women were more enraged than the men. On hearing this talk, such terror seized me that I thrashed about in those thorns. One of them said:

— She will certainly come to look for her cross: let us leave everything, sure that we will catch her.

At last they went away, and I no longer had the strength to get up and go away: blood was flowing from every part, and in that painful state I fainted. I gave a cry, calling on my God to help me. After a long time, having recovered from the stupor, I found myself — where? Lying on my cross! A light was shining, and I looked at my hands: they were pierced, but the blood had stopped; my whole body was one single pain. My God! tomorrow those people will arrive and they will kill me.

My voice:

— No! it will not be granted to them to find the road any more. Here is what is Mine, being destined for My beloved ones.

How will it go? — I said within myself — My God! how ill I feel! Give me Your strength, that I may toil and bring this ground into order according to Your most holy will.

And I fall asleep. Three loud knocks in the air awaken me. Having risen, I set out on my way: and where to? — I said within myself — Hard is the road of this earth, which forms my exile and divides me from my Good: the earth is untilled, the mountain rugged! I was ever terrified by the thought that the angry shepherd might arrive. It was a mass of gigantic thoughts that kept my mind preoccupied: always alone, from one hill to another unknown people lying in wait for me…

While I was walking, a thought seized me, so fierce, that I had abandoned the cross without trying to take it apart before going away, so that those brigands might not trample on it. I wanted to go back and set it right, and I turned round to go there. My voice, loudly:

— Stop! what you did not think to do, your angel has done. Walk on!

And more than ever I quickened my pace, with a strong inner agitation that took away even my breath. A beautiful discourse on the experience of «consummating union».

At last I see a temple in the distance. Oh! my Love! shorten this road, that I may soon come to You! A sweet flight, and I find myself at the door of the church. Who was there? A holy shepherd, who comforted me and told me not to be afraid, that he would be my defense in everything. I did not know how to answer; I was very much afraid. Can it be true? He, an angel of the Church, willing to stoop to defend me? My God! this is a mystery to me.

When I was admitted to holy Communion, I asked my God how I was to conduct myself.

Behold, my faithful soul said to me:

— He will be your defense, and in him and through him you will have great things. My fields will yield better fruits, and in many of these I shall take delight. His heart is free of every stain and upright: trust him. And the fields of the Lord will yield fruits and flowers that will give forth a fragrance of paradise.
