He told me other very beautiful things. I was in ecstasy; the sweetness I felt cannot be described.

— Many things will still have to be set right — He added; and vanished.

Having come to myself, I went on for a long while thanking my God.

My voice:

— It is time for work!

At once I went to cultivate the ground assigned to me. While I was working, my mind went deep into a rather beautiful discourse. I was happy and did not notice that I was working, but it was as if another person had been with me and together we were reasoning about the love of my Lord, about what one experiences and the degrees of this exquisite and incomprehensible sweetness. Pausing on the innermost consummating part, I desired to know to what point the creature can possess this infinite treasure; and I had very eloquent explanations. 94. At last it seemed to me that I was reaching the point where I desired better explanations, when behold, a crush arises among the workers, running up close to me.

I had to devote myself entirely to them, and to tell the truth I could understand them very little, and I only tried, with tact and good manners, to calm them and relieve them, quieting them with gentleness. I was not troubled by anything, always most happy to do in everything the most holy will of my God.

Apparition, in a dream, of the Immaculate Virgin, 14 November 1892.

In a most agitated dream — for I found myself amid hardships, my breast was panting with fear and I was wrapped in terror, thinking what way to take to come out of so painful a state — a monster was tormenting me and trying to make me turn from my road. When I saw myself lost, all the nerves of my body were shaking, and I seemed to be like a leafy branch in the wind. Alas! then I am lost!

On top of this there was added the apparition of the great Sovereign of heaven and earth, the great Mother of God, Mary Immaculate. Oh! how and why do I say that it was added to such anguish? Because she was wrapped in a thick veil: it was not given to me to see her face.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — why so veiled?

A deep voice, but clear enough, said to me:

— The monster is near you: so I must remain.

And she fell silent.

— Ah! merciful Virgin, Mother of sinners! take off your veil, or else I feel myself dying!

An uproar made by the monster, and she vanished. My God! I am lost! I went ever further into the darkness and felt a true torment at it. The dragon won, and did so much that he very nearly devoured me.

Ever in my mind was that beautiful and white Immaculate One.

— Virgin Mary, Mother of my God! release me from so cruel a state! If my Savior has bound me and tied me tightly to this chain, oh! I am ready to remain in it; but if it is a diabolical art, help me, for pity’s sake!

And I kept thinking of the veil. Oh! this clearly indicates to me that this is a horrid hovel [?].

Awakened from so terrible a sleep, I set myself to pray. I sought help from Saint Francis, my Father of Assisi, and truly I had light and clarification of my dream. But how am I to unfold my distress fully and at length? Where was my mind to take refuge so as to calm itself? I had recourse to the Passion of my Savior, and peace returned to my greatly troubled soul.

The monster withdrew from my eyes. And I began to walk along my usual path; it was very stony, but the pains I felt were a relief to me compared with the great hardships I had suffered.

Mystical, experiential effusion, with an importunate shepherd.

I found a shepherd who, having come near, asked me where I was going. With a deep sigh I told him that I did not know.

— How can it be as you say? — he replied to me — Look well at what you are doing, because whoever walks without a guide is sure to walk badly. Oh! — I said within myself — this was all that was needed to reopen my wound! I took courage and said to him:

— No! the one who guides me cannot err.

— So then — he resumed — you have a guide?

— Yes! — I answered.

And he insisted that I tell him about it.

— I do not know why I should tell you my affairs, when my Master does not permit me to. If you think you can lead me astray, you are mistaken. I beg you to leave this subject and to speak only of the greatness of God and of His omnipotence and mercy: these three subjects alone give me great satisfaction, both in hearing them spoken of and in pausing to reason on them by myself, because in them is found an immense greatness where the soul feeds and delights in its center, which is God, being a portion of Him. 95.

Oh! the mind reasons, and in such immensity has room to run without ever finding a stumbling-block to halt its reasoning; the intellect unfolds to the greatest knowledge of the soul with its God, that boundless ocean of greatness, of power and of mercy. The further the mind advances into Him, the greater it sees the space to be, and ever new themes unfold, and the majesty of a God is discerned in ever clearer proportions; and how the soul is ever from Him and in Him subject to Him. If I may so express myself, it is a most sorrowful groan when the soul itself feels and experiences its separation from Him, because of the darkness in which it sees itself wrapped in the mire of sin.

Ah! do unfold this delightful reasoning. I am certain that, with your theory, you will find such eloquent terms for it that I shall listen with the greatest pleasure to so delightful a reasoning.

He looked at me:

— I am not here to preach sermons or to develop themes; I only wish to know how you were able to enter into the cultivation of so beautiful a field, and who brought you to it.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — your question is very curious after I have told you that I occupy myself with nothing else than knowing the will of God in order to strive to fulfill it.

He flies into a rage and rebukes me harshly. And I, with all the greatest respect, go away, laughing within myself. I did not dare turn round for fear he might catch up with me.

Another shepherd who can speak only of justice.

I entered a field where many workers were attending to certain tasks so as to finish them and then recollect themselves in order to give the soul other nourishment.

I thought of joining them and tried to follow as best I could what they had laid down to make this time less delightful, indeed penitential.

We came upon a shepherd, so rude, who knew how to speak of nothing but justice. And he explained to us how rigorously we would be punished in everything; he always showed us our Teacher and Master as severe, an inexorable judge; and (he said that) whoever called down His mercy upon human miseries would never obtain it, but we would have provoked His justice. Oh! what terror! Can it be? He admitted everything as illusion. In short, he depicted my Lord to me only as a most severe judge.

My Love! I indeed know that I deserve all the indignation of Your justice, but Your mercy!… Have pity, my God!

Having approached him, with all humility I asked him to reconcile me with my God by means of Penance. Oh! how he treated me! But I was not troubled in the least: I know that I deserve everything. What was I to do? He would have wanted me to tell him — what? He remained so irritated that, in the middle of the field, where all the workers were gathered, he vented his feelings at length.

What did I gain from it? The grace of peace and of resignation to the dear and holy will of God. He had asked me nothing; so what was I to tell him? Oh! how my Teacher takes delight thus in His slave.

I met that shepherd again, and with such fury he accused me of an immensity of things, all wrongly done, calling my conscience to witness these deeds. All of a sudden I became sad and was left dismayed. Having withdrawn alone, at the foot of the cross, I wept, because I knew myself guilty of nothing.

At last, after a long time, my God dispelled the cloud, and I was left so sweetly relieved that I remember little or nothing of what the shepherd said to me. 96.

The holy shepherd chosen by God for His Work.

Many years before, it had been announced to me that I would have the good fortune to meet a holy shepherd, that he would be the only one to set the fields of my Master in good order, and would secure them so that in the future no one could give the workers any other direction; which for this poor slave would be a great relief, bringing peace and a work less labored, without the fear of succumbing beneath it.

As though awakened from a most sweet sleep, I found before me the shepherd who had been announced to me. From his manner and from what my voice told me, it was he. The fear of erring kept me perplexed; my voice, with affirmative words, assured me that it was he.

Many times, thrown to the ground, clinging to the cross, I asked to be better assured. My voice:

— You will see it by the facts.

And then I felt an assurance placed within me. And my voice:

— It is he!

I paid no more heed to my fear, but informed him of everything, resolving to hide nothing from him. I submitted all the workers to him, and I found perfectly that he had the true spirit of my Teacher: upright, for inexorable justice; charity equal for all (yet I never told him what I went through within me, no, only little things); jealous of the fields, vigilant over order, delicate to a scruple. Oh! I was not mistaken. While I was praying fervently, my Lord showed me how dear he was to Him and that He had chosen him for His Work, and that he would do very much good, that his every action would be done for the benefit of the fields. God was greatly pleased with him.

How tranquil I feel in this! As though I were leaning against a great poplar, I rest in everything; in the struggles against certain shepherds I am not afraid. Tranquilly I dream my dreams. Oh! how can I thank my God for it! 97.

XIII

«Be calm! your sorrow is Mine»

Thinking thus, I fell asleep. Two great dragons, with their noisy coming, woke me. Horrible terror! One was of a size…; its two horns joined together, with their two points, formed something like pincers; this huge one was furiously trying to hurl itself upon me as if it wanted to drive those horns into my face, but at a short distance it stopped and turned aside, going to plunge elsewhere. The other, smaller one stopped and, as if it did not care about me and had the mission of giving me pain, kept circling in front of me; but after a few turns it vanished. I fell asleep again, and in a dream I had sufficient explanation of what those two dragons wanted to do to me; but my Master, my God, permitted them nothing; and they, disheartened, went back.

A great shepherd was trying to obstruct my road, calling to his aid other shepherds, so as to be able to enter the fields entrusted to me by my Lord. The plot was well woven and they had already set to work to enter, when my Master, with an invincible strength, drove them out and put them to flight.

I was sitting on a stone, worn out by the struggle I had sustained, and a very lovely child comes near me. At the mere sight of Him I was enchanted and gazed at Him as if in ecstasy. He, standing still, said nothing to me for a long while. He calls me by name, comes near and says to me: — Be calm! Your sorrow is Mine. Take, eat this bread, and rise to go to work.

He vanished. Oh! my Love! You were close beside me; but how? I had no power to act, nor to speak, nor to throw myself to the ground and pray to Him: nothing! It was He! — I kept saying within myself — He was close to me! One by one I repeated His words. I threw myself face down on the ground and kissed that soil where He had set His most holy feet, and I gathered up the earth as best I could, to keep it. The bread that He had placed near me so that I might eat it no longer came to my mind, although, repeating His words to myself, I was saying also: «Take, eat this bread»; and so I eagerly gathered up the earth.

My voice:

— Leave this work: this is not what you were commanded. Eat the bread!

I left everything and, having risen, saw the bread; I pressed it to my breast and did not have the courage to eat it. Many times I kissed it and kissed it again, always repeating: My God! I am not worthy of it. But, fearing not to fulfill His most holy will, I knelt down and ate it, moistening it with tears from so much compunction and veneration, while it seemed to me that I was unworthy of all this.

She wishes to offer herself as a victim for the triumph of the Church.

When I had finished eating, I felt the strength of a giant. Having set out on the way to go to work, I met certain people who were suspicious to me; I did not know whether to turn back or to continue on my way. My voice:

— Forward!

— My God! who are these people?

My voice:

— Do not be afraid! These are a specimen of those devils who have overrun the earth. All their struggle is against My beloved Bride, the Church. From now on you will see, you will know of their plots and how they have taken possession of so many souls.

I asked Him to let me see this horrible war; He answered me:

— You will see a great portion of it, but certain abominations — these, no!

— I would like to know whether, by offering myself as a victim (always with Your permission), I could obtain the triumph of the Church.

— No! — He answered me — this is not what I want from you. 98.

Reasoning thus and running, I found myself on an immense road, shaded by great oaks; nothing could be heard but a murmuring of great eagles; I saw several of them: they frightened me; at each of these sights I gave a loud scream.

One could see neither the end of this road nor any houses: only immense meadows on both sides of the road. Meanwhile I went on walking in the hope of managing to see some farmhouse: nothing!

True sweetness can be had only in God.

Night was drawing on. My God, what agitation! by how many fears I felt oppressed! When I hear a murmur; and I could just make out that it was the chatter of women. Here they are, all making merry, coming up to me and inviting me to go along with them. I did not answer at once. I asked them where they came from and who they were. They answered me that they desired nothing but the good of creatures and that they helped many of them.

— Come — they kept repeating to me — and you will be happy.

— Tell me: in what does your happiness consist?

They stop:

— Why do you ask us this?

— You speak to me of the happiness of this world, where all is weeping and sorrow?

— What kind of talk is this? We are happy, and in our revels we feel great pleasure.

— And has the world many delights to give you? — I continued.

— Perhaps you are an anchoress and do not know these delights; but if you come with us we will let you taste them.

I looked at them very carefully, and then I began to weep:

— Oh! unhappy creatures! Your deceitful delights last but a short time, and then?… Oh! true sweetness can be had only in God!

They laugh at this talk of mine. But I, having dried my tears, began to describe to them the sweetness of the religious life: how God prepares for those who serve and love Him an eternity of good. Noticing that they were no longer laughing and were listening to me attentively, what eagerness I felt within me! I would have wished to make them understand everything in a single word.

Night was drawing on, but they begged me to remain in that field so as to continue my account. So it was. The whole night was spent speaking always of God and of His Bride the Church. I was able to learn that these were eight young women who, having fled from their fathers’ houses, wanted to go and throw themselves into the darkest whirlwind of the filthy world. In the end, enamored of the delights of the Creator, they promised me to leave everything and come with me, to cling to the dear Crucified One and to give heart and affections to Him alone.

They said to me:

— We have never heard of such things. Mamma and Papa spoke to us of nothing but the world and of what was beautiful in it.

— Oh! poor creatures! how unhappy you have been! Unhappy parents, what a terrible account they will have to render to God for it!

Having made them quite secure and given them into the care of a good overseer, I went where my voice directed me». 99. A most noble lady, benefactress of the Work of God.

Amid the most terrible anguish on a journey I had undertaken, I was warned by a holy creature that, at the very point where I had to pass, there were evil-minded people who had planned to do me harm. But it was the will of God that I should pass that way. Fear and anxiety overwhelmed me. Having reached the place, (the fear) vanished from my mind and at last, having regained heart, after a very long stretch I found myself at the place where God had sent me. Two days after I had been living in that cottage, a gracious matron came. On meeting her, at once I felt a certain something within me. Who can she be?

My voice: — A most noble lady who will do much good for My brides.

— Oh my Love! she is married 100 and young: how can that be?

I received nothing more. Several times I happened to see her, and I felt for her a certain confidence; and I told her many things about the Work of the Lord. I left that delightful cottage and remained a long time without seeing her again; but in thought I always seemed to have her near.

I had to return to that field, and we found ourselves more closely bound than the first time; and I told her much about how I came to be in this field, that it was all the work of my Master and had been created by His Vicar on earth, and that I was only its poor slave and good for nothing; that He alone worked, and that so great was my incapacity and ignorance that many times I undid what He had done. And I tried to make her understand well how ignorant I was. But the lady did not take offense at my condition, but quite on the contrary took delight in the work and in the beautiful labor, by which God was making delightful gardens spring up. Every day this matron grew in affection for the Work, and I saw clearly the work that the divine Majesty was doing in that heart, upright, simple and very great in loving.

She desired to have children, and I prayed much that the Holy Mother would obtain them for her. Once I was misled by this answer that I heard: — She will have more than one!

Oh! I rejoiced at it; but when I had the explanation, that they were not natural but spiritual (those daughters), there arose in me a certain mixed feeling for her soul: I rejoiced at it, but at the thought that she would suffer materially from it I felt sorrow. And then I kept thinking: how can it be that she will remain at the head of a field when she is so well accompanied? How many prayers and struggles did I not have to sustain!

Meanwhile one could see that her heart was inclining wholly toward the Work of the Lord, and that the labor of the mystical Gardener was gaining ground, and that that heart could no longer have anything more pleasing to satisfy it.

She works and, like one of the most zealous laborers, devotes herself entirely to the fields. Very intelligent, endowed with a very lofty mind and sound judgment, as soon as she was able to enter thoroughly into a matter, there she is, promptly forming an exact judgment of it, and she is very firm in the resolutions she has taken. But how can I describe the nobility of her heart? She was endowed with so gentle a feeling that she had the greatest charity for all. She preferred to undergo every privation and even renounced certain persons dear to her, provided she knew she was doing a favor and satisfying in whatever way the pleasure of others, sacrificing herself. And this came to her so easily, in appearance, that one would have believed her indifferent, whereas I can assure you that it was quite otherwise. At last she sets her hand to another, more beautiful work: she is preparing a large building in which to place certain creatures who are to learn to cultivate the fields well and meanwhile, in their solitude, will praise God and will strive to serve Him as well as possible. What will she have from God for this? The graces of the Lord have no end. Oh! blessed are you who have responded so well to the voice of the Lord!

Her thoughts, her longings are all for the Work of God; she rejoices in thinking of her beautiful and lovely field, where with such eagerness she desires to see the plants grow soon. But the dragon, powerful enemy of so proud and beautiful a plantation, rages, stirs up disputes about it and weaves snares so that it may not come about. Horror! how fiercely he clutches on every side!

But the mighty hand of God (will not fail); I see clearly from this cottage that his efforts are stones thrown into the water. Oh! beautiful work of omnipotence, so that that beautiful field may be purified and have strong foundations! Let the enemy make its soil firm, let him fertilize it with his fiery persecutions!» 101.

«Your suffering is enough to put a check on everything»

What a terrible storm! While I thought to rest for a moment in a cottage, behold, there arises a storm so fierce, a multitude of thunderclaps and lightning flashes terrified me. Furiously one of these devastates a wall. Where was I to take refuge? The agitation becomes terrible. I see clearly that a malignant dragon is whispering in the ear of that shepherd in whom I had placed my hopes, and a real combat takes place within him. How are these terrible disasters to be averted?

Certain caves open wide before me, into which it is given me to penetrate. Dreadful spectacle! what did they contain? With both hands I covered my face and wept bitterly with sorrow. A lovely worker, already dwelling among the chosen souls of heaven, came to comfort me, but it was of no avail. The tumults increased, and ever more terrible became the entanglements of that game of Satan, who took great delight in it. He went furiously now here, now there; he seduced the laborers, assuring them of his proud future; and the shepherd, his mind bound, wrapped in a black cloud, acted — how? His way of acting was so painful to me that, I must say, my breast tightened and my nerves writhed. Why this? It was the sight of the harm that would come of it to the great field of the Lord.

Having thrown myself to the ground and made a long prayer, after no short time I felt an assurance that in nothing would that dragon win, and that the foot of the most holy Virgin would crush him. But still I felt horribly tormented by it. Run? and where? and how to get out of this labyrinth? There is no escape; it is necessary to suffer and be resigned.

— No! — my voice — here in My field no one will be able to touch a hair of your head. Your suffering is enough to put a check on everything.

— My God! is this painful road of mine acceptable to You?

— Very much so! — my voice.

I felt myself revive and, as if He had taken a great weight from me, I regained strength and with courage set out for work. Along the way, other sufferings came upon me; but on arriving at the cottage I found the workers much aged, because it was many years since I had seen them. At once I felt sadness at it, but after some time I grew used to it, and indeed I tried to relieve them in their little vexations, for they cannot be called sufferings.

Meanwhile the news sent to me about the cottage I had left was so bad that it gave me terrible pain, and I felt it acting so fiercely on my nerves; and above all my head suffered from it. Oh! when will it be that You put this diabolical monster in irons? He is making such a din in that field!… Surely, my Lord, You will have pity on me and on Your workers.

What was heard was so horrible that, seized with terror, I screamed at the top of my voice. I called to my help the souls in purgatory and my two helpers, whom I always found ready; but on this occasion everything was closed; nothing appeared to free me from so fierce a combat. Wherever I turned my gaze there were horrible phantoms, whose only aim was to oppress me. Horrible turmoil! The worker, as though victorious, remained sure of her case; but, dissembling, she played her part very well; she felt secure in her powerful support. But nothing is secure for one who believes herself strongly defended by man. Oh! how fitting in this case, O my Lord, are Your words: Cursed is the man who trusts in man (Jer 17:5); his security will melt like ice in the sun.

These monsters tried to make me feel the most dreadful sufferings; when from afar I see a lovely dove advancing in slow flight; but seeing it fly so slowly, it seemed that, instead of drawing nearer, it stopped every now and then. What can it be? does it stop in the air? Surely it is waiting for something.

Breathless and tired from watching, I almost lost hope that it would come to me any more. Can it be that the contrary winds are carrying it elsewhere? I thought of a thousand possibilities. Then the thought came upon me: What can this dove have to bring me? Has it been until now an illusion of mine? The dove takes flight and comes straight to me, stopping at my feet. I did not delay an instant in taking it up in my hands; it did not want to lower its wings, but shook them as if it wished to say to me: Look! I lifted the feathers, and in shining words there was written: My field, victorious and radiant, will suffer nothing of what they wish to do to it.

Oh! dear little creature, so lovely! and I held it tight. What now? I looked again under its wings to see whether there was still more writing: nothing! It struggled in my hands, because I held it tight for fear it would escape me. And so it happened: in a flash it rose swiftly, took flight and I saw it no more.

I sat down on a rock and thought about the words I had read under those wings. Very consoling to me, my God, are these words; but only You, my most mighty Lord, can take from me the fright, the anxiety, the pain I feel within.

— How so? — my voice resumes — everything is in My power: in due time it will be taken away.

Thus tired, I fell asleep leaning against the trunk of a tree, which served me as a pillow. I slept deeply. A voice from afar woke me, calling me by name, so that I might go to the aid of people who were sure of their case, namely that, because of the beatings I had received, I would no longer be able to move. But, once awake, I found myself full of vigor. My voice:

— Run to the people who wish to lay snares for My fields; and do not stop again until you have an order from Me.

Full of vigor I rose and, running, arrived at the field. When I set to work, the field took on vigor, and so all heard that I was coming near them. They were frightened and tried to come to their senses. The workers worked the ground with alacrity. God showed me, by means of a worker, how beautiful the great field of His Work had become. My voice:

— It is not the time to stop, but rather you must run along this narrow path to arrive where your Teacher awaits you.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — I will stop no more, and always, day and night, I will try to walk so as to arrive at seeing my Beloved!

— Your eagerness is most pleasing; but this is not how I want it. Take care! for you must remain a long while on this path.

Alas! I stopped. Then is there no middle way? […] 102.

Tired in mind and in continual anxiety, I fell asleep. On waking, I found myself in a lovely field, but through the inertia of the keeper much tares were springing up in it. A good shepherd was advising the workers to come in search of me. On seeing me, without having called me, oh! how they blessed God!

At once, having recovered from the journey, I set myself to root out that weed which was gnawing at the good wheat; and so I gave heart to the poor workers. My God! the heart of creatures is a real heap of inclinations: now it clings to one, then it lets itself go to another affection; it bends to everything it feels to be pleasing to it. Oh! what a vexation! this accumulation of attachments makes the mind heavy, and it can no longer think of anything but earthly things…

Meanwhile I try to restore order as far as possible and to rouse them from their torpor. It consoles me that, by means of a most beautiful light, I was assured that the field is very pleasing to my Master. And for this reason I strive as much as possible not to err by setting foot outside the path. These poor workers are very worn out by their labor; gaunt and emaciated are their faces. At once I inquired about their maintenance. Certainly, I did not find it very good; but it is not so with the keeper, who has her food apart. Oh! how I feel compassion for them! I would have wished to find promptly the means to remedy (this evil). Meanwhile I try to relieve them in every way.

Among these there is one who is very devout and prays much. When I think that my Lord is greatly (pleased), I would very willingly (have stayed). But now I hear my voice commanding me to leave this cottage and go elsewhere. So, without further ado, I am preparing for departure.

At last today that good worker, who so intelligently consoled me greatly with her dear expressions of confidence in my Lord, and placed all her work in Him, sure that its outcome would be splendid — oh! how, without her noticing it, my God is working her very well! Her pliable judgment and her following of the inspirations of God: how the creature is seen to walk upright, with a sure foot, in the delightful way of the Lord. While I was thus, thinking of the dear and gracious worker, how many things crowded into my mind in beautiful ideas; but I did not notice that, leaning on the palm of my hand, I was resting there very well.

No! I felt an agitation invading me and bringing me little by little into the most desolating anguish. I tried to shake myself, but to no avail. I would have wished that it had become light, while I was in the darkness of midnight. Alas! — I exclaimed — how shall I be able to bear so fiercely so many hours more, so alone and tossed by this terrible agitation! I invoked all my holy protectors; I begged the most holy Virgin to come to my aid: nothing!

I abandoned myself to sorrow and, clasped to the cross that I held, I redoubled my sobs, but without uttering a word. So alone, my God, I am! It is true, my treasure — looking at the cross — for me you are always my companion! While I was saying this, it seemed to me that a voice came out of it which wished to tell me something comforting; but I could not understand; I held it pressed to my breast. My voice: — Only from the cross does one learn to love!

My God! Yes, my Love! I feel that you are in it, my Lord!

Having said this, I gained strength and, rising with vigor, I went to work.

A presumptuous «warden», severely struck by a Matron.

I found that ground very hard. There were moments when I would have left everything and gone elsewhere, so much did I doubt that I could manage to bring that soil to receive the good seed. When I believed I had succeeded in breaking that hard and stony ground, behold, the devil clings to the warden and goes whispering in her ear certain fears and, still more, makes her believe that she is the one looked upon with disfavor, because she has not known how to do well.

But I saw clearly that she added much to it, because she would have wished to be praised and confirmed in her ideas, and would have wished to be made a sharer in everything, whereas this was not possible. What happened? The enemy made use of this state of irritation of hers to fill her mind with a bundle of thoughts, which upset her, took away her peace and made her irascible in a singular way. I noticed it at once, but I had great trouble in being able to calm her.

I prostrated myself to pray. What was my surprise! At first I understood nothing of what was to happen to me; I understood that it must be some terrible event, but I dared neither to ask nor to rouse myself from prayer, because an inner fear greatly invaded me. I held myself back from making the smallest movement; when I see before me a great personage. Who can it be? Horrible spectacle! My voice: — He would like to torment my fields; he will achieve nothing, and see what his end will be.

My God! a horrible scourge struck him to the ground. My God! have pity on him!

At the same time, that seductress, who was making every effort to obtain from the shepherd what she wanted, and was seeking every means to overturn that heart which had done so much good to the fields of the Lord, was trying to sow tares on every side. My voice: — Pray for her. Oh! how many graces she would have had if she had corresponded to the impulses and calls she had!

But now: oh, what terror! A Matron rose from her throne and struck her hard. Poor victim! Crying out loudly, I asked her why she was doing so, that she should have thought of her. With a strong voice she answers me that everything was prepared.

But with a threat, this I understood, she will tell me. I was left so shaken that I trembled: what can it be?

This unhappy woman went on doing worse; her intrigues were something…

One could see that she was helped by an evil spirit that guided her horribly. There was something great in her maneuvers. She answered everything tremendously, she succeeded in the work; to whoever was given to see it, it cannot be denied that it was a spectacle, an action always different one from the other; and if from anyone some hindrance came to her cunning, she became a viper: such was the turmoil that arose in her; and she was not slow to put out the venom.

But that Matron, who struck her so severely, gave assurance that she would see to putting an end to all her subterfuges. There was truly in her an abyss of ever new deceits, which she tried to carry out, and she persuaded herself that she was most sure of her case and of the good result. Oh! how every passion has blindness as its beginning, never letting us see the end of what we passionately feel!

«While humanity suffered, the spirit rejoiced».

Reasoning thus along the way, I met an excellent shepherd whom at another time, long ago, I had the good fortune to meet; and there was a time when very often he approached on my way and spoke very well of God, and I listened with pleasure to his reasonings. At some moments I deluded myself that I could have some direction from him. Alas! I had not yet formed the desire when my Lord removed him in such a way that I could not reach him. And once, when I hoped I had arrived at my aim, by a strong and rude action, which I clearly saw to have been the work of my Crucified One, I had to persuade myself never again to desire and seek, not even from such worthy shepherds, the least relief. My voice:

— Is it not enough for you, what I always repeatedly tell you is my will?

— It is painful, my God! but I feel resigned and happy to do your most holy will.

Thus, weary, I was repeating to myself, when a poor old man approaches me and tells me that he had always worked since childhood, because he was needy, and he went on working, though he was bent; but he felt very happy, because he had always done everything according to the will of God. Hearing him reason thus, I remained recollected in myself; he looked at me and I did the same. We stayed thus in silence a good while, and then I burst into a flood of tears. He said to me: — Learn not to complain any more if you have worked and are working, because this does not please God.

Continuing to weep, I asked him who he was, and that, if I had committed this, he should pray God to forgive me, for I would never again return to making such complaints. The poor old man, moved by my weeping and still more by my sorrow, threw his mantle over my head. I remained rapt in God, and he disappeared.

Having come to myself, I looked all around to see if I could see a human creature: nothing! But, so inebriated with love, I ran through those fields, so that I felt no weariness, nor did the body have need of anything. And on the way I was making, one by one I repeated to myself the beautiful and great things I had seen and heard. Oh! — every now and then I exclaimed — oh! majesty of a God! my Lord, sweet Teacher!

I did not notice that night was falling and that my feet were bleeding, because that road was so stony and certain thorns entered my feet from every side and my legs too. Having become aware of this through the pain that made itself felt, I was happy about it; on seeing that I was leaving traces of blood I rejoiced; and I began to reason about my God when, as a little one, He was returning from Egypt and the most holy Virgin noticed that His most holy feet were shedding blood. Oh! how my Redeemer must have suffered! So vividly these pains of His came to my mind, and He Himself so beautiful and gracious, running!…103..

Without noticing it, I went on into a field that was all bushes and big thorns, but nothing distracted me from my reasoning and from the vividness of my thought. And while humanity suffered, the spirit rejoiced in it exceedingly.

Comforted and instructed by the Master Himself, the supreme Good.

My angel said to me:

— Stop! go back: look where you are! Horrible sight! I look and, from the fright I received from such ugly people who were carousing, I gave a loud cry and held tight to the sword of my angel. I look around me and, alas, nothing but crags can be seen. He took me by the hand, and in a flash I found myself on a soft park — I say soft because of thick grass, barely ten centimeters high: it seemed that I was walking on velvet.

My angel cast a glance at my feet, which were bleeding, and with this grass I was healed. And he left me, while I hoped he would have many things to tell me; and still more I desired to hear something about my God: nothing! So mortified, I sat down on that grass and, weeping bitterly, I said:

— Why leave me thus? at least one word… So I must have done wrong in going on into that thicket of thorns: that carelessness of mine, certainly, not pleasing my Teacher, it will not be granted me to see Him any more. Oh! my Crucified One! ah! speak to me, if you do not want to see me die of sorrow! It is a horrible pain: speak to me!

And I cried out at the top of my voice. The sorrow became so strong that I fainted, abandoned on the ground: I felt nothing more, nor was I capable of understanding. A hand shakes me, saying to me:

— My beloved, look at me, for I am always with you!

Oh surprise! My Good! my Master! I knelt down and He gave me a sweet liquor to drink.

— Rise! I have many things to tell you. Who could describe what I experienced?

He gave me a long lesson: how I was to cultivate certain new fields that I would have, and the way in which I was to conduct myself with the shepherds who were in those fields, and what would happen to me. When I heard that so much suffering was being prepared for me, I interrupted Him:

— My God! will you always be with me?

He gave me a smile, and then:

— I am always with you!

A strong trembling seized me when I heard of terrible sufferings and entanglements of things. And He, pressing my hand, said to me:

— Do not fear! you have my strength, and only with this can you bear this.

He signed me on the forehead and disappeared.

On my knees where He had set His most divine feet, with joy I plucked that grass; much of it I tried to eat, because the long fast made itself felt, and the rest I kept for myself. Oh! how many kisses I gave it! I no longer understood that I was of this world, because my ears always kept that sweet sound of the voice of my Savior. My mind repeated to me all that I had heard. It was a joy! Oh! here, here let me stay for ever! Only on these herbs will I feed. Here, my God, leave me! I no longer want to move away from here! My voice, in an imperious tone: — Go where God has commanded you! His will must be your pleasure.

Alas! with my treasure of that grass I rose and, all mortified for having been so insistent, running with all the strength given me, I prayed God to forgive me: — Yes, my Lord! your poor slave asks your forgiveness; but with pleasure she will carry out your orders: but your Love!!!

And so, walking and sobbing, I ran for two days and nights; on the third day, numb with cold, I could no longer stand on my feet. I found good people and they invited me to warm myself near a large hearth; but my hunger was such that I seemed to have become a feather. Having thanked these good people, I went to feed on my God. And so great was the longing to have Him in my breast that I no longer cared about hunger. But, having had Him with me, I was satisfied and full of vigor, with a warmth so that I was burning.

The unfaithfulness of some workers compensated by the adherence of the others.

I resumed my way and with the strength of a giant I arrived at the large farmstead and, setting myself to work, I raised up the workers; in a few hours great life could be seen in all of them; one more than the other tried to make that ground well prepared to sow good wheat in it.

There was one who, with her chatter, seemed to want to do everything, and she was the laziest. She came around me wanting to persuade me that she was the whole of that field and that everything that was still there was she alone who had worked it and taken care of it.

My voice:

— All lies! take care, because not even her little garden is in order, and if she does not change and her little garden continues to give such infected fruits, certainly everything will dry up. She? — And then it said: — Woe!

Alas! but what was to be done? I looked at her fixedly, but she did not lose courage; rather, she grew bolder in throwing out her great boasts. Meanwhile the poor workers gave me compassionate glances, as if they wanted to say: She is deceiving you! But she, with two fierce eyes, was attentively watching them closely so that none of them should come near me. She could not help seeing the fine work I had ordered; but, with a cynicism all her own, she was actually pleased with it; and she repeated:

— This shake-up was needed to take the laziness out of these stupid workers.

My voice:

— Silence! in due time you will speak of it.

From one field I passed to another. At last, my voice:

— Go at once to the large farmstead, 104, because the Shepherd is ruining a worker there, trying to delude himself by persuading himself that his aim is holy. And she, so cunning, knows very well how to play the part. Meanwhile the others are left admiring, and already a great whispering is heard […]. 105.

Oh poor soul! how, fascinated by so many unworthy actions of hers, she came to be exceedingly defiled! And yet… This reasoning occupied me entirely.

I met good people, and yet they joined me to speak to me of this affair, to which they gave great importance: with many sighs and with warmth they expressed their pain, sympathizing with me, and they would have wished to unite themselves with me to relieve me.

Among these good people I saw my great worker. She, with the deepest sorrow, throws herself on my neck and almost weeps. Beautiful and generous soul! perfect and upright is your heart, and proud. I tried to raise her up, assuring her that God would come to our aid. She calmed down; but she was always sighing, and every now and then she thought of so horrible a deed and could not swallow it.

Meanwhile we thought about the great work that was prepared for her and which my Lord wanted to be done entirely by her, it being the first and very important for its quality, being a large farmstead that must hold many workers.

While we were reasoning thus, I cast a glance at the sufferings that would come to me, and already I felt their blows as if they were in reality being given to me. But then I added: Victory will come. 106.

The Virgin Mary: «Do not fear, God is with you… Victory will always be yours».

The dear worker goes away and I hear a murmuring of people who were reasoning in their own way. Who were they? Certain workers who had nothing good except (appearances). Their caprice made them act. I tried to make them reason and I thought I had persuaded them when I withdrew from them; but, having returned on that road, I met them — alas! — worse than before. They became furious and no reasoning availed; the others who arrived joined them. And truly I did not know where I could find words to bring them to reason. At last, with a very loud voice I ordered them to go back and stop that behavior of theirs. But they continued until they saw me enter the farmstead, and then they withdrew.

How the devil managed so well to possess one of them is not to be believed. He has so bound and fascinated her mind that there is no doubt [?] that she can free herself; she herself has consented to this bond, and only the most powerful hand of my Lord will be able to free her. It is very difficult: there are no reasons that avail to make her come back to herself.

My Lord, my Master! ah! do not permit that through such fierce obstinacy she be lost! She is a soul created and redeemed by you!

Meanwhile, seized by a fierce headache, I struggled at His feet and asked Him for mercy. In a flash my mind became clear, as if it were reflected in a great or, to put it better, immense hall, illuminated only by a splendor, and I found myself inside it: all that I saw was clear and beautiful as light itself; nothing else could be heard but a sweet zephyr, which also gave this most beautiful light an indefinable sweetness.

Where am I? where are you, my God? Why do you make me sigh so much? Ah! speak to me and teach me to root out of that mind and that heart that fascination. Tell me, for pity’s sake, that you are with me!

Nothing could be heard; all was silence! But yet this light and what I feel…: my Lord must be here. So breathlessly I called Him: nothing! At last I see a very beautiful cloud approaching: the closer it came, the larger it grew. All of a sudden it opens, and behold the most holy Virgin with joined hands, who says to me:

— Do not fear: God is with you! 107 and all this is because you must take strength, having much to fight. Do not fear: victory will always be yours!

And she disappeared. While so sweet a Mother was speaking to me, I felt that I had all strength in my power. But, left alone, oh! what a thought remained in my mind! The sweetness of having seen her, her words, everything was for me something delightful. Every now and then I repeated to myself: what will this combat be that requires so much strength? and where, most holy Virgin, shall I have to face it?

I was already in the dark: nothing could be seen; I did not even understand where I was to put my foot so as not to fall. Whatever am I doing in this darkness? If these people come, what shall I say? No! I set myself to pray and, having finished, rising full of vigor, I set out toward a field that needed to be set in order again, without thinking at all of what was to happen to me; my thought was turned only to the great Mother of God and to her beauty; as if she continued to be with me, I reasoned with her and asked her for clarifications about my doubts, which arose for me in various circumstances. I heard and saw no one, yet I heard answers to me so fitting that I hurried on with the questions: I desired answers to so many. I set myself to ask her how the scene of the worker with that shepherd would end; she answered me: — The Shepherd will come to his senses, but the worker is terribly tempted. Oh! what an ugly entanglement I saw! and so darkly she made me feel that he was deceived, while he believes one thing and the worker aims at another. And this shepherd did her no good at all, rather much harm to her soul; and he too has drawn much disadvantage for his own soul from it, giving real admiration, and believing that they were holy things. Meanwhile, see!

I remained so absorbed in such a spectacle that I could find no peace for the sorrow of seeing these two souls, especially the shepherd, go backwards so. I heard nothing more.

«You still have too much to work, my beloved!»

Overcome by weariness, I began to complain and said: But how long this road is! I am tired, I am cold and hungry, nothing is to be found here, the eye cannot reach to see either a haystack or a tree: all dry rocks! Certainly night will come and, if this road is still always like this, I shall die of sorrow. So there is no longer any hope for me of getting out of here; everything that lies before me is frightful.

And I walked. The road and all that lay before me became ever worse. The sun sets, hunger makes itself strongly felt, already my strength fails me: a strong panic seizes me that I must succumb in the midst of that great and stony ground. I look here and there to see if I can find a blade of grass, because I would gladly have eaten it, but nothing! My throat dry, my palate parched, and not even a brook could be seen to have a sip of water. I feel myself fainting and I kneel with joined hands. I called my Teacher, my Master, and, crying out, I told Him that I was dying:

— Ah! come, help me: I am lost!

And I fainted. A gentle voice says to me:

— Rise!

— Oh my Love! I am dying, you know?

He, with a smile:

— No! you have too much to work, my beloved! Do not fear: my strength has need of nothing. Run: before night you will find help.

And He leaves me. Must I go away from here? Oh no! My Good is here. And I kept looking fixedly at that place where I saw and heard Him. But my voice:

— Hasten to obey!

I seemed a giant in strength; I do not know whether I flew or really walked. At dusk I see in the distance a bell tower and I hear its clanging. Oh my Love! it is your dwelling: a temple! tomorrow I shall feed on you. Oh! what a strong embrace I shall give you in this heart of yours! 108. A thousand sweet and loving words I repeated, and I flew at full speed.

Having arrived at the door of the temple, the custodian was closing its doors. I begged and implored him to let me enter: to no avail. He said a thousand insults to me: that I was a vagabond, a wicked woman…, and a thousand other outlandish words. I answered nothing, and I huddled on a step. This grumbler, on seeing me thus, grew angrier still and wanted to kick me so that I would go away.

— Ah! for pity’s sake, let me stay here until tomorrow comes.

— No! away! — he said, shouting.

An important lady welcomes her into

her palace, and then she becomes an apostle of the fields of the Lord.

A good old woman stops and comes near me:

— Come with me; it is not fitting that you stop here. Meanwhile that man went on grumbling and calling me a vagabond: it was the least of the titles. This poor woman looked at me, and then said to the grumbler:

— Why do you abuse her so badly? Do you know that she is such as you believe?

— Certainly! — he answered.

And the woman, in a resentful tone:

— I tell you that you are mistaken. Correct your words. I am astonished and I shall tell my mistress, who will certainly take this woman’s part.

And a pretty squabble followed. I kept silent; she went on saying:

— You must know that my mistress was informed by a person that this creature was to arrive in the village and that she was to be given lodging and refreshment.

Within myself I felt a shiver, thinking of the words of my Lord: that I would find help. I looked at the woman, who took me by the hand, looked me over well and said:

— It is she: the description is exact.

She wanted to give me her arm, telling me that she saw me so suffering that she feared I might be unwell. I thanked her. A few steps on, she entered a magnificent palace; the gracious lady came to meet me and said very loudly to the woman that she wanted me to be refreshed at once. And she begged me to be willing to tell her where I came from, how it was that she saw me so suffering; and she would have liked to know how I came to be in such a state.

I was anxious to know who had told this lady that I was in such a state and had put so much charity in her heart; but I did not dare. She, however, did not stop putting questions to me; I tried not to reveal anything and answered her little. But she was not satisfied. She began to say in a more serious tone:

— But who are you?

I answered her:

— I am a poor slave of the Lord; through obedience to Him I am here. And with joined hands I turned to her, asking her who had told her that I was in such need. She looked at me, and then added:

— A noble gentleman, on a graceful horse, passed before me while I was in my garden, and told me to send my maidservant to the door of the church, that there was a creature there who had great need of being helped, and that for all I would do for her God would reward me abundantly. And I had to carry it all out, because such an impulse remained in me that I had to fulfill what he told me. So I feel that I love you, and I feel an affection for you that I know I have never experienced for any creature. I am alone, I live retired in this castle and I try to love and serve God.

Having said this, I gave a great sigh:

— Oh! blessed soul! May God reward you for what you are doing for this poor slave.

She looked at me and then added:

— I see you so unwell that I beg you to go and take some rest; but tomorrow I want to hear from you.

And she handed me over to the maidservant, who took me to rest. But, the room being closed, I threw myself on the ground and, weeping, thanked my Master for it. Overcome by weariness and sleep, I fell asleep on the floor, so badly that my head remained resting against a piece of wood. Oh surprise! having woken after two hours — so a clock that was there showed — under my head I had a pillow so soft that my head lay very well on it. But who ever put it there for me? I went to see: the door was closed, everything was well secured; I kept saying to myself: who put it there for me? And from the thinking I was doing, a fear came over me that someone might be hidden. Already I felt a strong heartbeat. My voice:

— Be calm! It is your angel, who was ordered by me to do so.

Oh! how I settled down on the floor and, with the soft pillow under my head, I had another sleep, which one would call contemplation rather than sleep. My voice reasoned with me and taught me many things; likewise it told me how it had come about that I found that lady so full of charity, who showed herself so affable to me. My Lord had put in her heart so great an affection toward His slave that she would no longer be able to live without loving me, and that she would give me much help to take wherever the need made itself felt. (My voice) woke me: — Rise and pray: the rest you have taken is enough!

Having risen at once, I set myself to pray. No more than two hours had passed when I heard a knock at the door. I asked who it was and what was wanted; the maidservant answered me, telling me that the lady wanted me with her. I set off through such beautiful rooms, all elegantly furnished, and finally I arrived in her room. She was lying in bed; I thought the hour to go to church was near, when she makes me come near her bed and asks my pardon because it was not yet three o’clock and she had had me woken. The maidservant answers that I had not yet gone to sleep; but with tact and persuasive words I tried to assure the lady that I had already slept enough, and I begged her to be at peace on my account and to tell me what she desired. She sent the woman away and, putting her arms around my neck, said to me:

— Ah! do not abandon me! I greatly desire to love God, but there is something that prevents me.

I gave her courage and, at last, she revealed her secret to me and, set on the right way, she assured me that she would do everything I had told her. She burst into a flood of tears and said:

— You have saved me!

She came with me to church and, at last, she made her holy Communion after a well-made confession. Oh! how much I prayed that she might make up her mind! How much goodness, my Lord, you have!

We returned to her house, where she gave me a large sum for the poor workers of the Lord. She wanted me to remain another day with her, to know how I had become a slave; and she longed for me to speak to her of my Master, and in what way I served Him, where these creatures were working… I told her everything they did in the vineyard of the Lord, and that many more would be needed to sow His word everywhere, that the field of His Bride the Church was very great and that it had need of many workers.

She took delight in it and did not want to leave me for a moment; but on the following day my voice said to me: It is time to go away: you will return many other times. I took my leave; but the poor dear shed tears over it. I promised her to return; and not long after she called me together with other workers and entrusted to us a magnificent field. She became an apostle of the fields of the Lord. How powerful God is in His works!

When she was working thus with vigor, a big shepherd came and interrupted her work, and she stopped. Oh! how I wept over it! But he enjoined her to undertake another way of life by making her living comfortable, a thing to which human nature is at once ready to consent for its own comforts, and so to give itself to the softness of life, which lasted her but a short time. He tried everything to remove me from that heart and it was not possible for him: what God has done, man cannot destroy. So it came about, and she continued to give much to the poor workers.
